blocks.title: Independent study material

blocks.text: Exam AI-200, Developing AI Cloud Solutions on Azure, is for back-end developers who build the services around an AI application. You don't train models here. You host, feed, connect, secure and observe what runs around them: containers that serve a model-backed API, databases that hold documents and embeddings, queues and events that move work between components, and the secrets, configuration and telemetry that keep everything running. The audience profile asks for Azure and third-party SDKs, data services, messaging and eventing, vector databases, monitoring and troubleshooting, containers, and Python. That's why every code sample in this pack is Python.
blocks.title: What the exam measures

blocks.text:
• A score of 700 or more passes. It's a scaled score, so it doesn't have to equal 70% of the points.
• Associate exams without labs give you 100 minutes, and 120 minutes of seat time. Most Microsoft exams have 40 to 60 questions, but the number varies. Microsoft doesn't publish the question types for an exam, so try the exam sandbox to see the interface.
• On associate and expert exams you can open Microsoft Learn in a split screen during the exam, but the clock keeps running while you search, so don't rely on it. The exam technique lesson covers this and the other rules.
• Most questions cover generally available features. A preview feature can appear if it's commonly used. This pack says "preview" wherever one comes up.
• The study guide points to a Microsoft practice assessment for this exam (sign-in required). This pack doesn't use it.

blocks.text:
• Skill lessons: one for each of the 27 study-guide skills, in study-guide order. Each explains what the service does and how it works, then gives Python and CLI samples, a worked example, the exam traps and a self-check. Try the self-check before you read its solution.
• Labs: six worked builds that join several skills into one small solution: KEDA scaling in Container Apps, vector search in Cosmos DB, retrieval-augmented generation with pgvector, dead-letter handling in Service Bus, a Flex Consumption function app, and secrets with telemetry. Read a lab after the skill lessons it draws on.
• Cross-cutting lessons: Commonly confused pairs, Exam technique and Final revision. They come last because they assume you have met the services.
• Flashcards: short facts for spaced review, tagged by skill.
• Practice: learning sessions by skill or domain, with an explanation after every answer.
• Short mock: 20 questions in 40 minutes, weighted like the exam and never taken from a paper you haven't sat. Use it as a timed check between study blocks. It never counts towards readiness.
• Papers A to E: five fixed mock papers of 50 questions each, with a 100-minute deadline. Each holds exactly one case study of five questions and mixes single and multiple choice, matching (including Yes/No statements), dropdown, ordering and numeric questions. A paper scores out of 50 points and shows a pass at 35 or more.
blocks.title: What is in the pack

blocks.text:
The papers are reserved for mocks. No learning session or short mock serves a question from a paper you haven't taken, so each paper stays unseen until you sit it. After you sit a paper, its questions, including the ones you missed, can come back in practice.

Readiness counts the papers only. The pack recommends booking the exam when your latest three completed papers meet all of these:
• each was completed within the last 90 days;
• each scored more than 80% fully correct, where only answers that are entirely right count (partial credit earns points but not this percentage);
• each used only questions you hadn't seen before.

The rule always looks at your latest three papers, with no cherry-picking: a newer paper that falls short, or one that expires before you finish, breaks the streak. A paper you have sat is no longer fresh, so a retake can't count, and as your newest paper it breaks the streak too. With five papers, that leaves room for at most two weak papers, and only if they come before three strong ones in a row. So don't spend papers early: sit the first one only once you have worked through every domain.

The 35-point pass line approximates the exam's 700 and is separate from readiness. Readiness is a practice signal, not a prediction of your exam result.

If you used release 1.0.0 in the same database, progress on lessons that kept their IDs and your mastery carry over, revised lessons are marked as revised, and readiness starts again in 1.1.0. Questions you saw in 1.0.0 count as seen, while all five papers are new.
blocks.title: Papers and readiness

blocks.text: Spend about an hour a day. Sit each paper in one go, like the exam: 100 minutes, no notes. If a week runs over, shorten the review rather than skipping a domain.

lessons.title: 1.1 · Azure Container Registry: images, tags, locks and clean-up
lessons.summary: Store and version images in a registry, choose a SKU, tag for building and for deploying, lock what you release, keep storage under control and work with the registry from Python.

blocks.text:
A registry stores container images and other OCI artifacts. Images that share a name form a repository. Each image has a manifest, which lists its layers and is identified by a SHA-256 digest. A tag is a readable alias that points at one manifest, and one manifest can carry several tags or none.

The three SKUs, Basic, Standard and Premium, expose the same programmatic capabilities and data-plane APIs, and every SKU gets zone redundancy in regions that support it. They differ in included storage (10, 100 and 500 GiB), throughput and limits (webhooks, for example, are capped at 2, 10 and 500). Standard and Premium add anonymous pull access and artifact cache rules. Only Premium offers geo-replication, private endpoints through Private Link, connected registries, dedicated agent pools for tasks and the retention policy for untagged manifests. A SKU change causes no downtime. Moving down from Premium switches the Premium features off, and some resources, such as geo-replications and connected registries, must be deleted first.
blocks.title: What a registry holds

blocks.text:
Two tagging styles serve two purposes:
• Stable tags (python:3.12, app:1) are reused on purpose. Publishers move them to a newer digest whenever they patch the image, so they suit the base images you build from.
• Unique tags (a build ID or the digest itself) are never reused. A Git commit hash is only semi-stable, because a base-image rebuild runs from the same commit. Deploy from unique tags, so that a restart or a scale-out pulls exactly the build you tested.

Lock what you deploy. Setting write-enabled to false stops an image being overwritten or deleted, and delete-enabled false on its own blocks only deletion. You can lock by tag, by manifest digest (repo@sha256:...) or a whole repository. Tag and manifest attributes are separate: locking a tag doesn't lock its manifest.

Storage needs housekeeping. Untagging (az acr repository untag) removes only the tag. Deleting by tag or by digest removes the manifest and the layers no other image shares. When a stable tag moves, the old manifest stays behind untagged and still occupies storage. Two automated options exist, and both are preview: the acr purge command, usually run as a scheduled ACR task, and the Premium retention policy, which covers only manifests that become untagged after you turn it on.
blocks.title: Tags, locks and clean-up

blocks.text:
Clients authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID, so each person, pipeline or workload uses its own identity and a role scoped to the registry: AcrPull to pull, AcrPush to push and pull. The admin user is disabled by default; it is one account per registry with full access, meant for a single user and mainly for testing, so keep it off and use individual identities instead.

The azure-containerregistry package wraps the data plane. ContainerRegistryClient takes the endpoint (the login server with its https scheme), a credential and the Azure Resource Manager audience. Without a credential it works anonymously, which only succeeds on a registry that allows anonymous pull. The client lists repositories, tags and manifests, updates their attributes (the same locks as the CLI) and deletes manifests by digest.
blocks.title: Signing in and working from code

blocks.text:
# Digest and tags of every manifest in a repository
az acr manifest list-metadata --registry myregistry --name ranker-api -o table

# Lock the manifest that production runs (by digest, so the manifest itself is locked)
az acr repository update --name myregistry \
  --image "ranker-api@$PROD_DIGEST" --write-enabled false

# Remove a tag only; the manifest and its other tags stay
az acr repository untag --name myregistry --image ranker-api:canary

# Weekly clean-up task (acr purge is preview): old tags and untagged manifests
PURGE_CMD="acr purge --filter 'ranker-api:.*' --ago 30d --untagged"
az acr task create --registry myregistry --name weekly-purge \
  --cmd "$PURGE_CMD" --schedule "0 3 * * Sun" --context /dev/null
blocks.title: Azure CLI · inspect, lock by digest and schedule a purge

blocks.text:
import os

from azure.containerregistry import ArtifactManifestOrder, ContainerRegistryClient
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential

KEEP = 15
endpoint = os.environ["ACR_ENDPOINT"]   # the registry login server with its scheme
audience = os.environ["ACR_AUDIENCE"]   # the Azure Resource Manager audience

with ContainerRegistryClient(endpoint, DefaultAzureCredential(),
                             audience=audience) as client:
    newest_first = client.list_manifest_properties(
        "ranker-api", order_by=ArtifactManifestOrder.LAST_UPDATED_ON_DESCENDING)
    for position, manifest in enumerate(newest_first):
        if position < KEEP or not (manifest.can_delete and manifest.can_write):
            continue  # recent builds and manifests locked by digest stay
        client.delete_manifest("ranker-api", manifest.digest)
blocks.title: Python · prune_manifests.py (azure-containerregistry)

blocks.text:
A research group runs a workshop and wants attendees to pull a demo image, embed-demo, without Azure accounts. A docs page should list which demo versions exist.
• SKU: anonymous pull isn't available on Basic, so the registry needs Standard (Premium also works, but nothing here needs its extras).
• Turn on anonymous pull access (az acr update --anonymous-pull-enabled). It applies to every repository in the registry, so the group keeps private images in a separate registry.
• The docs page script creates ContainerRegistryClient with the endpoint only, no credential, and reads get_manifest_properties("embed-demo", "latest").tags to print every tag on that build.
• The group's own release pipeline still signs in with its Entra identity and AcrPush to publish new demo versions; anonymous access covers pulls only.
blocks.title: Worked example · a public demo image

blocks.text:
• A tag is an alias and a digest is the identity: two tags can name one manifest, and a moved tag names a different one.
• Untag, delete by tag and delete by digest are three different operations with different effects on storage.
• Locks set on a tag and locks set on a manifest are independent attributes.
• Zone redundancy keeps one region available; it does nothing for clients in another region.
• acr purge and the retention policy are preview features. Say so when you rely on them.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text:
Question: a release engineer locked ranker-api:2.4 with az acr repository update --image ranker-api:2.4 --write-enabled false. Next week prune_manifests.py deleted that build anyway. Why, and how should the lock have been set?

Solution: the CLI call set the tag's attributes. delete_manifest works on the manifest by digest, and the script reads the manifest's own can_delete and can_write, which the tag lock didn't change. Lock the build by digest (--image ranker-api@sha256:...) so that the manifest itself refuses deletion and the script skips it.

lessons.title: 1.1 · ACR Tasks: quick, triggered and multi-step builds
lessons.summary: Build and run images inside Azure with quick tasks, rebuild automatically on commits, base image updates and timers, and chain build, run and push steps in a multi-step task.

blocks.text:
ACR Tasks builds and runs containers inside Azure, for Linux (AMD64 by default, and ARM) and Windows, so a build agent needs no local Docker engine. Every task has a context, the source it builds from: a local folder, a Git repository (a branch, a subfolder or a commit), a remote tarball or an OCI artifact in a registry. Builds run in an isolated sandbox. You stay responsible for keeping secrets out of the context, and anything you pass on the command line can end up in diagnostic logs.

At the time of writing, the overview page notes that task runs are temporarily paused for subscriptions on Azure free credits.
blocks.title: What ACR Tasks is

blocks.text:
• Quick task: az acr build sends a context to the registry, builds the Dockerfile there and, by default, pushes the result to the same registry. Think docker build and docker push in the cloud.
• Triggered task: az acr task create defines a reusable task. On a Git context, the commit trigger is on by default and the pull request trigger is off. Source triggers need a personal access token so the task can install the repository webhook, and they don't work with GitHub Enterprise repositories. A timer trigger (--schedule, a cron expression) runs the task on a schedule, for example for maintenance.
• Multi-step task: a YAML file of build, cmd and push steps, so one task can build, run containers and then push. A cmd step can run detached and give the container an id that later steps use. Run variables such as {{.Run.ID}}, {{.Run.Registry}} and {{.Run.Date}} standardize tags.

Logs: a run you start by hand streams its log to the console. A run that a trigger started only stores its log, which you read in the portal or with az acr task logs.
blocks.title: How the three kinds of task work

blocks.text:
A task discovers the base image in the FROM line when it builds, so it must run at least once before it can react to that base image. The base image trigger is on by default for a new task (base-image-trigger-enabled True), and you can turn it off per task with az acr task update.
• It fires only when the stable tag it builds from gets a new digest. A brand-new version tag doesn't count.
• A base image in an Azure registry, in any region, triggers a run immediately. A public base image in Docker Hub or Microsoft Container Registry is checked at a random interval of 10 to 60 minutes.
• Only the final runtime image's base is tracked, not the base images of earlier build stages in a multi-stage Dockerfile. Learn recommends copying public base images into your own registry and building from that copy.
blocks.title: Base image updates

blocks.text:
# Quick task: build in Azure from the current folder, one unique tag per run
az acr build --registry myregistry --image ranker-api:{{.Run.ID}} .

# Triggered task from a subfolder of the release branch
az acr task create --registry myregistry --name ranker-release \
  --image "ranker-api:{{.Run.ID}}" \
  --context "$REPO_URL#release:services/ranker" --file Dockerfile \
  --git-access-token "$GIT_PAT"

# A frozen legacy image: keep its task, stop base image rebuilds
az acr task update --registry myregistry --name legacy-report \
  --base-image-trigger-enabled False

# Runs and their stored logs
az acr task list-runs --registry myregistry -o table
az acr task logs --registry myregistry --name ranker-release
blocks.title: Azure CLI · quick, triggered and scheduled tasks

blocks.text:
version: v1.1.0
steps:
  - build: -t {{.Run.Registry}}/ranker-api:{{.Run.ID}} -f Dockerfile .
  - build: -t {{.Run.Registry}}/ranker-migrate:{{.Run.ID}} -f Dockerfile.migrate .
  - push:
      - {{.Run.Registry}}/ranker-api:{{.Run.ID}}
      - {{.Run.Registry}}/ranker-migrate:{{.Run.ID}}
blocks.title: YAML · release-task.yaml (multi-step task)

blocks.text:
A platform team maintains py-base:1, a shared image with Python, certificates and logging set up, in the same registry as the services that build on it. Six services each have a triggered task whose Dockerfile starts FROM that image.
• When the team pushes a patched py-base:1, the tag stays the same but its digest changes, so the six service tasks rebuild their images from the one patched base, with no change to their own repositories.
• A seventh service, a report generator that must stay byte-for-byte unchanged for an audit, keeps its task for manual runs but has base-image-trigger-enabled set to False.
• Each run tags with {{.Run.ID}}, so deployments pick up a rebuild only when someone points them at the new tag.
blocks.title: Worked example · one platform base, many services

blocks.text:
• The pull request trigger is off by default, unlike the commit trigger.
• The --file path is relative to the source code root folder of the context.
• Logs of triggered runs aren't streamed anywhere; they're stored for later retrieval.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text:
Question: what does each part of the context <repository URL>#release:services/ranker tell a task?

Solution: the part before # is the repository. release is the branch, and services/ranker is the subfolder that becomes the build context, so paths in the Dockerfile and --file are relative to that folder. A commit hash can take the branch's place to build one fixed commit.

lessons.title: 1.2 · Containers on Azure App Service: settings and secrets
lessons.summary: Run a custom container on App Service, pull it from Azure Container Registry with a managed identity, and supply environment variables and Key Vault secrets through app settings.

blocks.text:
App Service pulls your image, starts the container and sends HTTP traffic to it. It assumes the container listens on port 80. If your server listens on another port, set the WEBSITES_PORT app setting to that port number. A container can expose only one port for HTTP requests.

Pulling from a private registry works two ways. You can store registry credentials on the app. The better way is a managed identity: give the app's identity the AcrPull role on the registry and set the acrUseManagedIdentityCreds site property to true. For a user-assigned identity, also set acrUserManagedIdentityID to its client ID. The registry must accept Azure Resource Manager audience tokens (az acr config authentication-as-arm). If it doesn't, pulls fail with an UNAUTHORIZED token validation error.

The first start pulls every layer. Later restarts reuse the cached layers and pull only what changed. On Linux, container console output needs container logging switched on (az webapp log config --docker-container-logging filesystem), and az webapp log tail then streams it.

Start-up on Linux: the platform pings a newly started container until it answers or until the start time limit runs out. That app setting (its name is in the CLI sample below) defaults to 230 seconds and accepts 10 to 1,800 seconds. A container that isn't ready in time fails the startup attempt, which the platform retries, and callers see 503 errors meanwhile. The ping path and the status codes that count as ready can be set with WEBSITE_WARMUP_PATH and WEBSITE_WARMUP_STATUSES.

Windows containers only: Docker host logs are on by default, the start limit defaults to 10 minutes, and an availability check mode setting decides what happens after three failed pings in a row (ReportOnly, the default, only logs it; Repair restarts the container; Off stops checking).

Multi-container apps built on Docker Compose retire on 31 March 2027. Sidecar containers replace them.
blocks.title: Running a custom container

blocks.text:
Every app setting is injected into the container process as an environment variable, so Python code just reads os.environ. The Env page of the app's Kudu (SCM) site shows what was injected. Registry credentials saved on the app are the exception: they are reserved variables that the application never sees. Any configuration change restarts the app.

Secrets belong in Key Vault. Instead of the value, the app setting holds a Key Vault reference in one of two forms:
• @Microsoft.KeyVault(...) wrapping SecretUri=<secret URI>, optionally with a version at the end of the URI
• @Microsoft.KeyVault(...) wrapping VaultName=<vault>; SecretName=<name>, with an optional SecretVersion The app resolves the reference with its system-assigned identity by default. To use a user-assigned identity instead, set keyVaultReferenceIdentity to its resource ID. That is also the way to go when a reference must resolve at creation time, before any system-assigned identity exists. With the Azure RBAC model, the identity needs the Key Vault Secrets User role.

Rotation and refresh: a reference without a version follows the latest version. App Service caches resolved values and refetches them every 24 hours. Any configuration change restarts the app and refetches at once, and an authenticated POST to the app's Key Vault references refresh endpoint (under config/configreferences in Resource Manager) forces resolution. Because each environment should have its own vault, mark settings that hold references as slot settings so they don't move during a swap.

When a reference can't be resolved, the app receives the literal @Microsoft.KeyVault(...) string. The portal shows the resolution status when you edit the setting, and a diagnostics detector for Key Vault application settings (under Diagnose and solve problems) explains failures.
blocks.title: Settings become environment variables

blocks.text:
# Start from a public image; switch to the private one once the identity can pull
az webapp create --resource-group rg-app --plan plan-linux --name ranker-web \
  --container-image-name "$PUBLIC_IMAGE"

principal=$(az webapp identity assign -g rg-app -n ranker-web \
  --query principalId -o tsv)
az role assignment create --assignee "$principal" --role AcrPull \
  --scope "$(az acr show -n myregistry --query id -o tsv)"
az webapp config set -g rg-app -n ranker-web \
  --generic-configurations '{"acrUseManagedIdentityCreds": true}'

# The identity reads secret values through Key Vault RBAC
az role assignment create --assignee "$principal" --role "Key Vault Secrets User" \
  --scope "$(az keyvault show -n kv-ranker --query id -o tsv)"

az webapp config appsettings set -g rg-app -n ranker-web --settings \
  WEBSITES_PORT=5000 RANKER_TOP_K=8 WEBSITES_CONTAINER_START_TIME_LIMIT=600 \
  "SEARCH_KEY=@Microsoft.KeyVault(VaultName=kv-ranker;SecretName=search-key)"

az webapp config container set -g rg-app -n ranker-web \
  --container-image-name myregistry.azurecr.io/ranker-api:b412
blocks.title: Azure CLI · managed identity pull, port and a Key Vault reference

blocks.text:
import os

TOP_K = int(os.environ.get("RANKER_TOP_K", "8"))
SEARCH_KEY = os.environ["SEARCH_KEY"]

# An unresolved reference arrives as its literal text. Fail fast at startup.
if SEARCH_KEY.startswith("@Microsoft.KeyVault("):
    raise RuntimeError("Key Vault reference not resolved: check identity and role")
blocks.title: Python · settings.py (read the injected values)

blocks.text:
A Python container on App Service for Linux loads a large re-ranking model before its web server starts, and on a cold instance that takes about five minutes. After a scale-out the new instance never comes up: the log shows the startup attempt failing and starting again, and requests that reach it get 503 errors.
• The platform waits only for the start time limit (230 seconds by default) for the container to answer its start-up pings, so a five-minute load fails every attempt.
• Quick relief: raise the limit, for example to 600 seconds as the CLI sample does (the Linux maximum is 1,800).
• Better fix: start the web server first and load the model in the background, so start-up stays well inside the limit and the real routes answer once the model is ready.
• With WEBSITE_WARMUP_STATUSES set to 200, the app can answer the warm-up path with another status until the model is loaded, so no traffic is routed early, as long as loading still ends inside the limit.
blocks.title: Worked example · a slow-loading model container

blocks.text:
• App settings reach the process as environment variables; there's no separate configuration file to mount.
• The pull identity and the Key Vault reference identity are configured separately, even when they're the same identity.
• A reference without a version follows rotation; a version in the reference freezes it.
• Settings are environment variables in the process, so changing one means a restart, not a live update.
• Docker Compose multi-container apps are being retired in favour of sidecars.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text:
Question: the registry password is stored on the app, and a developer's startup code logs os.environ to debug the pull. The registry server URL, user name and password variables are missing from the output. Is the configuration broken?

Solution: no. DOCKER_REGISTRY_SERVER_URL, _USERNAME and _PASSWORD are reserved variables that App Service keeps away from the application on purpose. The pull itself uses them. Check the pull in the platform's logs instead, and prefer a managed identity so there's no password to hide.

lessons.title: 1.3 · Azure Container Apps: environments, revisions and secrets
lessons.summary: Deploy to a Container Apps environment, tell revision-scope from application-scope changes, manage revision modes, traffic and labels, and wire secrets and identities.

blocks.text:
An environment is the secure boundary around a group of container apps and jobs. Apps in one environment share a virtual network and send their logs to the same Log Analytics workspace, and Dapr apps there can use service invocation and a shared Dapr configuration. Workload profiles environments are the default type and run both the serverless Consumption profile and Dedicated profiles. Consumption-only environments are the legacy type. An environment that stays idle, or stuck in a failed or blocked state, for more than 90 days is deleted automatically.

Every change to a container app is one of two kinds:
• Revision-scope changes are edits under properties.template, such as the image, container settings, environment variables and scale rules. Each one creates a new revision. Revisions are immutable snapshots.
• Application-scope changes are edits under properties.configuration, such as secret values, ingress (including traffic splitting rules), registries and Dapr settings. They apply to every revision and don't create a new one.
blocks.title: Environments and the two kinds of change

blocks.text:
• Single (the default): a new revision is provisioned and scaled up, and it must pass its startup and readiness probes. Only then does traffic move to it and the old revision is deactivated. Until that point the old revision keeps all the traffic, so a bad image causes no downtime.
• Multiple: several revisions stay active, you split traffic between them by weight, and you decide when old revisions are deprovisioned. The weights must add up to 100%. This mode is the basis for blue-green and canary releases. A revision suffix such as a commit hash gives revisions predictable names (app--suffix).
• Deployment labels (preview) are a third mode built on labels. A label gives one revision its own stable URL. Moving the label to another revision switches that traffic without changing the URL, and labelled traffic doesn't need a weight. Container Apps keeps up to 100 inactive revisions by default. Changing that limit is a preview setting.
blocks.title: Revision modes, traffic and labels

blocks.text:
Secrets are defined at application level (configuration.secrets). An environment variable refers to a secret with secretref:<name>, and scale rules can refer to secrets too. A secret can also be mounted: in a volume of type Secret, each secret becomes a file whose name is the secret name and whose content is its value, and you can mount all secrets or pick some and give them file names.

A secret can be a Key Vault reference, keyvaultref:<secret URI>,identityref:<identity>, resolved by a managed identity that holds Key Vault Secrets User. A URI with a version pins that version. Without a version, the app picks up a newer version within 30 minutes, and active revisions that use it in an environment variable restart automatically. For a plain secret value that you change yourself, running revisions keep using the old value until a restart or a new revision.

To pull from Azure Container Registry without credentials, give the app a system-assigned or user-assigned identity that has AcrPull and pass it as the registry identity. With only a user-assigned identity, code that uses the Azure Identity library must be given that identity's client ID (for example in AZURE_CLIENT_ID).
blocks.title: Secrets, identities and image pulls

blocks.text:
az containerapp create -g rg-app -n ranker-api --environment cae-ranker \
  --image myregistry.azurecr.io/ranker-api:b412 --revision-suffix b412 \
  --user-assigned "$UAMI_ID" \
  --registry-server myregistry.azurecr.io --registry-identity "$UAMI_ID" \
  --secrets "search-key=keyvaultref:$SEARCH_KEY_URI,identityref:$UAMI_ID" \
  --secret-volume-mount "/mnt/secrets" \
  --env-vars "AZURE_CLIENT_ID=$UAMI_CLIENT_ID" \
  --ingress external --target-port 5000
blocks.title: Azure CLI · an API with a mounted Key Vault secret

blocks.text:
az containerapp revision set-mode -g rg-app -n ranker-api --mode multiple
az containerapp update -g rg-app -n ranker-api \
  --image myregistry.azurecr.io/ranker-api:c7e0 --revision-suffix c7e0
az containerapp ingress traffic set -g rg-app -n ranker-api \
  --revision-weight ranker-api--b412=75 ranker-api--c7e0=25
az containerapp revision label add -g rg-app -n ranker-api \
  --label green --revision ranker-api--c7e0
blocks.title: Azure CLI · blue-green on the API app
Python · secrets.py (read a mounted secret)

blocks.text:
A ranking API needs a search service key, which security rotates every month, and a client certificate password that must change only in a planned release.
• The search key is a Key Vault reference without a version. A new version reaches the app within 30 minutes, and because the API reads it through an environment variable, its active revisions restart to pick it up. The team accepts that short restart, so no one has to touch the app after a rotation.
• The certificate password is a Key Vault reference with a version in the URI. It never changes by itself. The release that ships a new certificate also updates the reference.
• The rotation runbook notes that the search key's restart is expected, so on-call staff don't treat it as an incident.
blocks.title: Worked example · two secrets, two rotation policies

blocks.text:
• Revision scope is the template; application scope is the configuration. Ask where a property lives.
• Mounting secrets as files and referring to them with secretref are two ways to read the same application-level secret.
• Container Apps and App Service refresh unversioned Key Vault references on different schedules. Learn each platform's figure separately.
• A user-assigned identity needs its client ID passed to Azure Identity in code.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text:
Question: in single revision mode, a new revision is created but traffic stays on the old one. What must the new revision do before traffic moves?

Solution: provision successfully, scale up to the previous revision's replica count (within its own minimum and maximum), and have every replica pass its startup and readiness probes. Until then the old revision keeps all the traffic.

lessons.title: 1.3 · Event-driven scaling with KEDA in Container Apps
lessons.summary: Scale container apps on HTTP, TCP and event sources with KEDA-based rules: limits, the scaling algorithm, timing, and how scalers authenticate.

blocks.text:
Container Apps scales each revision horizontally with KEDA (Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling). You don't install or run KEDA yourself; you declare scale limits and rules on the revision.
• Limits: a minimum and a maximum replica count per revision, defaults 0 and 10, configurable up to 1,000. Set the minimum to 1 or more if an instance must always be running.
• Rules: HTTP (concurrent requests), TCP (concurrent connections) or custom. A custom rule accepts any ScaledObject-based KEDA scaler, such as azure-servicebus, azure-queue or Event Hubs, and CPU and memory rules are custom rules too. Event-driven Container Apps jobs use ScaledJob-based scalers instead.
• If you define no rule, the default HTTP rule applies (0 to 10 replicas). When an app has several rules, it starts to scale as soon as the first condition of any rule is met. Scaling is horizontal only: vertical scaling isn't supported. An app that scales to zero incurs no usage charges.
blocks.title: What KEDA does in Container Apps
How custom rules behave

blocks.text:
A scaler needs to read its source. Two options:
• A Container Apps secret, mapped to the scaler's TriggerAuthentication parameter (the auth array, or --scale-rule-auth on the CLI).
• A managed identity, for Azure Queue Storage, Service Bus and Event Hubs scalers: set identity to a user-assigned identity's resource ID or to system (--scale-rule-identity on the CLI). Learn prefers this, because no secret is stored in the app. The portal can't configure managed identity for scale rules, so use the CLI, ARM or Bicep.

The identity needs data-plane rights on the source. The Container Apps pages don't name a role for a scaler's identity. For Service Bus, Learn's AKS KEDA workload identity tutorial assigns Azure Service Bus Data Owner to the scaler's identity; that is AKS guidance, the nearest documented choice.
blocks.title: Authentication for scalers

blocks.text:
az containerapp create -g rg-app -n thumb-worker --environment cae-media \
  --image myregistry.azurecr.io/thumb-worker:a91f \
  --user-assigned "$UAMI_ID" \
  --registry-server myregistry.azurecr.io --registry-identity "$UAMI_ID" \
  --min-replicas 0 --max-replicas 30 \
  --scale-rule-name thumbnails --scale-rule-type azure-queue \
  --scale-rule-metadata "accountName=stmedia" "queueName=thumbnails" \
    "queueLength=25" \
  --scale-rule-identity "$UAMI_ID"
blocks.title: Azure CLI · a Storage queue worker scaled with a managed identity

blocks.text:
scale:
  minReplicas: 0
  maxReplicas: 30
  rules:
    - name: thumbnails
      custom:
        type: azure-queue
        metadata:
          accountName: stmedia
          queueName: thumbnails
          queueLength: "25"
        identity: <user-assigned identity resource ID>
blocks.title: YAML · the same rule as an ARM-style template fragment

blocks.text:
A thumbnail worker reads jobs from an Azure Storage queue. It must cost nothing overnight, must not hold a storage key and may use at most 30 replicas because a downstream API has a rate limit.
• Ingress stays off: nothing calls the worker over HTTP.
• Limits: minimum 0, so idle nights cost nothing, and maximum 30 to protect the downstream API.
• Rule: a custom azure-queue rule with queueLength 25, meaning each replica should have about 25 waiting jobs.
• Authentication: the app's user-assigned identity, set with --scale-rule-identity from the CLI because the portal can't set it, and given data-plane read access to the queue.
• The same identity has AcrPull for image pulls, so the app holds no credentials at all.
blocks.title: Worked example · designing a media worker's scaling

blocks.text:
• Scale rules belong to the revision template, so editing one is a revision-scope change.
• CPU and memory scaling are custom rules, not separate rule categories.
• The polling interval belongs to custom rules; HTTP and TCP rules measure load differently.
• Stabilization windows and the cool down period are different settings with the same 300-second value.
• Managed identity for a scaler: CLI, ARM or Bicep, never the portal.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text:
Question: a team wants an API to add replicas when memory use climbs, and asks which of the three rule categories to pick. What do you tell them, and what limit should they not expect to change?

Solution: memory is a custom rule (CPU and memory are custom metrics). It adds replicas; Container Apps doesn't scale vertically, so the memory of each replica stays what the container definition sets.

lessons.title: 1.4 · AKS: deploy and manage applications with manifests
lessons.summary: Describe workloads on Azure Kubernetes Service in manifest files: Deployments, resources, probes, disruption budgets, Services and namespaces, and pull images from Azure Container Registry.

blocks.text:
AKS runs Kubernetes with a managed control plane and comes in two cluster modes, AKS Automatic and AKS Standard. Nodes are grouped in node pools: the system node pool hosts critical system pods such as CoreDNS, and user node pools host your application pods. AKS creates a second resource group, the node resource group, for the cluster's virtual machines, scale sets and storage.

Namespaces divide a cluster for creating, viewing and managing access to resources. AKS creates default, kube-node-lease, kube-public and kube-system. kube-system holds cluster components such as coredns, konnectivity-agent and metrics-server, and Learn advises against deploying your own applications there.
blocks.title: What AKS gives you

blocks.text:
You describe the desired state in YAML manifest files and apply them with kubectl apply -f <file>, and Kubernetes works to make the cluster match. kubectl delete -f <file> removes what the file created.
• A Deployment declares the replica count, a label selector and a pod template: containers, images, ports, environment, resources and probes. Learn recommends at least two replicas for resilience. A pod is one or more containers that share network and storage, usually one.
• Resource requests and limits: set CPU and memory limits for every pod so one workload can't exhaust a node. A container that goes over its memory limit is killed (OOMKilled).
• Probes: the kubelet uses a readiness probe to decide whether a pod receives traffic, a liveness probe to decide when to restart a container, and a startup probe to hold the other two back until a slow starter is up.
• A Pod Disruption Budget keeps a minimum number of pods running during voluntary disruptions such as upgrades. Rolling updates are tuned with maxSurge and maxUnavailable, and topology spread constraints spread pods across nodes or zones. A cluster's availability zone setup can't be changed after creation.
• A Service gives the selected pods a stable address. ClusterIP (the default) is internal only, NodePort maps a port on each node, LoadBalancer creates an Azure load balancer with an external IP, and ExternalName maps to a DNS name. A new LoadBalancer Service shows EXTERNAL-IP as <pending> until the address is assigned.

To pull from Azure Container Registry, attach the registry (az aks create or az aks update with --attach-acr). That grants AcrPull to the cluster's kubelet identity. Attaching isn't supported for registries that use the ABAC repository permissions mode.
blocks.title: Manifests and the objects in them

blocks.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: search
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: embed-api
  namespace: search
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: embed-api}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: embed-api}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: myregistry.azurecr.io/embed-api:9d3e
          ports: [{containerPort: 7000}]
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: 500m, memory: 1Gi}
            limits: {cpu: "1", memory: 2Gi}
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: {path: /ready, port: 7000}
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: {path: /live, port: 7000}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: embed-api
  namespace: search
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector: {app: embed-api}
  ports: [{port: 80, targetPort: 7000}]
blocks.title: YAML · embed-api.yaml

blocks.text:
az aks update -g rg-search -n aks-search --attach-acr myregistry
kubectl apply -f embed-api.yaml
kubectl get pods -n search -l app=embed-api
kubectl get service embed-api -n search
blocks.title: Shell · attach the registry, apply and check

blocks.text:
A search team adds an embeddings API that only a gateway inside the same cluster calls.
• Namespace: a dedicated search namespace, not kube-system, so the team's access and clean-up stay separate from cluster components.
• Deployment: three replicas, CPU and memory requests and limits sized from load tests, a readiness probe on /ready so a pod still loading its model gets no traffic, and a liveness probe on /live.
• Service: ClusterIP, because no client outside the cluster needs it; the gateway calls embed-api.search through cluster DNS.
• Registry: the cluster's registry is attached once, so the manifest needs no image pull secret.
• One file holds the namespace, Deployment and Service, so kubectl apply -f creates or updates all three and kubectl delete -f removes them together.
blocks.title: Worked example · an internal embeddings service

blocks.text:
• Availability zones are chosen when the cluster is created and can't be changed afterwards.
• ClusterIP is the default Service type and is unreachable from outside the cluster.
• A Pod Disruption Budget protects against voluntary disruptions, not node crashes.
• --attach-acr grants a role to the kubelet identity, not to your user or a pod.
• kube-system is for cluster components, not application workloads.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text:
Question: a colleague proposes deploying a new API into kube-system "so it sits next to CoreDNS and starts with the cluster". What do you answer?

Solution: kube-system is the namespace Kubernetes uses for cluster components such as coredns, konnectivity-agent and metrics-server, and Learn doesn't recommend deploying your own applications there. Create an application namespace instead. Starting with the cluster comes from the Deployment, not from the namespace.

lessons.title: 1.4 · Monitor and troubleshoot AKS and Container Apps
lessons.summary: Diagnose failing pods, revisions and connections with state, events, logs and connectivity checks on AKS, and with console and system logs on Container Apps.

blocks.text:
Both platforms give you the same kinds of evidence, in different places:
• State: what the platform thinks is running (pod status and restarts on AKS; revision health and replicas on Container Apps).
• Events: short-lived records of what the control plane did. Kubernetes keeps them for about one hour and has no setting to change that.
• Logs: what the container wrote, and on Container Apps also what the platform wrote about the app.
• Connectivity: whether a request can reach a pod, through DNS, a Service or ingress. Container insights collects AKS logs, events and performance data into a Log Analytics workspace. AKS Automatic turns it on by default together with managed Prometheus; on AKS Standard you enable monitoring yourself.
blocks.title: What you have to work with

blocks.text:
Work from the outside in:
• kubectl get pods shows STATUS and RESTARTS. CrashLoopBackOff means the container keeps exiting and being restarted. Typical causes are bad configuration, missing environment variables, ConfigMaps or Secrets, a too-low limit or a misconfigured probe. ImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePull means the image can't be pulled. Exit code 137 with reason OOMKilled means the memory limit was exceeded.
• kubectl describe pod <pod> ends with the pod's events. They explain image pull and probe failures and other warnings. kubectl get events lists events for a namespace, while they still exist.
• kubectl logs <pod> shows output, and -c <container> picks a container. --previous shows the last run of a container that has restarted.
• Connectivity: kubectl describe service shows the selector and endpoints, and a test pod can call the pod IP and the Service IP to see which hop fails. Check network policies too. az aks check-acr tests whether the cluster can reach and authenticate to a registry.
blocks.title: Troubleshooting AKS: state, events, logs, connectivity

blocks.text:
Container Apps separates log categories:
• Console logs are what your container writes to stdout and stderr.
• System logs come from the platform: revision provisioning (including ErrImagePull, Timeout and ContainerCrashing errors), traffic weights, Dapr components, volume mounts, domain binding and authentication.
• HTTP logs come from the ingress layer once you turn them on in diagnostic settings. Stream console or system logs with az containerapp logs show --type console or --type system, adding --follow for a live stream or --tail for the last messages; --revision, --replica and --container pick one container. In Log Analytics the tables are ContainerAppConsoleLogs_CL and ContainerAppSystemLogs_CL, with columns such as ContainerAppName_s, RevisionName_s and Log_s (the console table adds ContainerGroupName_g, the replica).

Common symptoms and what to check:
• A revision stays Provisioning, or becomes Degraded: check the health probes and the image pull.
• Requests fail: check that ingress is enabled, which callers it accepts, and the target port.
• Responses come from the wrong version: check traffic weights and deploy with unique image tags.
• The log stream reports that the revision is scaled to zero: run it with a minimum of one replica while you debug. az containerapp revision list shows each revision's health, and az containerapp replica list shows its replicas.
blocks.title: Troubleshooting Container Apps

blocks.text:
kubectl get pods -n search -l app=embed-api
kubectl describe pod "$POD" -n search
kubectl logs "$POD" -n search -c api
kubectl top pod "$POD" -n search

az containerapp revision list -g rg-app -n ranker-api -o table
az containerapp replica list -g rg-app -n ranker-api \
  --revision ranker-api--c7e0 -o table
az containerapp logs show -g rg-app -n ranker-api --type system --tail 50
blocks.title: Shell · inspect a failing AKS pod and a Container Apps revision

blocks.text:
ContainerAppSystemLogs_CL
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Log_s has "Error provisioning revision"
| project TimeGenerated, ContainerAppName_s, RevisionName_s, Log_s
| order by TimeGenerated desc
blocks.title: KQL · revision provisioning errors (Container Apps)

blocks.text: During a load test, API pods keep restarting, and kubectl describe pod shows the last state as terminated with exit code 137, reason OOMKilled. kubectl top pod confirms that memory climbs to the container's limit. The container, not the node, ran out of its allowance. The team raises the memory request and limit in the Deployment (kubectl set resources does this from the command line), then investigates why each request allocates so much memory.
blocks.title: Worked example · restarts under load

blocks.text:
• Read the evidence in order: state, then events, then logs, then connectivity. Each narrows the next.
• ImagePullBackOff means the image never ran; CrashLoopBackOff means it ran and its process exited.
• kubectl top shows current use; kubectl describe shows the limits and the last terminated state.
• Exit code 137 with OOMKilled points at the container's limit, not at the node.
• A scaled-to-zero revision has no replica to stream logs from.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text:
Question: a pod runs the API container and a log-shipping sidecar. kubectl logs <pod> doesn't print the API's output and asks you to choose a container. What do you run?

Solution: kubectl logs <pod> -c api, naming the container from the pod spec (kubectl describe pod lists them). On Container Apps the equivalent is az containerapp logs show with --container, together with --revision and --replica when the app has several.

lessons.title: Lab · Scale a Container Apps queue worker with KEDA
lessons.summary: Hands-on: build a Python Service Bus worker in Azure Container Registry, deploy it to Container Apps with a KEDA scale rule and a managed identity, fill the queue and watch it scale out and back to zero.

blocks.text: You build a small Python worker that drains a Service Bus queue, deploy it to Azure Container Apps with no ingress, and let a KEDA azure-servicebus rule scale it from zero. One user-assigned identity pulls the image, authenticates the scale rule and lets the code read the queue, so no connection string or password appears anywhere. Allow about 45 minutes. The resources cost little, and the last step deletes them.
blocks.title: Goal

blocks.text:
• An Azure subscription where you can create resource groups and role assignments (task runs are paused on free-credit subscriptions at the time of writing, so the build step needs a paid one).
• Azure CLI, signed in with az login, with the containerapp extension (az extension add --name containerapp).
• Python 3.10 or later with azure-identity and azure-servicebus, to send test messages.
• A bash shell. Role assignments can take a few minutes to apply; if a step fails with an authorization error, wait and retry.
blocks.title: Prerequisites

blocks.text:
RG=rg-keda-lab; LOC=westeurope
ACR=acrkedalab$RANDOM; SB=sb-keda-lab-$RANDOM
az group create -n $RG -l $LOC
az acr create -g $RG -n $ACR --sku Basic
az servicebus namespace create -g $RG -n $SB --sku Standard
az servicebus queue create -g $RG --namespace-name $SB -n jobs

az identity create -g $RG -n id-keda-lab
UAMI_ID=$(az identity show -g $RG -n id-keda-lab --query id -o tsv)
UAMI_PRINCIPAL=$(az identity show -g $RG -n id-keda-lab --query principalId -o tsv)
UAMI_CLIENT=$(az identity show -g $RG -n id-keda-lab --query clientId -o tsv)

# Image pulls
az role assignment create --assignee-object-id $UAMI_PRINCIPAL \
  --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal --role AcrPull \
  --scope "$(az acr show -n $ACR --query id -o tsv)"
# Scaler and worker. The Container Apps pages name no scaler role; Data Owner follows
# Learn's AKS KEDA tutorial. The worker alone would need only Data Receiver.
SB_ID=$(az servicebus namespace show -g $RG -n $SB --query id -o tsv)
az role assignment create --assignee-object-id $UAMI_PRINCIPAL \
  --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal \
  --role "Azure Service Bus Data Owner" --scope $SB_ID
# You, to send test messages
az role assignment create --assignee "$(az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv)" \
  --role "Azure Service Bus Data Sender" --scope $SB_ID
blocks.title: Azure CLI · step 1, resource group, registry, queue and identity

blocks.text:
import os
import time

from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.servicebus import ServiceBusClient

# Only a user-assigned identity is attached, so AZURE_CLIENT_ID names it.
credential = DefaultAzureCredential()
fqdn = os.environ["SERVICEBUS_FQDN"]

with ServiceBusClient(fqdn, credential) as client:
    # No max_wait_time: the receiver keeps waiting for messages while the replica runs.
    with client.get_queue_receiver("jobs") as receiver:
        for message in receiver:
            time.sleep(2)  # stand-in for real work
            print("done", message.message_id, flush=True)
            receiver.complete_message(message)
blocks.title: Python · worker.py (the container's program)

blocks.text:
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir azure-identity azure-servicebus
COPY worker.py .
CMD ["python", "worker.py"]
blocks.title: Dockerfile · next to worker.py

blocks.text:
az acr build --registry $ACR --image jobs-worker:v1 .

az containerapp env create -g $RG -n cae-keda-lab -l $LOC
az containerapp create -g $RG -n jobs-worker --environment cae-keda-lab \
  --image $ACR.azurecr.io/jobs-worker:v1 \
  --user-assigned $UAMI_ID \
  --registry-server $ACR.azurecr.io --registry-identity $UAMI_ID \
  --env-vars SERVICEBUS_FQDN=$SB.servicebus.windows.net AZURE_CLIENT_ID=$UAMI_CLIENT \
  --min-replicas 0 --max-replicas 6 \
  --scale-rule-name jobs-backlog --scale-rule-type azure-servicebus \
  --scale-rule-metadata "queueName=jobs" "namespace=$SB" "messageCount=10" \
  --scale-rule-identity $UAMI_ID
blocks.title: Azure CLI · step 2, build in Azure and deploy with a scale rule

blocks.text:
import os

from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.servicebus import ServiceBusClient, ServiceBusMessage

fqdn = os.environ["SERVICEBUS_FQDN"]  # exported in step 4

with ServiceBusClient(fqdn, DefaultAzureCredential()) as client:
    with client.get_queue_sender("jobs") as sender:
        batch = [ServiceBusMessage(f"job {n}") for n in range(200)]
        sender.send_messages(batch)
print("sent 200 jobs")
blocks.title: Python · send_jobs.py (step 3, create a backlog from your machine)

blocks.text:
export SERVICEBUS_FQDN=$SB.servicebus.windows.net
pip install azure-identity azure-servicebus
python send_jobs.py

az containerapp replica list -g $RG -n jobs-worker -o table
az containerapp logs show -g $RG -n jobs-worker --type console --follow
az containerapp logs show -g $RG -n jobs-worker --type system --tail 30
blocks.title: Shell · step 4, send the jobs and watch them

blocks.text:
• Before you send jobs, az containerapp replica list shows no replicas: with no backlog the worker sits at zero.

• The done lines stop once all 200 jobs are handled. Some minutes later the replicas are removed and the list is empty again.
• If no replica ever starts, read the system log: an image pull error points at the AcrPull assignment or the registry identity. If replicas start but print nothing, check the Service Bus role and that AZURE_CLIENT_ID holds the identity's client ID.

lessons.title: 2.1.1 · Cosmos DB for NoSQL: connect with the Python SDK and run queries
lessons.summary: Build one CosmosClient with Microsoft Entra ID, walk from database to container, and choose between point reads, single-partition queries and writes.

blocks.text:
Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL stores JSON items in containers, and containers live in databases inside an account. The azure-cosmos package mirrors that shape: CosmosClient for the account, then a database client, then a container client that offers the item operations. Each item must include an id key that identifies it, and Cosmos DB accepts only string id values.

Create one CosmosClient and reuse it for the life of the process. The Python client is thread-safe and handles connections efficiently, so one shared instance is the recommended pattern. In Python every request goes via the Cosmos DB gateway: the Python SDK offers no Direct connectivity.
blocks.title: What it is

blocks.text:
Pass a DefaultAzureCredential to CosmosClient and give the identity a data-plane role, either Cosmos DB Built-in Data Reader or Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor, assigned with az cosmosdb sql role assignment create. These are Cosmos DB's own role definitions, separate from Azure RBAC roles. Data-plane roles read and write data but don't manage resources such as databases and containers. Create those through the control plane, with Bicep, ARM or the CLI. A custom data role lists its allowed operations under dataActions, and the identity also needs readMetadata, which the built-in roles already include.

Setting disableLocalAuth to true on the account turns off key-based access, so every client must sign in with Microsoft Entra ID.
blocks.title: Signing in with Microsoft Entra ID

blocks.text:
Every operation is charged in Request Units (RUs), so the call you choose matters.
• Point reads: read_item with the id and the partition key value. They cost fewer RUs than queries, so use one whenever you know both values.
• Queries: query_items with parameters, never values pasted into the SQL text. When you pass partition_key, the query stays in one partition and the SDK skips a query-plan call to the gateway. A query without the partition key fans out to all physical partitions, so it gets slower and costlier as the container grows. max_item_count sets the page size; Learn recommends leaving it unset so the service picks the page size.
• Writes: create_item, upsert_item, replace_item and delete_item. Transactional batch is supported, but bulk requests aren't implemented in the Python SDK yet.
• Regions: preferred_locations is the ordered list of regions the client tries for reads. If every listed region fails, reads go to the write region.
The charge for the last call is in the x-ms-request-charge response header (read last_response_headers on container.client_connection).
blocks.title: How the operations work

blocks.text:
import os

from azure.cosmos import CosmosClient
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential

# One client per process, reused everywhere
credential = DefaultAzureCredential()
client = CosmosClient(os.environ["COSMOS_ENDPOINT"], credential=credential)
orders = client.get_database_client("shop").get_container_client("orders")

# Point read: id plus partition key value
order = orders.read_item(item="ord-1009", partition_key="cust-42")

# Parameterized single-partition query
rows = list(orders.query_items(
    query="SELECT c.id, c.total FROM c WHERE c.status = @status",
    parameters=[{"name": "@status", "value": "open"}],
    partition_key="cust-42",
))
headers = orders.client_connection.last_response_headers
print("RU charge:", headers["x-ms-request-charge"])
blocks.title: Python · cosmos_orders.py

blocks.text: A support tool looks up tickets with SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.id = @id, and the ticket number comes from a URL route declared as an int, so the parameter value is 50213, not "50213". The query runs without an error but returns nothing, even for tickets that exist. Cosmos DB only accepts string id values, and the Python SDK returns no results and no error message when a query by id passes another type. The fix is to convert the value with str() before it goes into parameters, and to keep ids as strings everywhere the app creates items.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
• Every SDK client needs the readMetadata data action: the SDKs read account and container configuration before they serve data requests. Forget it in a custom role, and the client can't work with the account.
• The Python SDK has transactional batch but no bulk mode. Learn's workaround is the async client, which can burn RUs very fast.
• Leave max_item_count unset unless you need a fixed page size. The service then picks the best size.
• Python writes True and False, and Cosmos DB stores true and false. The SDK converts them in both directions.
• A query over a subitem, such as FROM c.children, needs partition_key or enable_cross_partition_query, and with partition_key the partition key must be inside the subitems.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text: Question: a report query with GROUP BY c.region runs in Data Explorer, but the same query sent through query_items in Python fails. Why, and what can you do? Solution: the Python SDK lists Group By queries under its data-plane limitations, so it doesn't support them. Return the rows you need and aggregate them in Python, or keep a pre-aggregated item that your writes maintain.

lessons.title: 2.1.2 · Cosmos DB: optimize RUs with indexing policies and consistency levels
lessons.summary: See where Request Units go, tune the indexing policy so writes pay only for the paths you query, and pick the weakest consistency level your users can accept.

blocks.text:
A Request Unit (RU) is a single currency that covers the CPU, IOPS and memory an operation uses. You pay for RUs in one of three modes: provisioned throughput (RU/s set in steps of 100), autoscale, or serverless. Learn lists what drives the charge:
• Item size and the number of indexed properties raise the cost of reads and writes.
• Point reads cost fewer RUs than queries.
• For queries: the number of results, the number and nature of predicates, user-defined functions, the size of the source data and of the result set, and projections.
• Strong and Bounded staleness reads cost about twice as much as reads at the relaxed levels.
The same query on the same data always costs the same number of RUs, so you can measure a change by comparing the x-ms-request-charge header before and after it. For queries, populate_query_metrics=True returns execution metrics and populate_index_metrics=True shows which indexes were used and which ones Cosmos DB recommends.
blocks.title: What Request Units are

blocks.text:
By default every property of every item is indexed, with indexing mode consistent, which means the index is updated synchronously with each write. That makes any filter cheap to query but makes every write pay for every path. Tune the policy:
• Keep the root path /* included and exclude the paths you never filter or sort on, such as long text or large arrays. This is the recommended strategy, because new properties still get indexed. The alternative excludes /* and includes only the listed paths. In that case remember to include the partition key path.
• When an included path and an excluded path conflict, the more precise path wins.
• Sorting on several properties at once (ORDER BY a, b) requires a composite index whose paths follow the same order. Composite indexes also help some combinations of filter and sort.
• Indexing mode none turns indexing off for a pure key-value container.
id and _ts are always indexed in consistent mode, and _etag is excluded by default.
blocks.title: Indexing policies
JSON · indexing policy: exclude bulky paths, add a composite index

blocks.text:
From strongest to weakest: Strong, Bounded staleness, Session, Consistent prefix, Eventual. You set a default on the account. Strong and Bounded staleness need two replicas for every read (a minority quorum), while the other three levels use one, so for the same RUs the two strong levels give half the read throughput. Write throughput is the same at every level.

Session is the most widely used level. Within a session, a client reads its own writes because the SDK keeps a session token for each partition and sends it with reads. A brand-new client has no tokens yet, so until it writes it reads like Eventual. After you change the account default, restart the applications so their clients pick up the new level.
blocks.title: Consistency levels

blocks.text: A stock dashboard writes in one region and serves reads from two other regions. The business accepts that a regional reader lags behind, but never by more than 30 seconds or 50 updates of an item. Bounded staleness expresses exactly that: you configure K versions and T time, and the lag between regions stays below whichever is reached first. If a partition's lag exceeds the bound, Cosmos DB throttles writes for that partition until it catches up. Within one region, data always replicates to a local majority, so the staleness check applies only across regions. The price is on the read side: Bounded staleness reads consult two replicas and cost about twice the RUs of the relaxed levels. Learn calls Bounded staleness an anti-pattern for multi-region write accounts, where apps should read and write in their own region.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
• A query that repeats on the same data costs the same RUs every time, so a changing charge points to changed data or a changed policy, not to noise.
• Projections and result size are part of a query's cost. Returning only the fields you need is one lever.
• Bounded staleness suits single-region write accounts with several read regions. With multi-region writes it's an anti-pattern.
• When an included and an excluded path overlap, the more precise path decides.
• id and _ts are always indexed, whatever the policy says.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text: Question: a container's policy excludes /* and includes only /status/?. Queries that filter on the partition key property now behave unexpectedly. Why? Solution: with the exclude-root strategy, the partition key path isn't indexed by default, so you have to include it explicitly.

lessons.title: 2.1.3 · Cosmos DB for NoSQL: store embeddings and run vector search
lessons.summary: Define a vector embedding policy and a vector index, choose between flat, quantizedFlat and diskANN, and run VectorDistance queries for semantic retrieval.

blocks.text:
Cosmos DB for NoSQL works as a vector store: you keep each chunk's embedding as an array property next to its text and metadata, so one query can filter and rank. Vector indexing and search are on by default, with no feature to register or account capability to enable. A container needs two settings:
• A vector embedding policy that lists each vector path with its dataType (float32, float16, int8 or uint8), its dimensions and its distanceFunction (cosine, the default, or dotproduct or euclidean). float16 halves the storage that float32 needs, at some cost in accuracy.
• An entry under vectorIndexes in the indexing policy for the same path. Learn's examples also list that path under excludedPaths so the regular index skips it.

Once vector indexing and search are enabled on a container, they can't be turned off. Accounts with shared throughput don't support them.
blocks.title: What it is

blocks.text: Both quantized types (quantizedFlat, diskANN) only take effect once 1,000 or more vectors are indexed. Below that, a query runs a full scan and can cost more RUs. Learn's rule of thumb is quantizedFlat for searches scoped to 50,000 vectors or fewer and diskANN above that.
blocks.title: Vector index types
rows: 100% recall; stored with the other indexes
fast at scale; results can vary between runs

blocks.text: VectorDistance(c.embedding, @queryVector) scores each item, and ORDER BY VectorDistance(...) puts the nearest first. Always add TOP N, because without it the query tries to return far more results and costs more RUs and latency. Without ORDER BY, TOP N returns arbitrary items rather than the closest. Pass the query vector and N as parameters. Add WHERE filters on tenant, type or date, and pass partition_key, so the search stays narrow. For diskANN you can raise searchListSizeMultiplier in VectorDistance's options to trade latency for recall on a single query.
blocks.title: How a vector query works

blocks.text:
import os

from azure.cosmos import CosmosClient
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential

credential = DefaultAzureCredential()
client = CosmosClient(os.environ["COSMOS_ENDPOINT"], credential=credential)
# The container was created through the control plane (CLI, Bicep or ARM) with
# a vector embedding policy on /embedding and a vector index on the same path.
chunks = client.get_database_client("kb").get_container_client("chunks")


def nearest(query_vector, owner, k=5):
    sql = ("SELECT TOP @k c.id, c.text, VectorDistance(c.embedding, @v) AS similarity "
           "FROM c WHERE c.ownerId = @o ORDER BY VectorDistance(c.embedding, @v)")
    return list(chunks.query_items(
        query=sql,
        parameters=[{"name": "@k", "value": k}, {"name": "@v", "value": query_vector},
                    {"name": "@o", "value": owner}],
        partition_key=owner))
blocks.title: Python · cosmos_vectors.py

blocks.text: You can add new vector path configurations to a container or remove existing ones, but you can't change the settings of a vector embedding policy or vector index in place. To change one, drop the policy or index and add it back with the new configuration. Wildcard characters (* and []) and vector paths nested inside arrays aren't supported in a vector policy or vector index. Each vectorIndexes entry can also set quantizerType: product is the default, and spherical can index a little faster and keep recall steadier with very high-dimensional embeddings. Learn also asks you to limit the insertion rate: very large ingestion, beyond 5 million vectors in a short period, can need more index build time.
blocks.title: Changing vector settings

blocks.text: A retailer migrates its catalogue to Cosmos DB and plans to load 12 million product embeddings in one night, then switch search traffic over the next morning. Learn warns that the rate of vector insertions should be limited, and that very large ingestion, beyond 5 million vectors in a short period, might need more index build time. So the team spreads the load over several nights, in batches whose RU charge it watches, and keeps the old search service live until the load is done. Before the switch, it checks result quality with real queries embedded by the production model, because randomly generated test vectors say little about recall.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
• flat stops at 505 dimensions. quantizedFlat and diskANN go to 4,096.
• A vector query without TOP N tries to return far more results than you need and costs more RUs.
• Vector indexes are tuned for embeddings from real models. Randomly generated test vectors give misleading recall.
• Once vector search is enabled on a container, you can't turn it off.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text: Question: creating a container with a vector embedding policy fails in an account that uses shared throughput. Why? Solution: Learn lists vector indexing and search as not supported on accounts with shared throughput. Use an account without shared throughput for vector containers.

lessons.title: 2.1.4 · Cosmos DB: process the change feed
lessons.summary: Choose a change feed mode, read it from Python with the pull model or an Azure Functions trigger, and save your position so processing resumes where it stopped.

blocks.text:
The change feed is a persistent record of changes to a container. It has two modes:
• Latest version (the default) records creates and updates and gives you the current version of each changed item. Intermediate versions can be skipped, and deletes aren't recorded. To see deletions, write a soft-delete flag instead of deleting. You can start from the beginning of the container, from a point in time, from now or from a saved checkpoint. The precision of a start time is about five seconds, and you can't filter the feed by operation type.
• All versions and deletes (preview) records every create, update and delete in order, including deletes caused by TTL expiry, with metadata that tells you which operation happened. It needs continuous backup, and you turn it on in the account's Features page. It can start only from now or from a checkpoint inside the backup retention window.
blocks.title: What it is

blocks.text:
• The change feed processor library is for .NET and Java only. Python and Node.js use the pull model instead.
• Pull model: query_items_change_feed with start_time ("Beginning", "Now" or a datetime), or mode="AllVersionsAndDeletes" (preview; needs azure-cosmos 4.9.1b1 or later), optionally with partition_key or a feed_range (read_feed_ranges returns one per physical partition) so that several workers can split the work. You save the continuation token yourself (the etag response header) and resume with continuation=. A continuation token takes precedence over a start time, and it carries the mode it was created with.
• Azure Functions Cosmos DB trigger: the platform manages the reading and keeps its state in a lease container. For Python functions the trigger uses latest version mode.
blocks.title: How Python consumes it
Python · function_app.py (Cosmos DB trigger, v2 model)

blocks.text:
import os

from azure.cosmos import CosmosClient
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential

credential = DefaultAzureCredential()
client = CosmosClient(os.environ["COSMOS_ENDPOINT"], credential=credential)
articles = client.get_database_client("kb").get_container_client("articles")


def read_changes(saved_token=None):
    if saved_token:
        feed = articles.query_items_change_feed(continuation=saved_token)
    else:
        feed = articles.query_items_change_feed(start_time="Beginning")
    for item in feed:
        print("changed:", item["id"])
    # Persist this after the batch succeeds; pass it back next time.
    return articles.client_connection.last_response_headers["etag"]
blocks.title: Python · feed_pull.py (pull model with a saved checkpoint)

blocks.text: A bug in a summarizer went live at 14:00 UTC on 9 March, and every article written since then has a bad summary. Reading the whole history again would waste RUs, so a one-off Python job reads the change feed from a point in time instead: query_items_change_feed with start_time set to a timezone-aware datetime for 13:58 on that day. The two-minute margin covers the start time's precision of about five seconds with room to spare. Latest version mode gives the current version of each article changed since then, and the job rewrites its summary. When the job reaches the end, it saves the etag continuation token, so a rerun picks up only newer changes rather than starting at 13:58 again.
blocks.title: Worked example
Python · backfill.py (start from a point in time)

blocks.text:
• All versions and deletes mode is preview, needs continuous backup, and can't start from the beginning or from a point in time.
• The change feed processor library doesn't exist for Python. Check which consumption options a language really has before you design around one.
• A continuation token wins over start_time, and it keeps the mode it was created with.
• You can't ask the change feed for only inserts or only updates. Mark items yourself if the difference matters.
• A start time is precise to about five seconds, so start a little early and make processing safe to repeat.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text: Question: a worker processes a batch of changes, writes the results, then crashes before it saves its new continuation token. What happens when it restarts, and how should the handler be written? Solution: it resumes from the last saved token, so it reads that batch again. The change feed processor's own guarantee is at-least-once delivery, and a pull-model worker that saves after processing behaves the same way. Make the handler idempotent, for example by upserting results keyed by the item's id, so a repeat does no harm.

lessons.title: 2.2.1 · Azure Database for PostgreSQL: connect and query from Python
lessons.summary: Reach a flexible server over TLS, sign in passwordless with Microsoft Entra ID, and run parameterized queries with psycopg.

blocks.text:
This pack targets Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server, a managed PostgreSQL service. It speaks standard PostgreSQL, so Python uses an ordinary driver. The Learn quickstart uses psycopg (version 3, psycopg.connect) and connects over TLS with sslmode=require. Connections use port 5432, or port 6432 when they go through the built-in PgBouncer pooler.

A new server comes with a postgres database for your use, plus azure_maintenance, which the managed service uses for its own processes, and azure_sys, which holds Query Store and autonomous tuning data. You choose the networking method (public access with firewall rules, or private access) when you create the server, and you can't change it afterwards. With public access, a client outside Azure needs a firewall rule for its IP address, or its connection times out.
blocks.title: What it is

blocks.text:
Microsoft Entra authentication is the recommended option for production; PostgreSQL authentication alone is meant for quickstarts. The app gets an access token with DefaultAzureCredential for the PostgreSQL token scope (the ossrdbms-aad host under database.windows.net, ending in /.default) and sends that token as the password. The user name is the database role mapped to the Entra principal.

A Microsoft Entra administrator, which can be a user, a group, a service principal or a managed identity, has the same privileges as the PostgreSQL administrator and can manage both Entra roles and local password roles. The first one is added on the server's Authentication page in the portal or through the ARM API. After that, the administrator creates roles for other principals in SQL with pgaadauth_create_principal and lists them with pgaadauth_list_principals. Tokens expire, so production code needs a refresh strategy, and Learn advises reusing one credential so its token cache saves round trips to the identity provider.
blocks.title: Passwordless sign-in with Microsoft Entra ID

blocks.text:
import os

import psycopg
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential

credential = DefaultAzureCredential()        # one credential, reused
SCOPE = os.environ["PG_ENTRA_SCOPE"]         # the ossrdbms-aad .default scope


def connect():
    token = credential.get_token(SCOPE).token
    return psycopg.connect(host=os.environ["PGHOST"], port=5432, dbname="kb",
                           user=os.environ["PGUSER"], password=token,
                           sslmode="require")


with connect() as conn:
    with conn.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute("SELECT id, title FROM articles WHERE tenant = %s LIMIT %s",
                    ("t-17", 20))
        rows = cur.fetchall()
blocks.title: Python · pg_query.py (Entra token, parameterized query)

blocks.text: A search endpoint builds its SQL with an f-string, so a title such as O'Brien breaks the statement and a crafted value could change what the query does. The fix follows the pattern in Learn's quickstart: keep %s placeholders in the SQL text and pass the values as a separate tuple to cursor.execute, for example ("O'Brien", 20). Never format user text into the SQL string. A query with a single value still needs a tuple, which in Python means a trailing comma: ("O'Brien",).
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
• PostgreSQL authentication only is the quickstart setting. Production servers use Microsoft Entra authentication.
• A Microsoft Entra administrator can be a group, which makes administration easier to share.
• The PostgreSQL administrator can create only local password-based users. Entra roles come from an Entra administrator.
• Public access versus private access is fixed when you create the server.
• With public access, a timeout from a developer machine usually means its IP address has no firewall rule.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text: Question: on a brand-new flexible server, which database should your application's tables go in, and what are the other two databases you see for? Solution: use postgres (or a database you create). azure_maintenance serves the managed service's own processes, and azure_sys holds Query Store and autonomous tuning data.
