lessons.title: 2.2.2 · PostgreSQL: model schemas and choose data types for embeddings
lessons.summary: Enable pgvector, design tables that keep text, metadata and embeddings together, and pick between vector, halfvec and dimension-free columns.

blocks.text: pgvector adds vector storage, distance operators and vector indexes to PostgreSQL. On flexible server the extension is called vector, not pgvector. Allow-list it in the azure.extensions server parameter, for example with az postgres flexible-server parameter set (check with SHOW azure.extensions), then run CREATE EXTENSION vector in each database that needs it. After that you can create vector columns next to ordinary columns, or add one to an existing table with ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN.
blocks.title: What it is

blocks.text:
Keep source documents and their chunks in separate tables. A document has many chunks, and each chunk holds its text, the metadata you filter on and its embedding.
• The embedding column is the pgvector vector(n) type, with n equal to the model's output size (1,536 for text-embedding-ada-002). A column needs fixed dimensions before ivfflat or hnsw can index it, and those indexes take at most 2,000 of them. For larger embeddings, half-precision vectors (halfvec) or half-precision indexing reach 4,000 dimensions.
• Plain columns: Learn's own examples use bigint or bigserial keys and text for the content.
• Put metadata that queries filter on (tenant, category, date) into ordinary columns, so you can index it with B-tree, write partial indexes for common predicates, or partition the table, for example by a date range or by tenant.
Load data in bulk with COPY, and upsert with INSERT … ON CONFLICT … DO UPDATE.
blocks.title: How to model the schema

blocks.text: Both types store up to 16,000 dimensions; the limits above are for indexing.
blocks.title: Vector column types
rows: ivfflat and hnsw up to 2,000 dimensions
only through an expression index with a cast, per length

blocks.text:
-- After 'vector' is allow-listed in azure.extensions
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

CREATE TABLE articles (
    id        bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    tenant    text NOT NULL,
    title     text NOT NULL,
    category  text NOT NULL,
    published date NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE chunks (
    id         bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    article_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES articles(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    tenant     text NOT NULL,
    chunk_no   int  NOT NULL,
    content    text NOT NULL,
    embedding  vector(1536) NOT NULL,
    UNIQUE (article_id, chunk_no)
);

CREATE INDEX chunks_tenant ON chunks (tenant);   -- B-tree for the filter column
blocks.title: SQL · schema.sql

blocks.text: A team evaluates two embedding models side by side: one returns 768 dimensions and the other 1,024. Rather than two tables, it keeps one table keyed by (model_id, item_id) with a dimension-free vector column. A plain vector column can't be indexed directly (CREATE INDEX fails because the column has no dimensions), so the team creates one expression index per model: it casts the column to that model's length and adds a partial-index WHERE on model_id. Each query repeats the same cast and the same model_id filter, so the planner can use the matching index. When the evaluation ends, the winning model's vectors can move to a fixed vector(n) column.
blocks.title: Worked example
SQL · two models in one column

blocks.text:
• ivfflat and hnsw index at most 2,000 dimensions. Storing longer vectors works; indexing them that way doesn't.
• A vector column without dimensions can't be indexed as it is. Fix the length, or cast in an expression index.
• An expression or partial index serves only queries that repeat its expression and its WHERE condition.
• Every vector(n) value takes 4 bytes per dimension plus 8. Halving the precision halves that.
• Filter values that live only inside the chunk text can't be indexed. Give them their own columns.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text: Question: how much storage does one 1,024-dimension embedding take in a vector(1024) column, and in a halfvec(1024) column? Solution: 4 × 1,024 + 8 = 4,104 bytes as vector, and 2 × 1,024 + 8 = 2,056 bytes as halfvec, before any index.

lessons.title: 2.2.3 · pgvector: index for low latency and less compute
lessons.summary: Match the operator class to the distance operator, choose and tune IVFFlat, HNSW and DiskANN, and read the query plan before you change anything.

blocks.text:
pgvector compares vectors with three distance operators: <-> (Euclidean, L2), <=> (cosine distance) and <#> (negative inner product). An index serves a query only when it was built with the matching operator class: vector_l2_ops for <->, vector_cosine_ops for <=>, vector_ip_ops for <#>. A nearest-neighbour query orders by the distance expression and ends with LIMIT. For vectors normalized to length 1, such as OpenAI embeddings, Learn suggests inner product for best performance.

Without a vector index the search is exact but reads every row (a sequential scan, possibly in parallel). Approximate indexes trade some recall for speed. When possible, load the data before you build the index: the build is faster and the resulting layout is better.
blocks.title: Operators and operator classes

blocks.text: ivfflat and hnsw index at most 2,000 dimensions. DiskANN product quantization (pg_diskann 0.6 and later) is preview, and so is its support for up to 16,000 dimensions.
blocks.title: Approximate index types
rows: fast, little memory; needs a training step on existing rows
lists at build; ivfflat.probes at query time (default 1)
start with lists = rows/1000 (up to 1M rows) and probes = lists/10
slower and more memory; no training, can be built on an empty table
graph index built for very large sets
flexible server feature; install with CREATE EXTENSION pg_diskann CASCADE

blocks.text:
• Read the plan first: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, VERBOSE, BUFFERS) shows whether your index or a sequential scan answers the query, and whether the query ran in parallel. A mismatched operator class or a missing ORDER BY … LIMIT keeps the index out of the plan.
• Tune per query, not per server: SET LOCAL ivfflat.probes, hnsw.ef_search or diskann.l_value_is inside a transaction changes only that transaction. Higher values give better recall but cost more latency and CPU.
• Builds take memory. Raise maintenance_work_mem for the build session and watch pg_stat_progress_create_index.
• Fewer dimensions mean less work. Reduce dimensions, or use half-precision vectors, which also extend indexing to 4,000 dimensions.
blocks.title: Cutting vector compute overhead
SQL · index, tune and check

blocks.text: A catalogue table holds 9 million product embeddings, and the team wants an IVFFlat index as a starting point before it measures recall. Learn's starting values change above 1 million rows: lists becomes the square root of the row count and probes the square root of lists. The square root of 9,000,000 is 3,000, so the index is built WITH (lists = 3000), after the rows are loaded so that k-means has data to train on. The square root of 3,000 is about 55, so queries start with SET LOCAL ivfflat.probes = 55. From there the team raises or lowers probes against a test set, checking recall and latency each time.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
• The index's operator class must match the operator in ORDER BY, or the planner can't use the index.
• Higher probes, ef_search or l_value_is mean better recall but more latency and CPU. Set them with SET LOCAL for the queries that need them.
• Load first, then index: the build is faster and the layout better.
• DiskANN on flexible server comes from the pg_diskann extension, which depends on vector. Allow-list it, then create it with CASCADE.
• DiskANN product quantization is preview.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text: Question: your embeddings are normalized to length 1, and you want the fastest ranking that Learn suggests for them. Which operator do queries use, and which operator class must the index have? Solution: inner product, the <#> operator, with an index built using vector_ip_ops.

lessons.title: 2.2.4 · PostgreSQL: size compute, memory and storage for vector workloads
lessons.summary: Choose a compute tier and size, estimate how much storage the vectors need, and plan for storage that can only grow.

blocks.text:
• Burstable runs on CPU credits. It suits workloads that are idle or below baseline most of the time and isn't meant for production. When the credits run out, the server can become unreachable, and it gets no built-in PgBouncer.
• General Purpose has 4 GiB of memory per vCore and suits most production workloads.
• Memory Optimized has 6.75 to 9.5 GiB per vCore. Choose it when vector indexes and hot data must stay in memory.
You can change the number of vCores up or down after creation.
blocks.title: Compute tiers

blocks.text: Storage only grows: you can increase the size, but you can't shrink it, and the storage type (Premium SSD or Premium SSD v2) is fixed when you create the server. Premium SSD disks go up to 32,767 GiB. Premium SSD v2 has no fixed sizes and goes up to 64 TiB (65,536 GiB). Premium SSD v2 lets you set capacity, IOPS and throughput separately and reaches higher maximums (80,000 IOPS and 1,200 MB/s). Storage autogrow is GA for Premium SSD and preview for Premium SSD v2. A server switches to read-only mode when storage use reaches 95 percent, so Learn recommends alert rules on storage used or storage percent.
blocks.title: Storage

blocks.text: A team plans a corpus of 4 million chunks with 1,536-dimension embeddings. pgvector stores each vector in 4 × dimensions + 8 bytes, so one embedding takes 6,152 bytes and the vectors alone come to about 24.6 GB. The same embeddings as halfvec(1536) take 2 × 1,536 + 8 = 3,080 bytes each, about 12.3 GB. On top of that come the chunk text, the other columns, and every index, including the vector index, which needs memory as well as disk. Because storage can't shrink later and the storage type can't change, the team starts with a size that covers the next growth step, sets an alert on storage percent and turns on autogrow.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
• Storage size goes up only. Getting smaller means dump and restore to a new server.
• Premium SSD disks stop at 32,767 GiB. Premium SSD v2 reaches 64 TiB.
• Memory per vCore is what separates General Purpose (4 GiB) from Memory Optimized (6.75 to 9.5 GiB).
• Storage autogrow on Premium SSD v2 is preview.
• Size for vectors, text and every index, not for the raw embeddings alone.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text: Question: a server was created on Premium SSD, and a year later the team wants Premium SSD v2 for its separate IOPS settings. Can it switch the existing server? Solution: no. The storage type can't be changed after the server is created, so moving to Premium SSD v2 means a new server and a migration.

lessons.title: 2.2.5 · PostgreSQL: vector similarity search and RAG with metadata filters
lessons.summary: Retrieve the chunks a user may see with a filtered similarity query, build a grounded prompt, and keep the cost of each step in view.

blocks.text: Retrieval-augmented generation grounds a model's answer in your data in three steps. Retrieve: query an index or data store for the content most relevant to the question. Augment: combine the question and that grounding data into a prompt. Generate: the model answers from the supplied content, which reduces guessing and lets the answer cite its sources. In PostgreSQL, the retrieve step is a vector query with ordinary WHERE clauses for the metadata (tenant, category, date) that limit it to rows the user may see. Keep fields that improve citations, such as titles and source names, next to the chunks.
blocks.title: What RAG is
How filtered retrieval works

blocks.text: Embeddings can come from your application or from the database. The usual path is to call the embedding model from the application and pass the vector as a query parameter. The azure_ai extension can also call an Azure OpenAI deployment from SQL: its azure_openai.create_embeddings function takes a deployment name and text, after you store the endpoint and key with azure_ai.set_setting or use a system-assigned managed identity. The extension's AI functions, including embedding generation, are labelled preview.
blocks.title: Where the embeddings come from

blocks.text:
import numpy as np
import psycopg
from pgvector.psycopg import register_vector

SQL = """
SELECT c.content, a.title
FROM chunks c JOIN articles a ON a.id = c.article_id
WHERE c.tenant = %(tenant)s AND a.category = ANY(%(cats)s)
ORDER BY c.embedding <=> %(q)s
LIMIT %(k)s
"""


def retrieve(conn: psycopg.Connection, query_vec, tenant, cats, k=5):
    register_vector(conn)  # lets psycopg send numpy arrays as vector values
    params = {"q": np.asarray(query_vec, dtype=np.float32), "tenant": tenant,
              "cats": cats, "k": k}
    return conn.execute(SQL, params).fetchall()


def grounded_prompt(question, rows):
    sources = "\n".join(f"[{i}] {title}: {text}"
                        for i, (text, title) in enumerate(rows, 1))
    return ("Answer only from the numbered sources and cite them as [n]. "
            "If they don't contain the answer, say so.\n\n"
            f"{sources}\n\nQuestion: {question}")
blocks.title: Python · rag_retrieve.py (filtered retrieval, grounded prompt)

blocks.text: A support assistant retrieves the 25 nearest chunks for every question, and long chunks push the prompt past the chat model's token budget, so requests fail or cost far more than planned. Learn's guidance for an exceeded token budget is passage filtering, ranking or summarization. The team lowers k to 6, ranks the candidates and keeps only those that fit a fixed token allowance, and shortens very long chunks when it splits documents. A smaller, better-ranked set of passages also cuts input tokens on every request, one of the costs that RAG adds.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
• azure_ai embedding generation is preview. Embedding in the application is the path that doesn't depend on it.
• With an approximate index the WHERE clause runs after the scan, so check how many rows a filtered query really returns.
• RAG quality depends on chunking, the embedding model and the search configuration, not only on the prompt.
• Store titles or source names with the chunks, or the answer can't cite where a fact came from.
• Prefer Microsoft Entra ID to API keys for the services a production RAG app calls.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text: Question: compared with sending the question straight to the model, which three costs does a RAG request add? Solution: the retrieval round trip and its compute, an embedding of the question at query time (on top of embedding the content at indexing time), and more input tokens, because the retrieved passages go into the prompt.

lessons.title: 2.2.6 · PostgreSQL: optimize connections for throughput and latency
lessons.summary: Understand what each connection costs, budget connections against the server's limit, and pool them in the application and in the built-in PgBouncer.

blocks.text: Every PostgreSQL connection, idle or active, uses server resources, and opening one is expensive. Many short-lived connections (under 60 seconds) drive CPU up, because the server spends time connecting and disconnecting. max_connections defaults to a value that depends on the compute SKU, for example 859 on a 2-vCore General Purpose server, and the server reserves 15 of those for replication and monitoring. Changing max_connections needs a server restart. Learn advises against raising it and recommends PgBouncer in transaction mode instead. When clients exceed the limit, they get FATAL: sorry, too many clients already.
blocks.title: Why connections cost

blocks.text:
• Pool connections: Learn's pooling guidance is to keep a cache of connections and hand them out again instead of opening a new one per request. The sample below does this inside each process with psycopg_pool.
• Pool at the server: the built-in PgBouncer listens on port 6432 at the same host name (direct connections use 5432) and supports Microsoft Entra authentication. You switch it on with the pgbouncer.enabled server parameter, and no restart is needed. It can multiplex up to 10,000 client connections.
• Limits: there's no PgBouncer on the Burstable tier. A restart, scale operation or failover restarts PgBouncer, so clients must reconnect. In transaction mode, only protocol-level prepared statements are supported, and only after the max_prepared_statements parameter is set above 0. Statement mode can't be used with prepared statements at all.
The three pool modes are session (one server connection for the whole client session), transaction (one connection for each transaction) and statement (one connection for each statement).
blocks.title: Pooling in the app and at the server

blocks.text: pool_mode sets when a server connection can go to another client. These parameters appear on the Parameters pane only after pgbouncer.enabled is set to true.
blocks.title: Built-in PgBouncer parameters

blocks.text:
import os

import psycopg
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from psycopg_pool import ConnectionPool

credential = DefaultAzureCredential()
SCOPE = os.environ["PG_ENTRA_SCOPE"]  # the ossrdbms-aad .default scope


class EntraConnection(psycopg.Connection):
    @classmethod
    def connect(cls, conninfo="", **kwargs):
        kwargs["password"] = credential.get_token(SCOPE).token
        return super().connect(conninfo, **kwargs)


conninfo = (f"host={os.environ['PGHOST']} port=6432 dbname=kb "
            f"user={os.environ['PGUSER']} sslmode=require")
pool = ConnectionPool(conninfo, connection_class=EntraConnection,
                      min_size=1, max_size=5, open=True)

with pool.connection() as conn:
    rows = conn.execute(
        "SELECT id, title FROM articles WHERE tenant = %s LIMIT 20", ("t-17",)
    ).fetchall()
blocks.title: Python · pg_pool.py (Entra token for each new connection)

blocks.text: A reporting API runs on 12 App Service instances, each with an application pool that may open up to 80 direct connections, against a General Purpose server with 4 vCores. Learn's table gives that size 1,718 maximum connections, of which 1,703 are for users once the 15 reserved slots are taken out. The pools together can open 12 × 80 = 960 connections, which fits today. The plan is to grow to 24 instances, and 24 × 80 = 1,920 would not fit. The budget per instance is 1,703 / 24, about 70, before anything else connects, and admin sessions, migrations and monitoring tools need room too. The team caps each pool at 60, so 24 instances open at most 1,440 connections, and it writes the cap into the scale-out plan so that the next growth step is checked against the same budget.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
• max_connections includes slots the server reserves. Check reserved_connections and superuser_reserved_connections before you budget.
• A new max_connections value needs a restart, and Learn advises against raising it.
• A restart, scale operation or failover restarts PgBouncer too, so clients must reconnect.
• The PgBouncer parameters stay hidden on the Parameters pane until pgbouncer.enabled is set to true.
• Enforcing TLS on the server with require_secure_transport also enforces it for the built-in PgBouncer.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text: Question: during a traffic burst, some clients connected through the built-in PgBouncer are disconnected after their queries wait about two minutes without ever reaching the server. Which PgBouncer setting is at work? Solution: pgbouncer.query_wait_timeout, which defaults to 120 seconds. A query that isn't assigned a server connection within that time gets its client disconnected.

lessons.title: 2.3.1 · Azure Managed Redis: caching, expiration and invalidation
lessons.summary: Settle the creation-time choices, use cache-aside with expiration, keep the cache consistent on writes, and watch memory before it runs out.

blocks.text:
Azure Managed Redis is the current service, built on Redis Enterprise software. Azure Cache for Redis is retiring: its Basic, Standard and Premium tiers on 30 September 2028, and its Enterprise and Enterprise Flash tiers on 31 March 2027. The tiers are Memory Optimized (8:1 memory to vCPU), Balanced (4:1), Compute Optimized (2:1) and Flash Optimized, which moves less-used data from RAM to NVMe storage. Some large SKUs are preview.

Clients connect over TLS on port 10000 (Azure Cache for Redis used 6380). New caches have Microsoft Entra ID enabled and access keys disabled, and Learn recommends Entra ID with managed identities.

Settle these at creation:
• Clustering policy. OSS is the default and the fastest, but the client must speak the Redis Cluster API. Enterprise gives a single endpoint. Non-clustered is preview and available only for caches up to 25 GB. OSS and Enterprise can't be changed in place.
• Modules (Redis 7.4). RediSearch, RedisJSON, RedisBloom and RedisTimeSeries must be selected when you create the cache and can't be added later. Flash Optimized supports only RedisJSON.
blocks.title: What it is and the choices you make at creation

blocks.text:
Cache-aside: read the key, and on a miss load from the data store, write the value to the cache and return it. The pattern suits caches that don't provide read-through or write-through themselves, so your code does the loading. Keep the cache consistent on writes in one of two ways:
• Invalidate on write: update the store, then delete the key, and the next read repopulates it. The write path stays simple, but a reader may briefly miss or see old data.
• Write-through: update the store and the cache in the same operation. Readers see the new value straight away, at the cost of more work on every write. Use it only for read-heavy paths that need read-after-write freshness.
Cache-aside never guarantees consistency. Another process can change the store at any moment, so pair it with expiration.

Expiration and memory: set a TTL on cached keys (SET with EX, or EXPIRE). Expiration removes keys proactively instead of waiting for memory pressure. Too short a TTL wastes the cache, and too long a TTL serves stale data and fills memory. The default eviction policy on Azure Managed Redis is volatile-lru, which evicts only keys that have a TTL, so a cache full of keys without TTLs evicts nothing.
blocks.title: Caching, expiration and invalidation

blocks.text:
import json
import os

import redis
from redis_entraid.cred_provider import create_from_default_azure_credential

# REDIS_SCOPE holds the Azure Managed Redis .default token scope
provider = create_from_default_azure_credential((os.environ["REDIS_SCOPE"],))
r = redis.Redis(host=os.environ["REDIS_HOST"], port=10000, ssl=True,
                credential_provider=provider, decode_responses=True)


def get_product(product_id, load_from_db):
    key = f"product:{product_id}"
    cached = r.get(key)
    if cached is not None:
        return json.loads(cached)
    product = load_from_db(product_id)
    r.set(key, json.dumps(product), ex=600)  # expire after ten minutes
    return product


def save_product(product, write_to_db):
    write_to_db(product)
    r.delete(f"product:{product['id']}")  # invalidate after the write succeeds
blocks.title: Python · redis_cache.py (Entra ID, cache-aside, invalidation)

blocks.text:
A private cache lives in the memory of one process. It's fast, but each application instance holds its own copy, so instances can answer the same query differently as the data changes. A shared cache, such as Azure Managed Redis, sits in a separate service, so every instance sees the same cached data and the cache scales on its own. It's slower to reach than local memory and adds a service to run.

When several instances modify the same cached data, choose a concurrency approach. Optimistic: check that the value hasn't changed since you read it, then write; suited to infrequent updates and rare collisions. Pessimistic: lock the data while you update it; it prevents collisions but can block other instances, so keep it for short operations where collisions are likely.
blocks.title: Private and shared caches, and concurrency

blocks.text: A pricing API runs on eight instances, and each instance keeps the exchange-rate table in an in-process dictionary that it refreshes every 15 minutes. Because each copy refreshes at a different moment, two calls a second apart can quote different prices. Moving the table into Azure Managed Redis as a shared cache gives every instance the same view: one key holds the table with a TTL, a miss reloads it from the rates service, and all eight instances read that one copy. The cost is a network round trip per read instead of a memory lookup, which this API accepts in exchange for consistent quotes.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
• With Redis 7.4, modules are chosen when you create the cache and can't be added afterwards, and OSS and Enterprise clustering can't be changed in place. Plan module and policy choices before you create it.
• Port 10000 with TLS. Prefer Entra ID, because access keys are disabled on new caches.
• Watch Used Memory Percentage, not raw Used Memory, and scale up when it stays above 75%.
• A TTL that's too short wastes the cache. One that's too long serves stale data and fills memory.
• A cache is a copy. Don't treat it as the authoritative store for critical data.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text: Question: several instances occasionally update a shared feature-settings value in the cache, and two updates rarely collide. Which concurrency approach does Learn suggest, and why not the other? Solution: optimistic concurrency, which checks that the value hasn't changed since it was read before writing it. It suits infrequent updates with unlikely collisions. Pessimistic locking prevents collisions but can block other instances and hurt scalability, so Learn keeps it for short operations where collisions are likely.

lessons.title: 2.3.2 · Azure Managed Redis: vector indexing and similarity search
lessons.summary: Plan a cache that can index vectors, build a RediSearch index with FLAT or HNSW, run KNN queries with metadata filters, and use the cache for semantic caching.

blocks.text: Vector search in Azure Managed Redis needs the RediSearch module, which you must enable when you create the cache: modules can't be added later, and you can't load or update modules yourself. RediSearch is available on the Memory Optimized, Balanced and Compute Optimized tiers, and not on Flash Optimized. It isn't supported with the OSS clustering policy. Learn's pages differ on which policy to use instead: the vector search overview, the clustering page and the quickstart allow Enterprise or the preview Non-clustered policy, while the Well-Architected guide says RediSearch requires Enterprise and the NoEviction eviction policy. The GA path is Enterprise with NoEviction. Size the cache for the vector data and the index overhead, and store metadata such as document ID, title, source, category, timestamp, tenant ID or access-control fields next to each vector.
blocks.title: What you plan at creation

blocks.text: Vectors can live in hashes or in JSON documents. Index types: FLAT is an exact brute-force index for smaller sets, and HNSW is an approximate graph index for larger sets where latency matters more than an exhaustive search. Distance metrics are L2, COSINE and IP (inner product). Cosine is a common choice for text embeddings, but the right metric depends on the model and on how its vectors are normalized. Use one embedding model consistently for an index, with the dimensions and metric that model needs. A KNN query returns the top K most similar vectors, and hybrid queries combine a metadata filter with the vector search, for example only the documents the current user may see.
blocks.title: How vector search works

blocks.text:
import numpy as np
from redis.commands.search.field import TagField, TextField, VectorField
from redis.commands.search.index_definition import IndexDefinition, IndexType
from redis.commands.search.query import Query

DIM = 1536


def create_index(r):
    fields = (
        TagField("tenant"),
        TextField("body"),
        VectorField("vec", "HNSW",
                    {"TYPE": "FLOAT32", "DIM": DIM, "DISTANCE_METRIC": "COSINE"}),
    )
    r.ft("idx:docs").create_index(
        fields, definition=IndexDefinition(prefix=["doc:"], index_type=IndexType.HASH))


def add(r, doc_id, tenant, body, vec):
    r.hset(f"doc:{doc_id}", mapping={
        "tenant": tenant, "body": body,
        "vec": np.asarray(vec, dtype=np.float32).tobytes()})


def knn(r, tenant, vec, k=4):
    expr = "(@tenant:{%s})=>[KNN %d @vec $v AS dist]" % (tenant, k)
    q = (Query(expr)
         .sort_by("dist").return_fields("body", "dist").dialect(2))
    blob = np.asarray(vec, dtype=np.float32).tobytes()
    return r.ft("idx:docs").search(q, query_params={"v": blob}).docs
blocks.title: Python · redis_vectors.py (redis-py search commands)

blocks.text: Semantic caching reuses an earlier LLM answer when a new prompt means the same as an old one. The app embeds the prompt with the cache's embedding model, searches the cached prompt embeddings, and returns the cached response when the closest entry is within the threshold and belongs to the right partition. On a miss it calls the model and stores the prompt, response, embedding, metadata and a TTL. There are two implementation paths. In your own code, RedisVL's SemanticCache gives you lookup, storage, TTLs, metadata, filters and a COSINE-distance threshold. At a gateway, Azure API Management's llm-semantic-cache-lookup and llm-semantic-cache-store policies use Azure Managed Redis as the external cache.
blocks.title: Semantic caching

blocks.text: Four internal apps, each owned by a different team, call the same chat deployment through Azure API Management, and the platform team wants one semantic cache in front of the model without changing any app's code. That points to the gateway path: configure Azure Managed Redis as the external cache and add the lookup policy before the backend call and the store policy after the response. An app-level RedisVL cache would need code in all four apps. One trap remains when the platform team copies settings across: RedisVL's distance_threshold is in Redis COSINE distance units from 0 to 2, while API Management's score-threshold runs from 0.0 to 1.0, so a value can't be moved between them without validating it.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
• OSS clustering doesn't support RediSearch.
• Modules can't be added to a cache after creation, and you can't load or update them yourself.
• Size the cache for the vectors plus the index overhead, not for the raw vectors alone.
• Store the metadata you filter on and cite next to each vector.
• For a semantic cache, track hit rate, lookup latency and the distribution of match distances before you change the threshold.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text: Question: to keep costs down, a team wants vector search on a Flash Optimized Azure Managed Redis cache. Will it work? Solution: no. RediSearch, which vector search needs, isn't available on the Flash Optimized tier (Flash Optimized supports only RedisJSON). Choose Memory Optimized, Balanced or Compute Optimized.

lessons.title: Lab · Vector search in Cosmos DB for NoSQL
lessons.summary: Create an account, a container with a vector policy and your own data role from the Azure CLI, then load a few vectors from Python and rank them with VectorDistance.

blocks.text:
Goal: a working vector container that you query passwordless from Python. You need an Azure subscription where you can create resources and assign Cosmos DB data roles, the Azure CLI signed in with az login, and Python with the azure-cosmos and azure-identity packages.

To keep the lab free of an embedding model, the items carry hand-made 4-dimension vectors and the container uses a flat index, which is exact and works from the first item. A real app stores model embeddings, such as 1,536 dimensions, and picks quantizedFlat or diskANN, which need at least 1,000 vectors before they take effect. Delete the resource group at the end so nothing keeps costing money.
blocks.title: Goal and prerequisites

blocks.text:
RG=rg-vector-lab
ACCT=cosmos-vector-lab-$RANDOM   # account names are global
az group create --name $RG --location westeurope
az cosmosdb create --resource-group $RG --name $ACCT
az cosmosdb sql database create --resource-group $RG --account-name $ACCT \
    --name kb

# Look up the built-in data role by name, then assign it to yourself
ROLE_ID=$(az cosmosdb sql role definition list \
    --resource-group $RG --account-name $ACCT \
    --query "[?roleName=='Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor'].id" -o tsv)
ME=$(az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv)
az cosmosdb sql role assignment create --resource-group $RG \
    --account-name $ACCT --role-definition-id "$ROLE_ID" \
    --principal-id "$ME" --scope "/"

blocks.text:
import os

from azure.cosmos import CosmosClient
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential

client = CosmosClient(os.environ["COSMOS_ENDPOINT"],
                      credential=DefaultAzureCredential())
notes = client.get_database_client("kb").get_container_client("notes")

items = [
    ("n1", "billing", "Invoices are issued monthly", [0.9, 0.1, 0.0, 0.1]),
    ("n2", "billing", "Refunds take five days", [0.8, 0.2, 0.1, 0.0]),
    ("n3", "billing", "Office opening hours", [0.0, 0.1, 0.9, 0.3]),
    ("n4", "support", "Reset a password", [0.1, 0.9, 0.1, 0.0]),
]
for item_id, topic, text, vec in items:
    notes.upsert_item({"id": item_id, "topic": topic, "text": text,
                       "embedding": vec})

sql = ("SELECT TOP 2 c.id, c.text, VectorDistance(c.embedding, @q) AS score "
       "FROM c ORDER BY VectorDistance(c.embedding, @q)")
query_vec = [0.85, 0.15, 0.05, 0.05]
for row in notes.query_items(query=sql, partition_key="billing",
                             parameters=[{"name": "@q", "value": query_vec}]):
    print(row["id"], row["text"], round(row["score"], 3))
print("RU:", notes.client_connection.last_response_headers["x-ms-request-charge"])
blocks.title: Python · step 3: lab_vectors.py (load and rank)

blocks.text:
• The script prints n1 and n2, the two billing notes whose vectors point the same way as the query vector, with the closest first. With cosine as the distance function, a higher score means more similar. n3 is in the same partition but points elsewhere, and n4 is in another partition, so neither appears.
• Run the query again and compare the RU charge: the same query on the same data costs the same each time.
• Remove TOP 2 and the charge can rise, though on four items the difference may be small. Remove ORDER BY instead and the two rows are no longer guaranteed to be the closest.
• If upsert_item fails with 403, the role assignment hasn't reached the account yet. Wait a few minutes and run the script again.

lessons.title: Lab · Retrieval-augmented generation with pgvector
lessons.summary: Create a flexible server, enable pgvector, sign in with Microsoft Entra ID, then store a few vectors, index them and run the filtered retrieval step of a RAG pipeline from Python.

blocks.text:
Goal: the retrieval half of a RAG pipeline on Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server, from an empty subscription to a grounded prompt. You need an Azure subscription, the Azure CLI signed in with az login, permission to add yourself as a Microsoft Entra administrator on the server, and Python with psycopg, pgvector, numpy and azure-identity.

The lab uses a Burstable server because it's cheap and idle most of the time. That's the development choice: production servers use General Purpose or Memory Optimized. The rows carry hand-made 4-dimension vectors so no embedding model is needed. In a real pipeline the vectors come from an embedding model, and the question is embedded with the same model. Delete the resource group at the end.

PG=pgvector-lab-$RANDOM          # server names are global
MYIP="<your public IP address>"
az group create --name $RG --location westeurope
az postgres flexible-server create --resource-group $RG --name $PG \
    --location westeurope --admin-user labadmin \
    --admin-password "<a strong password>" \
    --tier Burstable --sku-name Standard_B1ms --storage-size 32 \
    --public-access $MYIP

    --server-name $PG --name azure.extensions --value vector

import os

import numpy as np
import psycopg
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from pgvector.psycopg import register_vector

SCOPE = os.environ["PG_ENTRA_SCOPE"]  # the ossrdbms-aad .default scope
token = DefaultAzureCredential().get_token(SCOPE).token
rows = [
    ("billing", "Invoices are issued monthly", [0.9, 0.1, 0.0, 0.1]),
    ("billing", "Refunds take five days", [0.8, 0.2, 0.1, 0.0]),
    ("billing", "Office opening hours", [0.0, 0.1, 0.9, 0.3]),
    ("support", "Reset a password", [0.1, 0.9, 0.1, 0.0]),
]

with psycopg.connect(host=os.environ["PGHOST"], dbname="postgres",
                     user=os.environ["PGUSER"], password=token,
                     sslmode="require") as conn:
    conn.execute("CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector")
    register_vector(conn)
    conn.execute("CREATE TABLE notes (id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, "
                 "topic text NOT NULL, body text NOT NULL, "
                 "embedding vector(4) NOT NULL)")
    for topic, body, vec in rows:
        conn.execute("INSERT INTO notes (topic, body, embedding) "
                     "VALUES (%s, %s, %s)",
                     (topic, body, np.asarray(vec, dtype=np.float32)))
    conn.execute("CREATE INDEX notes_topic ON notes (topic)")
    conn.execute("CREATE INDEX notes_hnsw ON notes "
                 "USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)")
    conn.commit()

blocks.text:
import os

import numpy as np
import psycopg
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from pgvector.psycopg import register_vector

SCOPE = os.environ["PG_ENTRA_SCOPE"]  # the ossrdbms-aad .default scope
SQL = ("SELECT body, embedding <=> %s AS distance FROM notes "
       "WHERE topic = %s ORDER BY embedding <=> %s LIMIT 2")

token = DefaultAzureCredential().get_token(SCOPE).token
question = "When do I get my money back?"
q = np.asarray([0.8, 0.2, 0.05, 0.0], dtype=np.float32)  # stand-in embedding

with psycopg.connect(host=os.environ["PGHOST"], dbname="postgres",
                     user=os.environ["PGUSER"], password=token,
                     sslmode="require") as conn:
    register_vector(conn)
    hits = conn.execute(SQL, (q, "billing", q)).fetchall()
    plan = conn.execute("EXPLAIN " + SQL, (q, "billing", q)).fetchall()

sources = "\n".join(f"[{i}] {body}" for i, (body, _) in enumerate(hits, 1))
print("Answer only from the numbered sources and cite them as [n].\n"
      f"{sources}\n\nQuestion: {question}")
print("\n".join(line for (line,) in plan))
blocks.title: Python · step 4: lab_ask.py (filtered retrieval, grounded prompt)

blocks.text:
• The prompt lists the two billing notes, refunds first, because their vectors are closest to the stand-in question vector. The password note never appears, because the WHERE clause keeps retrieval to the billing topic.
• The distance column is the cosine distance from <=>, which runs from 0 to 2, so smaller values mean more similar.
• Read the EXPLAIN output with Learn's checklist: was an index used, and which one? On a table of four rows the planner can choose a plain scan, so repeat the experiment after loading more rows before you judge the index.
• If the connection is refused or times out, check that the firewall rule holds your current IP address and that you were added as a Microsoft Entra administrator.

lessons.title: 3.1 · Azure Service Bus: queues, topics, sessions and dead-lettering
lessons.summary: Queue back-end work reliably: send and receive with the Python SDK, settle messages correctly, use sessions, duplicate detection and scheduling, fan out with topics and rules, and handle the dead-letter queue.

blocks.text:
Service Bus is a message broker for enterprise messaging. A message carries data under a contract between sender and receiver, which is why Service Bus suits transactional back-end work. Event Grid, by contrast, routes lightweight notifications that something happened, and Event Hubs ingests streams of telemetry.

A queue hands each message to one of several competing consumers, in roughly first-in, first-out order. A topic gives a copy of each message to every subscription whose rules match. Consumers read from the subscriptions, never from the topic itself, and each subscription behaves like its own queue.

The Basic tier offers queues only. Topics and subscriptions, sessions and duplicate detection need the Standard or Premium tier.
blocks.title: What Service Bus is

blocks.text:
• Peek-lock (the default in the Python SDK) is two-stage. The broker locks the message and hands it over, then your code settles it: complete (done), abandon (unlock it now for redelivery), defer (set it aside, to be fetched later by sequence number) or dead-letter (move it to the dead-letter queue with a reason). If the lock expires first, the message becomes available again. The lock lasts 1 minute by default and at most 5 minutes, so long work renews it with renew_message_lock or an AutoLockRenewer. A crash before complete means redelivery, which makes this at-least-once processing.
• Receive-and-delete marks the message consumed as soon as it's handed over. A crash loses the message, which makes this at-most-once processing.
• peek_messages only browses: a peeked message isn't locked or removed, and it can't be completed, deferred or dead-lettered.
Settle on the same receiver and connection that received the message. Closing the receiver before settling leaves the message locked until its lock expires, and then it is redelivered. The service's 10-minute idle timeout also releases the lock.
blocks.title: How it works: receive modes and settlement

blocks.text:
Every queue and every subscription has its own dead-letter queue (DLQ), at <queue>/$deadletterqueue or <topic>/Subscriptions/<sub> followed by /$deadletterqueue. Messages land there for several reasons:
• MaxDeliveryCountExceeded: the delivery count passed the entity's maximum, 10 by default. Every abandon, and every lock that runs out before settlement, adds one to the count.
• TTLExpiredException: the message expired while dead-lettering on expiration was enabled on the entity. With that option off, expired messages are simply dropped.
• A subscription filter threw an error while dead-lettering on filter evaluation exceptions was enabled.
• Your code called dead_letter_message with its own reason and error description. Put the exception type in the reason and the details in the description.
Nothing cleans the DLQ automatically: messages stay until you receive and complete them. Read it by passing sub_queue set to the DEAD_LETTER value of ServiceBusSubQueue, and look at each message's dead_letter_reason and dead_letter_error_description. A message that can't be auto-forwarded goes to the transfer dead-letter queue of the source entity instead.
blocks.title: How it works: the dead-letter queue

blocks.text:
Sessions give ordered, exclusive processing of related messages. A sender sets session_id on each message, and once sessions are enabled on a queue or subscription, clients must send with a session ID and receive by accepting a session.
• A session receiver holds an exclusive lock on every message with that session ID, including messages that arrive later. Only one receiver can hold a session at a time. Renew the session lock with receiver.session.renew_lock, or register the session with an AutoLockRenewer.
• In Python, get_queue_receiver and get_subscription_receiver need a session_id for a session-enabled entity: either a specific ID, or NEXT_AVAILABLE_SESSION to accept whichever session is free. Leaving session_id unset is only for entities without sessions.
• Session state: receiver.session.set_state stores an opaque value of up to one message's size, and get_state returns it (None if nothing was set). It lets another processor resume the work. The state stays until you clear it, even after every message in the session is consumed, and it counts towards the entity's storage quota.
• Sequence numbers fix the order in which messages are retrieved, not the order in which they finish processing. Two consumers can complete messages out of order, and sessions are what preserve processing order.
• A dead-lettered session message that is moved back to the queue gets a new enqueue time and sequence number, so it loses its original place in the session's order.
blocks.title: Sessions

blocks.text:
• Duplicate detection tracks the application-controlled MessageId of every message sent during a history window: 10 minutes by default, from 20 seconds to 7 days. A send whose MessageId is already logged is reported as accepted and the copy is dropped. Only the MessageId is compared. Derive it from the business operation, such as an order number plus a step name, so that a retry repeats it. Scheduled messages count too, and on a partitioned entity uniqueness is MessageId+PartitionKey.
• Time to live: a message sent without one takes the entity's default. A locked message isn't affected by expiry, and the broker may remove expired messages lazily.
• Scheduling: the sender's schedule_messages returns the sequence numbers of the scheduled messages, and cancel_scheduled_messages with those numbers calls them off while they are still pending. Setting scheduled_enqueue_time_utc on a message is the other way to delay it.
blocks.title: Duplicates, expiry and scheduling

blocks.text:
Every new subscription starts with a default rule, $Default, whose filter is the true filter, so the subscription receives everything until you replace that rule.
• A SQL filter evaluates a SQL-like expression over user properties and system properties (sys. prefix), including comparisons and LIKE patterns.
• A correlation filter matches exact property values, and its string comparison is case-sensitive. Learn prefers correlation filters where possible, because SQL filters lower throughput.
• Filters never read the message body.
Rules without actions combine with OR into one copy of a matching message, while each matching rule with an action produces its own copy.
blocks.title: Topics and rules

blocks.text:
import json
import os
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.servicebus import (AutoLockRenewer, ServiceBusClient, ServiceBusMessage,
                              ServiceBusSubQueue)

FQDN = os.environ["SERVICEBUS_FQDN"]  # <namespace>.servicebus.windows.net
SUPPORTED = {1, 2}
credential = DefaultAzureCredential()


def enqueue(shipment_id, version=2):
    body = json.dumps({"shipment": shipment_id, "v": version})
    with ServiceBusClient(FQDN, credential) as client:
        with client.get_queue_sender("shipments") as sender:
            msg = ServiceBusMessage(body, message_id=f"ship-{shipment_id}")
            sender.send_messages(msg)
            check_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc) + timedelta(hours=2)
            return sender.schedule_messages(ServiceBusMessage(body), check_at)


def work():
    renewer = AutoLockRenewer(max_lock_renewal_duration=600)
    with ServiceBusClient(FQDN, credential) as client:
        with client.get_queue_receiver("shipments", max_wait_time=30,
                                       auto_lock_renewer=renewer) as receiver:
            for msg in receiver:
                job = json.loads(str(msg))
                if job["v"] not in SUPPORTED:
                    receiver.dead_letter_message(
                        msg, reason="UnsupportedVersion",
                        error_description=f"version {job['v']}")
                    continue
                print("dispatching", job["shipment"])
                receiver.complete_message(msg)


def peek_dead_letters():
    with ServiceBusClient(FQDN, credential) as client:
        with client.get_queue_receiver("shipments",
                                       sub_queue=ServiceBusSubQueue.DEAD_LETTER) as dlq:
            for msg in dlq.peek_messages(max_message_count=20):
                print(msg.sequence_number, msg.dead_letter_reason, msg.delivery_count)
blocks.title: Python · shipments.py (send, schedule, receive, settle, peek the DLQ)

blocks.text:
import os

from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.servicebus import NEXT_AVAILABLE_SESSION, ServiceBusClient

FQDN = os.environ["SERVICEBUS_FQDN"]


def process_next_cart():
    with ServiceBusClient(FQDN, DefaultAzureCredential()) as client:
        with client.get_queue_receiver("cart-events", max_wait_time=20,
                                       session_id=NEXT_AVAILABLE_SESSION) as receiver:
            session = receiver.session
            handled = int(session.get_state() or b"0")  # resume after a crash
            for msg in receiver:
                print(session.session_id, msg.sequence_number, str(msg))
                receiver.complete_message(msg)
                handled += 1
                session.set_state(str(handled))
            session.set_state(None)  # clear the state once the cart is finished
blocks.title: Python · carts.py (session receiver with session state)

blocks.text:
import os

from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.servicebus.management import (CorrelationRuleFilter,
                                         ServiceBusAdministrationClient, SqlRuleFilter)

admin = ServiceBusAdministrationClient(os.environ["SERVICEBUS_FQDN"],
                                       DefaultAzureCredential())

admin.delete_rule("payments", "mobile-desk", "$Default")  # drop the catch-all rule
admin.create_rule("payments", "mobile-desk", "mobile-only",
                  filter=CorrelationRuleFilter(properties={"channel": "mobile"}))

admin.delete_rule("payments", "refunds", "$Default")
admin.create_rule("payments", "refunds", "refund-labels",
                  filter=SqlRuleFilter("sys.label LIKE 'refund-%'"))
blocks.title: Python · rules.py (replace the default rule on two subscriptions)

blocks.text: A billing worker sometimes receives a payment message before the order message it depends on. Rather than abandoning it and burning delivery attempts, the worker calls defer_message and records the payment's sequence number. When the order arrives, it fetches the deferred payment with receive_deferred_messages using that sequence number, processes it and completes it. The deferred message stayed in the queue the whole time, but no ordinary receive could have returned it.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
• A deferred message is reachable only by its sequence number. Record the number when you defer, or the message is hard to get back.
• Session state outlives the session's messages. Clear it with set_state(None) when the work is finished, or it keeps counting against the storage quota.
• Moving a dead-lettered session message back to its queue gives it a new sequence number, so its original place in the session's order is gone.
• Duplicate detection covers scheduled messages too: of a scheduled send and a plain send that share a MessageId, only the first is kept.
• Removing an app's Service Bus role doesn't cut it off at once. Its token stays valid until it expires (24 hours by default) or the app restarts.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text:
Question: a receiver pulls messages, puts them in an in-memory list and completes them twenty minutes later, and the complete calls start failing. Why?
Solution: first, the lock lasts 1 minute by default and 5 minutes at most unless it is renewed, so twenty minutes later every lock has expired and the messages have been handed out again. Second, the service closes a connection that stays idle for 10 minutes, which also releases the locks. Settle promptly on the same receiver, and renew locks if processing is long.

lessons.title: 3.2 · Azure Event Grid: custom events, filters, retries and dead-lettering
lessons.summary: Publish custom events, route them with event type, subject and advanced filters, and understand system topics, retries, delayed delivery and dead-lettering, naming the delivery model each time.

blocks.text:
Event Grid routes events, which are lightweight notifications that something happened, to subscribers that react to them. Compare Service Bus, which carries high-value messages for transactional work, and Event Hubs, which ingests streams. Sources come in two kinds:
• System topics carry events published by Azure services such as Storage. Only the Azure service can publish to one, so it has no endpoint or keys of its own.
• Custom topics carry your application's events, published to the topic's endpoint. A custom topic accepts the CloudEvents v1.0 schema or the Event Grid schema, chosen with the input schema when you create the topic. CloudEvents is the open, interoperable choice.

Event Grid comes in two models, and facts differ between them:
• Event Grid Basic: system topics, custom topics and domains, with push delivery only. The retry and dead-letter defaults below belong to this model.
• Event Grid Namespaces: namespace topics with pull delivery (consumers receive and then acknowledge, release or reject) as well as push delivery.
In Python, EventGridPublisherClient sends to both models (add namespace_topic= for a namespace), and EventGridConsumerClient handles namespace pull delivery. Authenticate with a topic access key (AzureKeyCredential) or Microsoft Entra ID (DefaultAzureCredential).
blocks.title: What Event Grid is

blocks.text:
• Event Grid allows only one system topic per source, such as a storage account, and creates it in the source's Azure subscription, usually in the source's resource group and region. For events at Azure subscription scope it uses the Default-EventGrid resource group in West US 2.
• Creating an event subscription directly on an Azure resource creates a system topic named <resource>-<GUID>, which is deleted automatically with its last event subscription. A system topic you create explicitly keeps its name and stays until you delete it. Learn recommends creating the system topic first, and the portal always does.
• If an Azure policy blocks the system topic resource, events still flow, but you lose the topic's metrics and diagnostics.
blocks.title: How it works: system topics

blocks.text:
By default a subscription receives every event type its source emits. Three kinds of filter narrow it:
• Event types: includedEventTypes lists the types to deliver.
• Subject: subjectBeginsWith and subjectEndsWith compare a prefix or a suffix of the event's subject, such as a container path or a file extension. Give custom events subjects that are easy to filter on.
• Advanced filters compare a key, which can be event data such as data.sizeMb or, in the CloudEvents schema, attributes such as source or eventtype, against values with an operator: NumberGreaterThan, NumberInRange, StringBeginsWith, StringIn, IsNullOrUndefined and others. Values listed in one filter combine with OR, separate filters combine with AND, and string comparisons ignore case. Arrays need advanced filtering on arrays switched on for the subscription. If the key is missing from the event, most operators evaluate as not matched, but NumberNotIn and StringNotIn match, and IsNullOrUndefined evaluates to true.
Limits: 25 advanced filters and 25 filter values across all filters of one subscription, 512 characters per string value, and no keys that contain a dot.
blocks.title: How it works: filtering an event subscription

blocks.text:
Delivery is at least once and not ordered, so make handlers idempotent and order-tolerant. Only 200 to 204 responses count as success. Event Grid waits 30 seconds for a response, then retries with exponential backoff (10 s, 30 s, 1 min, 5 min, 10 min, 30 min, 1 h, 3 h, 6 h, then every 12 hours up to 24 hours) with some randomization.

Each subscription's retry policy has two limits, and whichever runs out first ends delivery:
• maximum delivery attempts, 1 to 30, default 30
• event time to live, 1 to 1,440 minutes, default 1,440 (24 hours)
The time to live is checked only at the next scheduled attempt.

Some errors are never retried: 400 and 413, plus 403 for Azure resource endpoints and 401 and 403 for webhooks. Dead-lettering is off by default. Without it, those events and events that exhaust their retries are dropped. Turn it on by giving the subscription a Blob Storage container as its dead-letter location. Writes happen about five minutes after the last attempt, and if the storage location stays unavailable for four hours the event is dropped.

Three more delivery features:
• Delayed delivery: when deliveries to an endpoint keep failing, Event Grid delays retries and new deliveries to it, in some cases for several hours, to protect the endpoint and itself.
• Output batching is off by default, so each request carries an array with one event. Setting max events per batch (1 to 5,000) or a preferred batch size (1 to 1,024 KB) turns it on.
• Custom delivery properties add up to 10 HTTP headers to delivered events, each value at most 4,096 bytes, for webhooks, Service Bus, Event Hubs and Relay Hybrid Connections.
blocks.title: How it works: delivery, retries and dead-lettering (Event Grid Basic push delivery)

blocks.text:
A webhook endpoint must prove that it wants events before it receives any.
• Event Grid schema: Event Grid sends a SubscriptionValidationEvent. The endpoint either returns the validationCode in its response or calls the validationUrl, which stays valid for 10 minutes.
• CloudEvents v1.0 delivery uses CloudEvents abuse protection instead: an HTTP OPTIONS request with a WebHook-Request-Origin header, which the endpoint answers with WebHook-Allowed-Origin (and WebHook-Allowed-Rate).
Azure Functions with the Event Grid trigger, Logic Apps and Azure Automation webhooks handle validation for you.
blocks.title: How it works: webhook validation

blocks.text:
import os

from azure.core.credentials import AzureKeyCredential
from azure.core.messaging import CloudEvent
from azure.eventgrid import EventGridConsumerClient, EventGridPublisherClient
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential

# Event Grid Basic custom topic (CloudEvents input schema), access key auth
publisher = EventGridPublisherClient(os.environ["EG_TOPIC_ENDPOINT"],
                                     AzureKeyCredential(os.environ["EG_TOPIC_KEY"]))
publisher.send([CloudEvent(
    source="/apps/fleet", type="Fleet.Vehicle.Serviced",
    subject="depots/north/van-17", data={"odometerKm": 48210, "depot": "north"})])

# Event Grid Namespaces: pull delivery with Entra ID
consumer = EventGridConsumerClient(
    os.environ["EG_NAMESPACE_ENDPOINT"], DefaultAzureCredential(),
    namespace_topic="fleet", subscription="maintenance-planner")
batch = consumer.receive(max_events=10)
done = [d.broker_properties.lock_token for d in batch]
if done:
    consumer.acknowledge(lock_tokens=done)

blocks.text:
az eventgrid topic create --name fleet-events -g rg-fleet -l westeurope \
  --input-schema cloudeventschemav1_0
TOPIC_ID=$(az eventgrid topic show --name fleet-events -g rg-fleet --query id -o tsv)
az eventgrid event-subscription create --name north-depot \
  --source-resource-id "$TOPIC_ID" \
  --endpoint "$WEBHOOK_URL" \
  --included-event-types Fleet.Vehicle.Serviced \
  --subject-begins-with depots/north/ \
  --advanced-filter data.odometerKm NumberGreaterThanOrEquals 40000 \
  --max-delivery-attempts 18 --event-ttl 360 \
  --max-events-per-batch 50 \
  --deadletter-endpoint "$STORAGE_ID/blobServices/default/containers/fleet-dlq"
blocks.title: Azure CLI · CloudEvents topic, then a filtered subscription with batching

blocks.text: A pricing service's webhook failed every delivery for about an hour after a bad release. Once it was fixed, even events published after the fix arrived late for a while. That is delayed delivery: after a run of failures, Event Grid treats the endpoint as unhealthy and holds back retries and new deliveries to it, sometimes for hours, rather than flooding it. The team keeps a dead-letter container on the subscription so that nothing which runs out of retries during such an outage is lost, and keeps the handler idempotent because the backlog can arrive with duplicates and out of order.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
• The time to live is checked only at the next scheduled attempt, so an event can stay queued past its time to live until that attempt comes round.
• Output batching is off until you set a batch size or event count, so each delivery holds one event.
• A system topic created implicitly by an event subscription disappears with its last subscription. Create the system topic explicitly when you want it to stay.
• One source, such as a storage account, can have only one system topic.
• A custom topic's input schema is chosen when the topic is created.
• A subscription can add custom HTTP headers to deliveries, up to 10 of them.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text:
Question: a subscription has an advanced filter NumberNotIn on data.discountPct with the value 0, meant to deliver only discounted orders. An order event arrives with no discountPct field at all. Is it delivered?
Solution: yes. When the key is missing, NumberNotIn and StringNotIn evaluate to true, so the event passes. Add an IsNotNull filter on the same key (filters combine with AND) if missing values must be excluded.

lessons.title: 3.3 · Azure Functions: serverless APIs with triggers and bindings
lessons.summary: Build serverless APIs with the Python v2 programming model: triggers, input and output bindings, HTTP routes and access keys, identity-based connections and the Service Bus trigger's message handling.

blocks.text:
A function has exactly one trigger, which starts it, and any number of input and output bindings, which read and write data declaratively. Bindings are optional: a function can also create an SDK client itself.

The Python v2 programming model is the one recommended for new apps. You declare everything with decorators on a func.FunctionApp() object in function_app.py, with no function.json files. The v1 model, with a function.json file and __init__.py per function, is for legacy apps. Larger apps put functions in blueprints (bp = func.Blueprint()) and register them with app.register_functions(bp).
blocks.title: What triggers and bindings are

blocks.text:
• @app.route(route=..., methods=[...], auth_level=...) for HTTP.
• @app.timer_trigger with a schedule for timers. NCRONTAB has six fields, {second} {minute} {hour} {day} {month} {day-of-week}, so 0 */5 * * * * runs every five minutes. Schedules use UTC by default, and the timer parameter's past_due is true when a run starts later than scheduled.
• Trigger decorators such as @app.service_bus_queue_trigger and @app.cosmos_db_trigger (and @app.event_grid_trigger and others) for events and messages.
• Output bindings such as @app.service_bus_queue_output. The function writes through a func.Out[...] parameter by calling .set(value).
Inside an HTTP function, read route parameters from req.route_params and the query string from req.params. Routes get the api prefix by default. An HTTP function that sets no output returns 204 No Content.
blocks.title: How it works: common decorators

blocks.text:
With any authorization level other than anonymous, callers must send an access key in the x-functions-key header or the code query string. Keys are shared secrets, not user sign-in: for real authentication, put App Service Authentication or API Management in front.

Each key has a name, and the app and each function have a key named default. When a function key and a host key share a name, the function key is used. Keys are encrypted at rest, in a Blob Storage container of the AzureWebJobsStorage account by default. AzureWebJobsSecretStorageType moves them, for example to Azure Key Vault (keyvault). Several apps pointed at one vault share its secrets and can overwrite each other's keys, so give each app its own vault.
blocks.title: How it works: HTTP authorization and access keys

blocks.text: Never give the master key to third parties or ship it in client apps.
blocks.title: Access key types
rows: The admin level and the runtime REST APIs under /admin
Extension webhooks, such as the Event Grid trigger

blocks.text:
A binding's connection value names an app setting or a setting prefix. For identity-based connections you set the prefix plus __fullyQualifiedNamespace (Service Bus, Event Hubs) or the prefix plus __accountEndpoint (Cosmos DB), and give the app's managed identity a data-plane role, so no secret is stored.

The Service Bus trigger receives each message in peek-lock mode. By default the runtime completes the message when the function succeeds and abandons it when the function fails, and it renews the lock while a long run is in progress. Functions has no poison-message setting of its own: Service Bus dead-letters a message by its own delivery-count rules.
blocks.title: How it works: connections and the Service Bus trigger
Python · function_app.py (HTTP API, queue output, queue and timer triggers)
Python · billing.py (a blueprint that function_app.py registers)

blocks.text: A function_app.py has grown to forty functions across three areas: intake, billing and reporting. The team moves each area into its own module that defines bp = func.Blueprint() with that area's decorators, as billing.py does above, and the main file only imports each blueprint and calls app.register_functions(bp). Deployments are unchanged, and each area can be reviewed and tested on its own.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
• A function key and a host key with the same name: the function key wins.
• The runtime REST APIs under /admin need the master key, sent in the x-functions-key header.
• The Event Grid trigger's webhook is protected by a system key that the extension manages, not by a function key you hand out.
• NCRONTAB has six fields, and the first is seconds.
• For a Cosmos DB identity-based connection, the setting is the prefix plus __accountEndpoint.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text:
Question: two function apps store their access keys in Key Vault through AzureWebJobsSecretStorageType, both pointing at the same vault URI. Keys in one app start to change unexpectedly. Why, and what is the fix?
Solution: secrets in the vault aren't scoped to each app, so the two apps share and overwrite the same key secrets. Give each function app its own Key Vault instance.

lessons.title: 3.4 · Configure and deploy function apps
lessons.summary: Choose a hosting plan, understand Flex Consumption scaling, networking and billing, manage host.json and app settings, and pick the right deployment method for each plan.

blocks.text:
• Flex Consumption is GA, runs on Linux only and is the plan Learn recommends for new serverless apps. It scales to zero and out to 1,000 instances, offers virtual network integration and always-ready instances, and bills for execution time plus any always-ready baseline.
• Premium (Elastic Premium) and Dedicated (App Service plan) suit apps that need prewarmed or reserved capacity, deployment slots or containers.
• Container Apps can host containerized function apps.
• Consumption is a legacy plan. Hosting on Linux Consumption retires on 30 September 2028 and gets no new features or language versions, so don't choose it for new work: migrate those apps to Flex Consumption. Windows Consumption apps aren't currently affected.

The Python runtime runs only on Linux, on every plan. Default function timeouts are 30 minutes on Flex Consumption, Premium, Dedicated and Container Apps, and 5 minutes (maximum 10) on Consumption. Whatever the timeout, an HTTP-triggered function must respond within 230 seconds.
blocks.title: What the hosting plans are

blocks.text:
• Instance memory is 512, 2,048 (the default choice for most apps) or 4,096 MB, with about 0.25, 1 and 2 cores. You can change it at any time. The platform adds 272 MB per instance for system processes, which isn't billed.
• Per-function scaling: HTTP triggers scale together as the http group, Event Grid-based Blob triggers as blob, and Durable Functions triggers as durable. Every other function scales on its own instances, named function:<name>.
• Always-ready instances keep a minimum number of instances running for a group or function, which cuts cold starts. Without them, instances run on demand and are billed only for execution time. With zone redundancy each group or function needs at least two. The maximum instance count (1 to 1,000) limits on-demand instances only, for each group.
• The platform manages the scale-out rate: fast at first, more gradual at high instance counts. Always-ready instances aren't subject to it.
• All Flex Consumption apps in a subscription and region share a memory quota counted in cores, and always-ready instances count against it. A support request can raise it.
• Billing: the minimum billable execution is 1,000 ms, then it rounds up to the nearest 100 ms.
• One app per plan, no deployment slots, and app initialization times out after 30 seconds.
blocks.title: How it works: Flex Consumption scaling and billing

blocks.text:
• Virtual network integration needs a subnet delegated to Microsoft.App/environments (Premium and Dedicated use Microsoft.Web/serverFarms) and the Microsoft.App resource provider registered in the subscription.
• A /27 subnet is the minimum for one app, and /26 is recommended for several apps or very high scale. Instances don't get an IP address each: a pool of gateways shares the subnet's addresses.
• The subnet can't hold private endpoints or service endpoints, can't be delegated to another service, and can't be shared with an Azure Container Apps environment. Several Flex Consumption apps in the same region can share one.
• Azure Files shares can be mounted as local folders (SMB only; NFS isn't available), which keeps large binaries such as models out of the deployment package.
blocks.title: How it works: networking and storage on Flex Consumption

blocks.text:
• host.json carries runtime settings for the whole app, such as functionTimeout, and deploys with your code.
• App settings reach your code as environment variables. They hold connections (AzureWebJobsStorage, identity-based prefixes) and app configuration. Changing them restarts the app by default; on Flex Consumption, rolling updates (preview) can avoid the downtime.
• local.settings.json is for local runs only and isn't published. Because it can hold secrets, keep it out of source control, and encrypt it with func settings encrypt. func azure functionapp fetch-app-settings copies the app's settings down, overwriting local values with the same names.
• requirements.txt lists the Python packages that a remote build installs.
• On Flex Consumption many classic settings are deprecated. The language and its version move into functionAppConfig, the platform manages the runtime version setting, and content-share and build-during-deployment settings aren't used.
blocks.title: How it works: configuration

blocks.text:
• Flex Consumption: the code package goes into a blob deployment container, by default in the AzureWebJobsStorage account, and the app runs from it. Before switching to a new package, Azure starts it on a temporary instance, checks that the host reports ready and syncs triggers. That validation doesn't run your functions or call downstream services. A remote build is requested by a deployment parameter, and Core Tools and Visual Studio Code request it for Python. Classic ZIP deployment, external package URLs, source control, local Git and FTPS aren't available on this plan, but the Azure CLI's az functionapp deployment source config-zip, Core Tools and Visual Studio Code still work: on Flex Consumption they use package deployment.
• Premium and Dedicated: ZIP deployment is the default and recommended technology, running from the package with WEBSITE_RUN_FROM_PACKAGE=1. A remote build there is switched on with build settings, and WEBSITE_RUN_FROM_PACKAGE is then left unset.
• An external package URL (a .zip in Blob Storage) needs a manual trigger sync after every package change, which is why Learn doesn't recommend technologies that need one.
• func azure functionapp publish packages and deploys a project, and func pack builds a ready-to-run .zip without deploying it.
blocks.title: How it works: deployment

blocks.text:
az functionapp list-flexconsumption-locations --query "sort_by(@, &name)[].name" -o tsv
az functionapp create -g rg-orders -n func-orders --storage-account stordersfunc \
  --flexconsumption-location northeurope --runtime python --runtime-version 3.11 \
  --vnet "$VNET_ID" --subnet snet-func
az functionapp scale config set -g rg-orders -n func-orders --instance-memory 512
az functionapp scale config set -g rg-orders -n func-orders \
  --trigger-type http --trigger-settings perInstanceConcurrency=10
az functionapp config appsettings set -g rg-orders -n func-orders \
  --settings "ORDERS_API_HOST=orders.example.net"
func azure functionapp publish func-orders
blocks.title: Azure CLI · Flex Consumption app with virtual network integration

blocks.text: A team plans three Flex Consumption apps in one region that must reach a database inside a virtual network, and one of them may scale to several hundred instances. They create a /26 subnet, delegate it to Microsoft.App/environments and register the Microsoft.App provider. They keep the subnet free of private endpoints and out of the Container Apps environment that another team runs, and they watch outbound throughput at production scale, because shared gateways, not IP addresses, become the limit first.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
• A successful Flex Consumption deployment doesn't prove your functions work: validation only checks that the host starts and triggers sync. The Flex Consumption Deployment diagnostic tool shows history and package status.
• Flex Consumption subnets are delegated to Microsoft.App/environments, not Microsoft.Web/serverFarms.
• Mounted file shares on Flex Consumption are SMB only.
• Durable Functions on Flex Consumption supports only the Azure Storage and Durable Task Scheduler providers.
• Flex Consumption doesn't support PowerShell managed dependencies: upload the modules with the app content instead.
• Changing an app setting restarts the app by default on every plan; on Flex Consumption, rolling updates (preview) avoid the downtime.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text:
Question: a developer's local.settings.json points SEARCH_INDEX at a test index. After running func azure functionapp fetch-app-settings against the production app, local runs suddenly query the production index. Why?
Solution: fetch-app-settings overwrites existing local values with the app's settings from Azure (and adds missing ones). Keep local overrides under names the app doesn't use, or set them again after fetching.
