lessons.title: Lab · Dead-letter handling in Service Bus with Python
lessons.summary: Hands-on: create a queue with a low delivery limit, dead-letter messages two ways, inspect the dead-letter queue from Python, drain it, and clean up.

blocks.text:
Goal: see both ways a message reaches the dead-letter queue, read why it got there, and drain the queue yourself.

You need an Azure subscription, the Azure CLI signed in with az login, and Python 3.9 or later with the azure-servicebus and azure-identity packages (pip install azure-servicebus azure-identity). The lab signs in with your own Microsoft Entra account through DefaultAzureCredential, so no connection string is stored. It costs a few cents and takes about 20 minutes.
blocks.title: Goal and prerequisites

blocks.text:
RG=rg-sb-lab
NS=sblab$RANDOM
az group create --name $RG --location westeurope
az servicebus namespace create --resource-group $RG --name $NS --location westeurope
NS_ID=$(az servicebus namespace show -g $RG -n $NS --query id -o tsv)
ME=$(az ad signed-in-user show --query id -o tsv)
az role assignment create --role "Azure Service Bus Data Owner" \
  --assignee $ME --scope $NS_ID
export SERVICEBUS_FQDN=$NS.servicebus.windows.net
blocks.title: Azure CLI · step 1: create a namespace and give yourself a data role

blocks.text: Learn's quickstart uses Azure Service Bus Data Owner for local development, because the lab both manages a queue and sends and receives. A real app should get the narrowest role at the narrowest scope it needs. A new role assignment can take a minute or two to apply.
blocks.title: Why these choices

blocks.text:
import os

from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.servicebus.management import ServiceBusAdministrationClient

admin = ServiceBusAdministrationClient(os.environ["SERVICEBUS_FQDN"],
                                       DefaultAzureCredential())
admin.create_queue("lab-orders", max_delivery_count=2)  # low limit for the lab
print(admin.get_queue("lab-orders").max_delivery_count)
blocks.title: Python · step 2: lab_queue.py creates the queue

blocks.text:
import os

from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.servicebus import ServiceBusClient, ServiceBusMessage

FQDN = os.environ["SERVICEBUS_FQDN"]

with ServiceBusClient(FQDN, DefaultAzureCredential()) as client:
    with client.get_queue_sender("lab-orders") as sender:
        sender.send_messages([ServiceBusMessage(b, subject=b)
                              for b in ("good", "rejected", "flaky")])
    with client.get_queue_receiver("lab-orders", max_wait_time=10) as receiver:
        for msg in receiver:
            kind = str(msg)
            if kind == "good":
                receiver.complete_message(msg)
            elif kind == "rejected":
                receiver.dead_letter_message(
                    msg, reason="LabRejected", error_description="rejected on purpose")
            else:
                print("abandoning", kind, "delivery", msg.delivery_count)
                receiver.abandon_message(msg)  # comes back until the limit is passed
blocks.title: Python · step 3: lab_run.py sends three messages and settles them

blocks.text:
import os

from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.servicebus import ServiceBusClient, ServiceBusSubQueue
from azure.servicebus.management import ServiceBusAdministrationClient

FQDN = os.environ["SERVICEBUS_FQDN"]
credential = DefaultAzureCredential()

props = ServiceBusAdministrationClient(FQDN, credential).get_queue_runtime_properties(
    "lab-orders")
print("active", props.active_message_count,
      "dead-lettered", props.dead_letter_message_count)

with ServiceBusClient(FQDN, credential) as client:
    with client.get_queue_receiver("lab-orders",
                                   sub_queue=ServiceBusSubQueue.DEAD_LETTER) as dlq:
        for msg in dlq.peek_messages(max_message_count=10):
            print(str(msg), msg.dead_letter_reason, msg.dead_letter_error_description,
                  msg.delivery_count)
blocks.title: Python · step 4: lab_inspect.py verifies the dead-letter queue

blocks.text:
• Step 3 prints the flaky message's abandon lines until the delivery limit is passed, then the loop ends after 10 seconds without messages.
• Step 4 should report 0 active and 2 dead-lettered messages. The rejected message shows your own reason and description. The flaky one shows MaxDeliveryCountExceeded, the reason Service Bus records when the delivery count passes the queue's limit.
• Run step 4 again: peeking left both messages where they were, because a peek neither locks nor removes anything. Nothing expires them either, so they wait in the dead-letter queue until you act.
blocks.title: How to verify

blocks.text:
import os

from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.servicebus import ServiceBusClient, ServiceBusSubQueue

FQDN = os.environ["SERVICEBUS_FQDN"]

with ServiceBusClient(FQDN, DefaultAzureCredential()) as client:
    with client.get_queue_receiver("lab-orders", max_wait_time=5,
                                   sub_queue=ServiceBusSubQueue.DEAD_LETTER) as dlq:
        for msg in dlq:
            print("discarding", str(msg), msg.dead_letter_reason)
            dlq.complete_message(msg)  # log it first in a real system
blocks.title: Python · step 5: lab_drain.py empties the dead-letter queue

blocks.text: az group delete --name $RG --yes --no-wait
blocks.title: Azure CLI · clean-up

blocks.text:
• The dead-letter queue is a sub-queue of the entity, opened with sub_queue on an ordinary receiver.
• dead_letter_message records your reason at once; abandoning lets Service Bus dead-letter the message by its own count.
• Inspecting with a peek is safe; only completing a dead-lettered message removes it.

lessons.title: 4.1.1 · Key Vault: retrieving, protecting and rotating secrets
lessons.summary: Store and read secrets with azure-keyvault-secrets, choose the right access model and roles, understand soft delete and purge protection, and rotate secrets on Key Vault events.

blocks.text:
A secret in Azure Key Vault is a value, such as a password, token or API key, plus metadata: a content type, tags, an enabled flag and optional activation and expiry dates. Every write creates a new version, and the newest version is the one callers get unless they ask for a specific one.

From Python you use SecretClient from the azure-keyvault-secrets package, created with the vault URL and a credential such as DefaultAzureCredential from azure-identity. The same code then uses your developer sign-in locally and the managed identity in Azure.
• set_secret creates a secret, or a new version if the name is already in use.
• get_secret(name) returns the latest version, and get_secret(name, version) a specific one.
• update_secret_properties changes metadata such as enabled, tags or expires_on, for the latest version or a named one, without creating a version. It can't change the value.
• list_properties_of_secrets lists identifiers and attributes only, never values.
• begin_delete_secret and begin_recover_deleted_secret return pollers, because deleting and recovering take a few seconds in a vault with soft delete.
blocks.title: What it is

blocks.text:
Key Vault has two planes. The control plane (Azure Resource Manager) manages the vault resource itself, and the data plane (the vault's own endpoint) works with keys, secrets and certificates. Both authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID. The control plane always authorizes with Azure RBAC. The data plane uses either Azure RBAC or the legacy access policy model.

Azure RBAC is the recommended model, and from API version 2026-02-01 it's the default for newly created vaults. Learn recommends one vault per application per environment, with roles assigned at vault scope.
• Key Vault Secrets User reads secret contents.
• Key Vault Secrets Officer can do anything with secrets except manage permissions.
• Key Vault Reader reads metadata and can't see values.
• Key Vault Contributor manages the vault resource only and gives no access to its data.
The Key Vault data roles only work on vaults that use the Azure RBAC model. Watch who holds Contributor on a vault that still uses access policies, because a control-plane Contributor can grant themselves data access by adding an access policy.
blocks.title: How it works · Access

blocks.text:
Soft delete is on by default for new vaults and can't be turned off once enabled. Deleted vaults and objects stay recoverable for 7 to 90 days (90 by default). You set that period only at vault creation and can't change it later. Deleting permanently takes two steps: delete, then purge. A soft-deleted vault's name can't be reused until the period ends, or until the vault is purged, which purge protection blocks.

Purge protection is optional and off by default, needs soft delete, and stops anyone purging a deleted vault or object before the retention period passes. Deleted objects can still be recovered.

While an object is deleted, it can only be listed, recovered or purged; every other operation fails. Soft-deleting a whole vault also deletes integrations such as its Azure RBAC role assignments and Event Grid subscriptions, and recovering the vault doesn't bring them back.
blocks.title: How it works · Protection
How it works · Throttling and rotation

blocks.text:
import os

from azure.core.exceptions import ResourceNotFoundError
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.keyvault.secrets import SecretClient

client = SecretClient(vault_url=os.environ["KEY_VAULT_URL"],
                      credential=DefaultAzureCredential())

# A new version of the weather service key, with metadata that explains it
latest = client.set_secret("weather-api-key", os.environ["NEW_WEATHER_KEY"],
                           content_type="text/plain",
                           tags={"owner": "forecast-team"})
print("now serving version", latest.properties.version)

# Disable one older version so that nothing can read it any more
old_version = os.environ.get("RETIRED_VERSION")
if old_version:
    client.update_secret_properties("weather-api-key", old_version, enabled=False)

try:
    key = client.get_secret("weather-api-key").value  # latest version
except ResourceNotFoundError:
    raise SystemExit("weather-api-key isn't in this vault")

Worked example

blocks.text:
• Key Vault Contributor and Contributor are control-plane roles. Under Azure RBAC they give no access to secret values.
• update_secret_properties takes an optional version, so you can disable one old version and leave the latest alone.
• A deleted secret can't be read until it's recovered. begin_recover_deleted_secret brings back its latest version.
• backup_secret produces a protected blob that only Key Vault can use; restore_secret_backup reads it back.
• SecretNearExpiry has twins for keys and certificates; read the event name's prefix before you pick one.

blocks.text: Question: Learn recommends assigning Key Vault roles at vault scope. When does it accept role assignments on individual secrets? Solution: in exceptions, such as a secret that a single user must read (an SSH private key used through Azure Bastion) or a secret that several applications share. Otherwise use one vault per application per environment, with roles at vault scope.

lessons.title: 4.1.2 · App Configuration: settings, labels, feature flags and refresh
lessons.summary: Store settings centrally in Azure App Configuration, load them in Python with selectors and labels, keep secrets in Key Vault through references, use feature flags and refresh values without a restart.

blocks.text:
App Configuration stores non-secret settings and feature flags centrally, so many apps and environments share one source without redeploying.
• A key-value is a key, a value, an optional label, a content type and tags. Keys are case-sensitive Unicode strings, usually hierarchical (Forecast:Maps:Timeout). Any character except % is allowed, and a key can't be . or .. on its own. A key-value with all its attributes can be at most 10 KB.
• App Configuration treats each key as a whole and doesn't parse its delimiters.
• Labels create variants of the same key, typically one per environment or one per build (an app version or a Git commit ID). A key-value has no label by default, and the selector writes that as "\0".
• The content type helps the app interpret the value. App Configuration uses media types for its built-in types, such as feature flags, Key Vault references and JSON values.
blocks.title: What it is

blocks.text:
• The Python provider is azure-appconfiguration-provider. Its load() returns a dictionary-like provider and loads unlabelled key-values by default. Authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID (recommended) through a credential, or with a connection string. An async load() lives in the provider package's aio module and needs an async credential.
• selects=[SettingSelector(...)] chooses keys and labels, and when several selectors return the same key, the last one wins. trim_prefixes strips a prefix from key names, and a selector can load a snapshot instead.
• Values with a JSON content type arrive as Python objects. From version 2.2.0, JSON values may contain comments.
• Dynamic refresh: watch a sentinel by passing refresh_on a list with one WatchKey, or set refresh_enabled=True. The refresh interval defaults to 30 seconds, and your code calls refresh() where activity happens. Update the sentinel last, after all related keys, so apps reload a consistent set.
• Start-up: load() retries for up to startup_timeout (100 seconds by default). Replica discovery is on by default, so the provider fails over to the store's geo-replicas.
blocks.title: How it works · Loading and refresh

blocks.text:
• Key Vault references keep secrets in Key Vault. The provider resolves them through keyvault_credential, per-vault client settings or a secret resolver, so the app's identity needs App Configuration Data Reader on the store and Key Vault Secrets User on the vault.
• Feature flags load only when you ask for them, and the featuremanagement package's FeatureManager evaluates them with filters such as targeting and time window. Metric scorecards for flags are preview.
• Data-plane roles: App Configuration Data Reader (read) and App Configuration Data Owner (read, write, delete). Neither grants access to manage the store resource itself. App Configuration Reader and Contributor are control-plane roles.
blocks.title: How it works · Secrets, flags and access

blocks.text:
import os

from azure.appconfiguration.provider import SettingSelector, WatchKey, load
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential

credential = DefaultAzureCredential()
config = load(
    endpoint=os.environ["APP_CONFIG_ENDPOINT"],
    credential=credential,
    selects=[SettingSelector(key_filter="Forecast:*", label_filter="prod"),
             SettingSelector(key_filter="Shared:*", label_filter="prod")],
    trim_prefixes=["Forecast:", "Shared:"],
    keyvault_credential=credential,    # resolves Key Vault references
    refresh_on=[WatchKey("Forecast:Sentinel")],
    refresh_interval=60,
)


def map_timeout():
    config.refresh()  # checks the sentinel only when the interval has passed
    return int(config["Maps:TimeoutSeconds"])
blocks.title: Python · settings.py (azure-appconfiguration-provider)
Worked example

blocks.text:
• App Configuration isn't a secret store. Secrets stay in Key Vault, and a Key Vault reference only points to them.
• In a label filter, "\0" means no label, while * matches every label, the empty one included.
• The async provider needs the async credential from azure.identity.aio, not the synchronous one.
• A snapshot selector needs a code change to switch snapshots; a snapshot reference (provider 2.4.0 and later) switches at runtime.
• Control-plane roles manage the store resource; reading key-values through Entra ID needs a Data role.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text: Question: a team wants the settings that shipped with build 4.2.0 of a report service to stay available while build 4.3.0 rolls out, using one store and the same key names. How can it keep both sets side by side, and how does each build load its own? Solution: label each key-value with the build number. Each build loads with a SettingSelector whose label filter is its own version, such as "4.3.0". A filter such as "4.*" would match every 4.x label, so use the exact label.

lessons.title: 4.2.1 · OpenTelemetry: tracing distributed Python services
lessons.summary: Instrument Python services with an OpenTelemetry distro for Azure Monitor, enrich spans, follow one operation across services, and control what the distro collects.

blocks.text:
A trace is a tree of spans that share one operation ID. Each span is a unit of work, such as a request, a database call or a model call, with a start time, a duration, attributes and a status. In Application Insights, operation_Id (OperationId in the workspace tables) groups the telemetry of one end-to-end operation, and W3C Trace Context carries the trace across service boundaries.

Two Python packages send OpenTelemetry data to Application Insights. Don't initialize both in one app.
• The Microsoft OpenTelemetry Distro, package microsoft-opentelemetry. Learn's Python pages now lead with it: call use_microsoft_opentelemetry with enable_azure_monitor=True, and it reads the connection string from the Application Insights connection string environment variable. Apps already on the older distro need no action.
• The Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry Distro, package azure-monitor-opentelemetry, documented in the Python API reference. You call configure_azure_monitor() once at startup. It collects traces, metrics and logs, and enables bundled instrumentations for Azure SDK clients (Azure Core Tracing), Django, FastAPI, Flask, httpx, psycopg2, requests, urllib and urllib3.
The code in this lesson uses the second package, because the API reference documents it in full. That distro installs the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry exporters for you. Learn's FAQ links the standalone Python exporter package to its preview SDK reference, so treat that package as preview (prerelease).
blocks.title: What it is

blocks.text:
• Resource: the cloud role name, the node name on the Application Map, comes from the resource attributes service.namespace and service.name, falling back to service.name alone. The role instance comes from service.instance.id. OTEL_SERVICE_NAME and OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES set them.
• Instrumentations: the bundled ones are on by default. instrumentation_options switches individual ones off by library name, and an environment variable (shown in the code below) does the same with a comma-separated list of lowercase names.
• Extras: Live Metrics and performance counters are on by default (enable_live_metrics and enable_performance_counters). Learn's Live Metrics section carries a preview-terms notice.
• Sampling: both distros default to rate-limited sampling of five traces per second. The other strategy is a fixed rate (a ratio between 0 and 1). For azure-monitor-opentelemetry, sampling set through environment variables takes precedence over the sampling options passed in code, although other passed arguments win over their environment variables.
• Precedence: apart from sampling, every argument you pass to configure_azure_monitor wins over the related environment variable.
blocks.title: How it works · What the distro collects

blocks.text:
• Spans: get a tracer with trace.get_tracer(__name__) and open spans with tracer.start_as_current_span. Telemetry created inside the with block is attributed to that span.
• Attributes: span.set_attribute adds a value to one span. Attributes are exported as custom properties, in the customDimensions field of the requests, dependencies, traces or exceptions table.
• Span processors: a SpanProcessor passed through span_processors runs for every span. Learn's sample adds attributes in on_start, so they reach every span without touching the business code.
• Logs: records from the named application logger become traces, and a dict passed as extra becomes custom dimensions.
• Metrics: a meter from the OpenTelemetry metrics API creates counters, histograms and gauges.
Keep the providers alive for the life of the app and flush pending telemetry at shutdown.
blocks.title: How it works · Custom telemetry

blocks.text:
import logging
import os

from azure.monitor.opentelemetry import configure_azure_monitor
from opentelemetry import metrics, trace
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import SpanProcessor


class RingProcessor(SpanProcessor):
    """Stamps every span with the deployment ring it ran in."""

    def on_start(self, span, parent_context=None):
        span.set_attribute("app.ring", os.environ.get("DEPLOY_RING", "main"))


# Reads APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING; call once, at startup.
# OTEL_PYTHON_DISABLED_INSTRUMENTATIONS=urllib3 would skip one instrumentation.
configure_azure_monitor(logger_name="forecast",
                        span_processors=[RingProcessor()])

tracer = trace.get_tracer(__name__)
log = logging.getLogger("forecast")
scored = metrics.get_meter("forecast").create_counter("forecasts_scored")


def score(region, model):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("score-region") as span:
        span.set_attribute("app.region", region)
        result = model(region)
        scored.add(1, {"region": region})
        log.info("scored %s", region, extra={"model": "v7"})
        return result
blocks.title: Python · telemetry.py (azure-monitor-opentelemetry)

blocks.text: A forecasting API runs in two deployment rings, canary and main, and the team wants to compare their latency and failures in Application Insights. Its business code has dozens of spans, and nobody wants to edit each one. They write the small span processor shown above, whose on_start sets app.ring from an environment variable, and pass it to configure_azure_monitor through span_processors. Every request and dependency now carries app.ring as a custom property, so one query split by that property compares the rings. When the canary is promoted, only the environment variable changes.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text:
• Name the package: microsoft-opentelemetry uses use_microsoft_opentelemetry, and azure-monitor-opentelemetry uses configure_azure_monitor. Never initialize both.
• Span attributes become custom properties. Resource attributes describe the service as a whole.
• Live Metrics and performance counters are on unless you turn them off.
• Sampling is the exception to "passed arguments win": its environment variables beat the code options.
• azure-monitor-opentelemetry is set up in code with configure_azure_monitor; its README says automatic (no-code) instrumentation isn't supported yet.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text: Question: a nightly batch service that uses configure_azure_monitor must keep its traces and logs, but a cost review asks it to stop sending Live Metrics and performance counters. What does it pass? Solution: False for both enable_live_metrics and enable_performance_counters. Both default to True, and neither setting touches the trace or log pipelines.

lessons.title: 4.2.2 · KQL: querying logs and metrics in Azure Monitor
lessons.summary: Write Kusto Query Language queries against the workspace-based Application Insights tables: filter, shape, aggregate, join, parse and chart, and run queries from Python.

blocks.text:
Kusto Query Language (KQL) is the read-only query language of Azure Monitor Logs, Azure Data Explorer and other services. A query is a pipeline: a table, then operators joined by |, each taking the previous result as input.

Workspace-based Application Insights data lives in App* tables in the Log Analytics workspace. The pages saved for this pack show AppRequests (Name, DurationMs, Success, ResultCode, OperationId, AppRoleName), AppDependencies (Target, DependencyType, DurationMs, Success), AppExceptions (ExceptionType, OuterMessage, ProblemId) and AppTraces (Message, SeverityLevel). OperationId links the telemetry of one end-to-end operation across tables.
blocks.title: What it is

blocks.text:
• Filter early: where TimeGenerated > ago(1h) straight after the table, then the other conditions.
• Shape: project picks, renames and computes columns, and extend adds computed ones while keeping the rest. take, top N by and order by trim and sort.
• Aggregate: summarize count(), countif(), dcount(), avg(), sum(), max() or percentile() by one or more columns. Each unique combination of the by values is a group. Use bin() on a time column, because summarizing by raw TimeGenerated creates a group per value. With no by clause, summarize over no rows returns one row: count(), dcount(), sum() and similar give 0, while avg() and most others give null. With a by clause it returns no rows.
• Parse: parse Message with "Scored batch " Batch:long " in " Ms:long " ms" breaks a string that follows one pattern into typed columns; rows that don't match get null.
• Combine: join kind=inner or kind=leftouter on a key such as OperationId. The default flavour is innerunique, which removes duplicate keys from the left side first.
• Strings: has matches whole terms through the term index, while contains matches any substring and is slower. == is case-sensitive and =~ isn't. Learn prefers has, and case-sensitive operators where they do the job.
• Chart: render goes last and draws the result, for example as a timechart or a barchart.
blocks.title: How it works · Operators

blocks.text: azure-monitor-query's LogsQueryClient runs KQL with query_workspace(workspace_id, query, timespan=...), or with query_resource against an Azure resource ID. It takes a token credential such as DefaultAzureCredential. A result can come back partial (LogsQueryStatus.PARTIAL, with partial_error and partial_data). Since version 2.0, metrics queries have moved to the separate azure-monitor-querymetrics package.
blocks.title: How it works · From Python

blocks.text:
// Requests and failure share per operation in 15-minute buckets
AppRequests
| where TimeGenerated > ago(12h) and AppRoleName == "forecast-api"
| summarize failed = countif(Success == false), total = count()
    by Name, bin(TimeGenerated, 15m)
| extend failedPct = round(100.0 * failed / total, 1)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// Which problems touch the most operations today
AppExceptions
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| summarize operations = dcount(OperationId), hits = count() by ProblemId
| top 5 by operations
blocks.title: KQL · failure share per operation, then exceptions by reach

blocks.text:
import os
from datetime import timedelta

from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.monitor.query import LogsQueryClient, LogsQueryStatus

client = LogsQueryClient(DefaultAzureCredential())
query = "AppExceptions | summarize hits = count() by ProblemId | top 5 by hits"
result = client.query_workspace(os.environ["LOG_WORKSPACE_ID"], query,
                                timespan=timedelta(days=1))
if result.status == LogsQueryStatus.SUCCESS:
    tables = result.tables
else:
    print("partial result:", result.partial_error)
    tables = result.partial_data
for table in tables:
    for row in table.rows:
        print(list(row))

Worked example

blocks.text:
• parse handles strings that share one pattern; extract() with a regular expression suits strings that don't.
• If the right side of a join is small and the left side large, Learn suggests lookup instead of join. lookup fails if its right side is larger than several tens of MB.
• A let value used more than once is worth wrapping in materialize().
• Store and compare times as datetime, not as Unix-time numbers converted at query time.
• High-cardinality summarize keys (more than about a million) benefit from hint.shufflekey.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text: Question: a team's custom table stores each event time as Unix-epoch milliseconds in a long column, and every query converts it with a Unix-time conversion function before filtering. What do Learn's best practices suggest? Solution: keep times in a datetime column. Convert the Unix time once, during ingestion (Learn names update policies for this), rather than in every query, so time filters work on a real datetime column.

lessons.title: Lab · Read a Key Vault secret and trace it into Application Insights
lessons.summary: A hands-on walkthrough: create a vault and an Application Insights resource with the Azure CLI, read a secret from Python, send a custom span, then find it with KQL. About 30 minutes.

blocks.text: By the end you have a Python script that reads a secret from Key Vault with its own identity, wraps the work in a custom span with an attribute, and sends it to a workspace-based Application Insights resource. You then find that span with a KQL query run from Python, and remove everything.
blocks.title: Goal

blocks.text:
• An Azure subscription where you can create resource groups and assign roles.
• The Azure CLI, signed in with az login, and the application-insights CLI extension (step 2 adds it).
• Python 3.10 or later in a virtual environment with azure-identity, azure-keyvault-secrets, azure-monitor-opentelemetry and azure-monitor-query installed.
• Your user principal name, for the role assignment.
blocks.title: Prerequisites

blocks.text:
1. Run the step 1 commands to create the group and an Azure RBAC vault, give yourself Key Vault Secrets Officer at vault scope and store one secret. If the secret set command is refused at first, wait a few minutes for the role assignment to apply and try again.
2. Run the step 2 commands. They add the CLI extension, create a Log Analytics workspace and a workspace-based Application Insights resource linked to it, and export the vault URL, the connection string and the workspace ID (its customerId) for the scripts.
3. Run python lab_app.py (step 3). DefaultAzureCredential uses your CLI sign-in. The custom span and the Key Vault call made through the SDK go to Application Insights.
4. Wait a few minutes: Learn notes that data can take a few minutes to show up.
blocks.title: Steps

blocks.text:
rg=lab-secrets-rg
loc=westeurope
vault=<globally-unique-vault-name>

az group create --name "$rg" --location "$loc"
az keyvault create --name "$vault" --resource-group "$rg" \
  --enable-rbac-authorization true

# Data access is separate from owning the resource: give yourself a secrets role
sub=$(az account show --query id --output tsv)
scope="/subscriptions/$sub/resourceGroups/$rg"
scope="$scope/providers/Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/$vault"
az role assignment create --role "Key Vault Secrets Officer" \
  --assignee "<upn>" --scope "$scope"

az keyvault secret set --vault-name "$vault" --name lab-greeting \
  --value "hello from the vault"
blocks.title: Azure CLI · step 1: resource group, vault, role and secret

blocks.text:
az extension add -n application-insights

az monitor log-analytics workspace create --resource-group "$rg" \
  --workspace-name lab-logs --location "$loc"
ws_id=$(az monitor log-analytics workspace show --resource-group "$rg" \
  --workspace-name lab-logs --query id --output tsv)

az monitor app-insights component create --app lab-appinsights \
  --location "$loc" --resource-group "$rg" --kind web \
  --application-type web --workspace "$ws_id"

export KEY_VAULT_URL=$(az keyvault show --name "$vault" \
  --query properties.vaultUri --output tsv)
export APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING=$(az monitor app-insights \
  component show --app lab-appinsights --resource-group "$rg" \
  --query connectionString --output tsv)
export LOG_WORKSPACE_ID=$(az monitor log-analytics workspace show \
  --resource-group "$rg" --workspace-name lab-logs \
  --query customerId --output tsv)

blocks.text:
import os

from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.keyvault.secrets import SecretClient
from azure.monitor.opentelemetry import configure_azure_monitor
from opentelemetry import trace

configure_azure_monitor(logger_name="lab")  # reads the connection string
tracer = trace.get_tracer(__name__)

client = SecretClient(vault_url=os.environ["KEY_VAULT_URL"],
                      credential=DefaultAzureCredential())

with tracer.start_as_current_span("lab-read-greeting") as span:
    greeting = client.get_secret("lab-greeting").value
    span.set_attribute("lab.greeting_length", len(greeting))
    print("read a value of", len(greeting), "characters")

trace.get_tracer_provider().force_flush()  # send before the script exits

blocks.text:
import os
from datetime import timedelta

from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.monitor.query import LogsQueryClient

query = """
union AppRequests, AppDependencies
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where Name has "lab"
| project TimeGenerated, Type, Name, DurationMs, Properties
"""
client = LogsQueryClient(DefaultAzureCredential())
result = client.query_workspace(os.environ["LOG_WORKSPACE_ID"], query,
                                timespan=timedelta(hours=1))
for table in result.tables:
    for row in table.rows:
        print(list(row))
blocks.title: Python · verify.py (azure-monitor-query)

blocks.text: Run python verify.py. You should see a row for lab-read-greeting, a span with no kind that lands among the dependencies, with lab.greeting_length in its Properties column. If nothing comes back, wait a little longer and run the query again, or check that the connection string points to lab-appinsights. A 403 from Key Vault means the role assignment hasn't applied yet or is on another scope.
blocks.title: Verify

blocks.text: Delete the resource group with az group delete --name "$rg". The vault goes into the soft-deleted state rather than disappearing, so its name stays reserved until the retention period ends (90 days by default). Purge protection is off in this lab, so az keyvault purge --name "$vault" frees the name at once by deleting the vault permanently. Otherwise use a new vault name if you repeat the lab.

lessons.title: Commonly confused pairs across the 27 skills
lessons.summary: Twelve pairs of services, options and operators that look alike on the exam, with the one property that tells each pair apart.

blocks.text: Many wrong options on an associate exam are real features that solve a neighbouring problem. For each pair below, learn the deciding property, not a list of features. When a question names a requirement, ask which side of the pair that requirement belongs to. Each pair links back to the skill lessons, where the details and code live.
blocks.title: How to use this lesson

blocks.text:
Learn draws the line between a message and an event:
• A message carries the data itself, and a contract exists between publisher and consumer: the publisher expects the consumer to do the work. Service Bus is the enterprise messaging broker for that. It adds FIFO ordering through sessions, transactions and duplicate detection, and consumers pull messages at their own pace.
• An event is a lightweight notification that something changed, and the publisher has no expectation about how it's handled. Event Grid routes events reactively, in near real time, and its basic tier pushes them to handlers. It gives no ordering guarantee and no duplicate detection.
Both offer at-least-once delivery and dead-lettering, so neither of those decides the choice. Ask instead whether the receiver owes the sender some work (a message) or is simply being told about a change (an event).
blocks.title: Service Bus or Event Grid

blocks.text:
• A queue is point-to-point. Several competing consumers can read from it, but each message is processed by one consumer.
• A topic is publish/subscribe. Each subscription behaves like its own virtual queue and receives a copy of every message sent to the topic, and subscription filters decide which copies a subscription keeps.
The deciding question: how many independent receivers need to see the same message? One worker pool means a queue; several systems that each need their own copy mean a topic with one subscription per system. Consumers read from a subscription, never from the topic itself.
blocks.title: Service Bus queue or topic

blocks.text:
All three are ACR Tasks, so "use ACR Tasks" alone rarely settles a question.
• A quick task is az acr build: one on-demand build of a single image from a context you send, run in Azure and pushed to the registry by default. Nothing is saved for next time.
• A triggered task is a saved definition (az acr task create) that runs again on its own: on a commit or pull request in GitHub or Azure DevOps, on a base image update, or on a timer.
• A multi-step task is a YAML file of steps (build, cmd and push) that can build, test and push several images in one run. A triggered task can run a multi-step file.
Ask whether the requirement is a one-off build, a build that repeats on an event, or a workflow of several steps.
blocks.title: Quick task, triggered task or multi-step task

blocks.text:
• Azure Container Apps runs general-purpose containers and microservices on a managed platform built on Kubernetes, KEDA, Dapr and Envoy. It gives you revisions, traffic splitting, event-driven scaling including scale to zero, and jobs, but no direct access to the Kubernetes API.
• Azure Kubernetes Service gives you a managed Kubernetes platform with direct access to the Kubernetes API, and it can run any Kubernetes workload. In AKS Standard you manage the cluster configuration and operations.
• Azure App Service is fully managed hosting optimized for web applications and web APIs, deployed as code or as containers.
The deciding property is usually the Kubernetes API: a requirement for manifests, custom resources or cluster control points to AKS. A web app or API with no orchestration needs points to App Service, and containerized microservices that should scale on events without a cluster to run point to Container Apps.
blocks.title: Container Apps, AKS or App Service

blocks.text:
• In Container Apps you never install KEDA. You declare scale rules (HTTP, TCP, or custom rules based on a KEDA scaler such as a Service Bus queue), and the platform uses KEDA to apply them.
• In AKS the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) changes the number of pod replicas as CPU, memory or application metrics change. KEDA is an add-on there. It scales on external events such as queues and streams, and it can scale a workload to zero.
• In AKS, KEDA creates and uses an HPA internally. So don't add your own HPA to a workload that a KEDA ScaledObject already scales, because the two autoscalers would compete.
Rule of thumb: event backlog or scale to zero means KEDA (built into Container Apps scale rules, an add-on in AKS); steady CPU or request load on identical replicas means the HPA.
blocks.title: KEDA scale rules or the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler

blocks.text:
Two different sizing currencies:
• Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL charges every operation in request units (RUs), which abstract CPU, IOPS and memory. A point read of a 1 KB item by ID and partition key costs about 1 RU. With provisioned throughput you set RU/s in steps of 100 and pay hourly for what you provision. In serverless mode you provision nothing and pay for the RUs you consume.
• Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server is sized by compute: a pricing tier (Burstable, General Purpose or Memory Optimized), a number of vCores and the memory that comes with them, plus storage.
So a slow or expensive Cosmos DB query is tuned in RUs (indexing policy, consistency, query shape). A PostgreSQL vector workload is tuned in vCores, memory and storage.
blocks.title: Request units or vCores

blocks.text:
Without an index, pgvector runs an exact search: perfect recall, slow at scale. Each index trades some recall for speed in a different way:
• IVFFlat partitions the vectors into lists with k-means. It builds faster and uses less memory than HNSW, but its speed-recall trade-off is weaker.
• HNSW builds a multilayer graph. It takes more time and memory to build than IVFFlat and has the better speed-recall trade-off.
• DiskANN comes from the pg_diskann extension, which depends on the vector extension. Learn describes it as combining highly accurate queries with fast build times, and as scaling to very large datasets.
Learn the trade-offs first: build time, memory and recall.
blocks.title: HNSW, IVFFlat or DiskANN

blocks.text:
• Cache-aside: the application owns the cache. A read checks the cache, and on a miss it loads the item from the data store and adds it to the cache. A write goes to the data store and invalidates the cached item, which is loaded again on the next read. Between the write and that read, a reader can miss or briefly see stale data.
• Write-through: one write operation updates both the data store and the cache, so readers see the new value straight after a successful write.
Cache-aside suits caches that don't offer read-through or write-through themselves, and demand you can't predict. Learn points to write-through when read-heavy paths need read-after-write freshness. Neither pattern guarantees consistency when another process changes the data store behind the cache.
blocks.title: Cache-aside or write-through

blocks.text:
Both let configuration point at a Key Vault secret instead of holding its value, but different components resolve them:
• In App Service, the app setting holds a Key Vault reference. The platform resolves it with the app's managed identity and hands the secret to the app as an ordinary environment variable. The code doesn't change.
• In App Configuration, a key-value with a special content type holds the reference. The configuration provider in your code recognizes it and connects to Key Vault itself, using the credential you pass as keyvault_credential. So the app's identity needs read access to the App Configuration store and to the vault.
Ask who reads the secret: the hosting platform (App Service) or your code through the provider (App Configuration).
blocks.title: Key Vault references in App Service or in App Configuration

blocks.text:
• Access policies are the legacy permission model. Each entry grants a principal a set of permissions on secrets, keys or certificates, with up to 1,024 entries per vault. Anyone whose role lets them write the vault resource, such as Contributor, can grant themselves data-plane access by adding a policy.
• Azure RBAC is the model Learn recommends for new deployments. Built-in data-plane roles separate duties: Key Vault Secrets User reads secret contents, Key Vault Secrets Officer manages secrets, and Key Vault Administrator performs all data-plane operations. Learn recommends one vault per application per environment, with roles assigned at vault scope.
The data-plane roles work only on vaults that use the RBAC permission model.
blocks.title: Access policies or Azure RBAC in Key Vault

blocks.text:
Two different generations of Application Insights sampling share the same words:
• The Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry distro samples whole traces in your process. You choose fixed-rate sampling (a ratio between 0 and 1) or rate-limited sampling (a maximum number of traces per second).
• The classic Application Insights SDKs offer adaptive sampling (on by default in the ASP.NET and ASP.NET Core SDKs and in Azure Functions) and fixed-rate sampling.
• Ingestion sampling is set on the Application Insights resource and drops data where Azure Monitor ingests it. Learn treats it as a fallback, not recommended, for when you can't control sampling at the source, and it's available with either generation. For the classic SDKs, Learn adds that it applies only when no other sampling is in effect.
When you read a sampling question, first check which SDK the app uses. Adaptive sampling belongs to the classic SDKs, and the distro's settings are named differently.
blocks.title: Sampling in the OpenTelemetry distro or in the classic SDKs

blocks.text:
KQL splits each string into terms, which are runs of letters and digits, and indexes every term of three characters or more.
• has matches a whole term. It uses the term index, so it's fast.
• contains matches any substring. It can't use the term index and scans the column, which is much slower.
Both ignore case. Their _cs forms are case-sensitive and run faster. So for the value "Order Shipped", has "shipped" is true because has ignores case, while has_cs "shipped" is false and has_cs "Shipped" is true. Use has for whole words, add _cs when you know the exact case, and use contains only when you really need part of a term.
blocks.title: has or contains in KQL

One consumer per message / a copy for every subscription

lessons.title: Exam technique · How the AI-200 exam runs
lessons.summary: The exam rules that change how you answer: time, Microsoft Learn access, breaks, case studies, problem–solution sets, question kinds and partial credit.

blocks.text: Microsoft doesn't say which question types an exam uses. Instead it offers an exam sandbox, a demo of the role-based exam experience with the same introductory screens and instructions, where you can try each question type in the real interface. If you use assistive devices, it's also where you can see how they and the keyboard work in the exam interface. To use them in the exam itself you need an approved accommodation, because the secure exam browser blocks third-party applications. The sandbox doesn't run that secure browser.
blocks.title: Before the exam: try the sandbox

blocks.text:
• Associate role-based exams without labs give you 100 minutes of exam time inside 120 minutes of seat time. Seat time also covers the instructions, the candidate agreement and optional comments at the end. Exams that may contain labs give 120 minutes of exam time. Microsoft doesn't publish which exams have labs, so read the overview pages when you launch.
• Most exams have 40 to 60 questions. That works out at roughly 2 minutes a question on a 100-minute exam.
• The introduction screen states how many questions and case studies the exam has. Case studies aren't timed separately, and the clock keeps running while you review answers.
blocks.title: Time

blocks.text:
On associate and expert exams, a Microsoft Learn button in the left pane opens Learn in a split screen next to the question. You can open several tabs, drag the splitter and go full screen, and full screen shows the timer and question count. Ctrl+F (Command+F on a Mac) searches the current Learn page, but not the exam window.

The limits matter more than the feature:
• Browsing stays on the Learn domain. Q&A, practice assessments and your profile are blocked, as are links to other sites such as GitHub.
• No extra time is added, and the exam clock keeps running while you read.
• Microsoft says the resource is meant for questions where you may need to look something up. If you use it for every question you won't finish, and that is by design.
Use it for one specific fact, such as a limit or a parameter name, when you have already narrowed the options.
blocks.title: Microsoft Learn during the exam

blocks.text:
• Five minutes of break time are built into the exam time. You can take several breaks of any length, but the exam clock keeps running throughout. If time runs out during a break, the exam is scored on what you completed.
• Before a break starts, the exam shows how many questions you have seen, left unanswered or marked for review. After the break you can't return to any question you saw before it, even an unanswered or marked one.
• You can't take a break in the middle of a lab or a problem–solution set, only before or after one. You can take one during a case study, but you lose access to its questions seen before the break.
• Start a break from the exam interface. Unauthorized materials stay off limits during it.
So finish and review the questions you have seen before you take a break.
blocks.title: Breaks

blocks.text:
A case study describes a business and technical scenario, and several questions draw on it. You can refer back to the scenario details as often as you like while you answer its questions. A review screen at the end of the case lets you change your answers. Once you leave the case, you can't return to its questions.

A good habit: skim the requirements and constraints in the scenario first, then read each question, then go back to the scenario for the details that question needs. Treat the end of a case like a break and review before you move on. In this pack every paper has one case study of five questions, so practise this in each paper.
blocks.title: Case studies

blocks.text:
Some exams include sets of Yes/No questions that share one scenario and problem. Each question proposes a different solution, and you decide whether it meets the stated goal. More than one solution might work, or none of them. Microsoft's guidance for these sets:
• After you answer a question in the set, you can't return to it, and it doesn't appear on the review screen.
• Everything you need is in the problem statement, so don't overthink it. If a solution solves the problem only partly, or is just the first step, the answer is No.
• If you don't know, make your best guess, because you can't come back.
You also can't take a break inside a set. This pack's Yes/No grids are a different format: they put several statements on one screen, so use them for the knowledge, not for the one-way navigation.
blocks.title: Problem–solution sets

blocks.text:
Microsoft's sample videos show these kinds: multiple choice, build list, drag and drop, hot area, active screen, case studies and labs, along with the mark-for-review feature, the review screen, and navigation and the timer. A particular exam might use any of them. Questions that use a different way of scoring say so in the question text.

This pack's formats are practice versions of the same skills, not copies of the exam interface: single and multiple choice, ordering, matching (including Yes/No grids), dropdown completion and numeric answers. Use the sandbox to get used to the real controls.
blocks.title: Question kinds

blocks.text:
• Most multi-part questions give one point for each correct part, so you can earn all, some or none of their points. A question worth more than one point says so.
• Wrong answers cost nothing. There's no penalty for guessing, so answer every question.
• Some questions may be unscored, used only to gather data, and you can't tell which ones they are. Answer each one as if it counts.
• The pass mark is 700 on a scale of 1 to 1,000. It's a scaled score, so it doesn't have to equal 70% of the points. The score report shows your overall score and a bar per skill area, not the questions you got wrong.

In this pack, multiple choice, matching, dropdown and ordering questions give partial credit for each correct part, worth one point in total. Single choice and numeric questions are all or nothing. Partial credit counts towards a paper's 35-point pass line but not towards readiness, which counts only fully correct answers.
blocks.title: Scoring and partial credit

blocks.text:
• Taking a break with unanswered or marked questions: you can't go back to them afterwards.
• Leaving a case study before you review it: its questions are closed once you move on.
• Revisiting a problem–solution answer: you can't, so read the goal closely before you answer.
• Looking up every question on Learn: the clock doesn't stop, and that's by design.
• Leaving a question blank: a guess costs nothing and might score.
blocks.title: Exam traps

blocks.text: Say the introduction screen shows 50 questions, including one case study. Note the end time. At about 2 minutes a question, aim to be past question 25 by the 50-minute mark. Mark the questions you're unsure of and keep moving. When you reach the case study, read its requirements, answer its questions, and use its review screen before you leave. Keep Learn lookups for the few questions where one fact decides the answer. If you need a break, take it just after a review, never with marked questions behind you. Use the last 10 minutes on the final review screen.
blocks.title: Worked example · a 100-minute plan

blocks.text: Question: you're halfway through a case study, three of its questions are marked for review, and you need a break. What should you do first? Solution: review and settle the marked questions, because after a break you can't return to any question you saw before it. You can take the break during the case study, but its earlier questions are then closed, and the clock keeps running while you're away.

lessons.title: Final revision · The last week and the day
lessons.summary: A compact last-week checklist for each domain, weighted like the study guide, and what to do the night before and on the day.

blocks.text: Spend the week roughly in proportion to the domain weights below, and go first to the skills your progress page shows as developing or not started. For each checklist line, explain the answer aloud or on paper without notes. If you can't, reread that skill lesson's exam traps and do a short learning session on the skill. Leave new topics alone in the last two days: review flashcards and your missed questions instead.
blocks.title: How to use the last week

blocks.text: Shares are proportional to the midpoint of each published range (22.5, 27.5, 22.5 and 22.5%). Domain 2 has the most skills, so it gets the least time per skill: spend it on your weakest ones.
blocks.title: Weights and time

blocks.text:
• Registry: choose stable or unique tags, lock what you deploy and free storage from old manifests.
• ACR Tasks: tell a quick task, a triggered task and a multi-step task apart, and name each trigger.
• App Service: set the port, pull with a managed identity and resolve Key Vault references in settings.
• Container Apps: environments, revision modes, traffic splitting, secrets and identity-based image pulls.
• KEDA: write a scale rule for a queue and say how replicas scale out and back in.
• AKS: read a Deployment and Service manifest, and grant the cluster pull access to the registry.
• Troubleshooting: find logs and events for a failing container and test connectivity end to end.
blocks.title: Domain 1 · Containers

blocks.text:
• Cosmos DB SDK: one client per app, query within a partition, and authenticate with Entra roles.
• RUs: what raises a query's cost, and how indexing policy and consistency level change it.
• Cosmos DB vectors: vector policy, vector index types and a VectorDistance query.
• Change feed: the processor's lease container, start position and the modes it supports.
• PostgreSQL: connect with Entra tokens, choose vector types and design the chunks table.
• pgvector indexes: HNSW, IVFFlat and DiskANN, their tuning settings and the distance operators.
• Compute and storage: tier, vCores and memory for an index, and how storage grows.
• RAG: embeddings in the database, metadata filters with vector search, and filtering pitfalls.
• Connections: PgBouncer, pool modes and connection limits.
• Redis: cache-aside, expiry, eviction and invalidation, then vector indexes and semantic caching.
blocks.title: Domain 2 · Data management (the heaviest domain)

blocks.text:
• Service Bus: queues and topics, settlement, sessions, duplicate detection, filters and dead-lettering.
• Event Grid: system and custom topics, event schemas, filters, retries, dead-lettering and validation.
• Functions: Python v2 triggers and bindings, connections by identity, HTTP auth levels and keys.
• Deployment: hosting plans (Flex Consumption above all), app settings and the deployment methods.
blocks.title: Domain 3 · Connect and consume

blocks.text:
• Key Vault: SecretClient calls, RBAC roles, soft-delete and purge protection, and rotation.
• App Configuration: keys and labels, the Python provider, dynamic refresh and feature flags.
• OpenTelemetry: the Azure Monitor distro, resources and spans, context propagation and sampling.
• KQL: the Application Insights tables, where/summarize/join, percentiles, string operators and render.
blocks.title: Domain 4 · Secure, monitor, troubleshoot

blocks.text:
• Confirm your appointment time, and for an online exam, check your room, desk and computer against the provider's requirements.
• Run through the exam sandbox once more if the controls still feel unfamiliar.
• Reread Commonly confused pairs and the exam traps in your three weakest skill lessons. Don't start a new paper.
• Sleep. A tired candidate loses more points than one more hour of review gains.
blocks.title: The night before

blocks.text:
• Read the overview pages: they give the number of questions and case studies, and say whether there are labs.
• Watch the clock: about 2 minutes a question on 50 questions in 100 minutes. Mark doubtful questions and move on.
• Answer every question. Wrong answers cost nothing.
• Review before you leave a case study and before any break, because neither lets you go back.
• In a problem–solution set, judge each solution on its own. A partial fix or a first step is No.
• Use Microsoft Learn for one fact you can name, not to read up on a topic.
blocks.title: On the day

blocks.text: Pick the two skills your progress page shows as weakest. For each one, say in two sentences what problem the service solves and which option it's most often confused with. If you can't, that's tonight's reading: the skill lesson's exam traps, then the matching pair in Commonly confused pairs.

questions.prompt: Container apps in West Europe and East US pull a large image from a Standard registry in West Europe, and pulls in East US are slow. You need one registry name with network-close pulls in both regions. What should you do?

options.text: Keep Standard and rely on its default zone redundancy in West Europe
Upgrade the registry to Premium and add an East US geo-replica
Reference the image by digest instead of by tag in the East US apps
Create a second Standard registry in East US and push each build to both

questions.explanation: Geo-replication is a Premium feature that keeps one registry name while serving pulls from a replica in each chosen region, so East US pulls no longer travel to West Europe. A second registry means a second name and a second push for every build, and zone redundancy only spreads data across zones inside one region. Pulling by digest changes which image is pulled, not where it's served from.

questions.prompt: A team wants every production rollback to pull exactly the build that was tested. Which TWO image references should its deployments use? Select TWO.

options.text: A unique tag that carries the build ID
A major-version tag such as 1
A minor-version tag such as 1.4 that receives patches
The manifest digest (sha256) of the build
The latest tag, re-pushed after each build

questions.explanation: A unique tag is never reused and a digest identifies one exact manifest, so both keep pointing at the tested image after later pushes; Learn recommends unique tags for deployments. Stable tags such as latest, 1 or 1.4 are moved to newer images as patches ship, so a rollback through them can pull an image that was never tested.

questions.prompt: Complete the Azure CLI commands that protect images in the contosoai registry.

slots.text: Release docs-api:1.4.2 can be neither overwritten nor deleted: az acr repository update -n contosoai --image docs-api:1.4.2

options.text: --write-enabled false
--read-enabled false
--delete-enabled false

slots.text: The docs-api repository can't be deleted, but new tags can still be pushed: az acr repository update -n contosoai --repository docs-api

options.text: --delete-enabled false --write-enabled true
--read-enabled false --write-enabled true
--write-enabled false --delete-enabled true

slots.text: Recalled image docs-api:1.3.0 must no longer be pulled: az acr repository update -n contosoai --image docs-api:1.3.0

options.text: --write-enabled false
--read-enabled false
--delete-enabled false

questions.explanation: Setting write-enabled to false locks a tag against both overwrite and deletion, whereas delete-enabled false on its own still lets a push replace the tag. On a repository, delete-enabled false with write-enabled true stops deletion of the repository while pushes keep working; write-enabled false would lock every image in it. Only read-enabled false blocks pulls, because the write and delete flags leave reads allowed.

questions.prompt: A nightly build re-pushes docs-api:3 with OS patches, and registry storage keeps growing although the number of tags stays flat. What should you do?

options.text: Lock the docs-api:3 tag with write-enabled false so that it stops changing
Switch the nightly build to unique build-ID tags instead of docs-api:3
Move the registry to a tier that includes more storage in its daily rate
Delete the untagged manifests left behind, by manifest digest

questions.explanation: When a stable tag such as 3 moves to a new build, the previous manifest loses its tag but stays in the registry with its unique layers, so storage climbs while the tag list looks unchanged; deleting those manifests by digest removes them and their unique layer data. acr purge --untagged in a scheduled task and the Premium retention policy can automate this, but both are preview, and the policy covers only manifests untagged after it takes effect. Locking the tag would break the nightly patch builds, and unique tags or a larger tier leave the old manifests in place.

questions.prompt: For each statement about Azure Container Registry tiers, select Yes or No.

options.text: No
Yes

slots.text: Changing a registry from Standard to Premium causes a short outage for pulls.
A Premium registry with connected registries must have them deleted before it can move to Standard.
Basic registries can send webhook notifications.
Private endpoints can be used with a Standard registry.

questions.explanation: Changing tiers causes no downtime, but Premium-only resources such as connected registries have to be deleted before a move down to Standard or Basic. Every tier has webhooks (Basic allows two), while private endpoints need a Premium registry.

questions.prompt: An administrator put a CanNotDelete resource lock on a registry, yet a developer later deleted a released image tag from it. What would have prevented the deletion?

options.text: Setting write-enabled to false on the image with az acr repository update
Changing the registry's resource lock from CanNotDelete to ReadOnly
Relying on zone redundancy to keep a copy of the deleted image tag
Adding the same CanNotDelete lock to the registry's resource group

questions.explanation: Azure resource locks protect management operations on the registry resource, such as deleting the registry or its replications, and leave repository data alone, so tags and manifests stay deletable whatever lock type is used or wherever it's inherited from. An image lock set with az acr repository update and write-enabled false is what blocks both overwriting and deleting the image. Zone redundancy keeps the registry available during a zone outage; it doesn't keep deleted data.

questions.prompt: The tags ranker:latest and ranker:v3 point to the same manifest in the acrml registry. You must remove the latest tag while ranker:v3 stays pullable. Which command should you run?

options.text: az acr repository delete --name acrml --image ranker:latest
az acr repository untag --name acrml --image ranker:latest
az acr repository delete --name acrml --image ranker@<digest of latest>
az acr repository update --name acrml --image ranker:latest --list-enabled false

questions.explanation: Untagging removes only the tag reference, so the manifest, its layers and the v3 tag stay in the registry. Deleting by tag deletes the manifest together with every tag that points to it, which would take v3 as well, and deleting by digest has the same effect. list-enabled is a changeable attribute of the image, so setting it changes how the image is listed and leaves the tag in place.

questions.prompt: During a release, deployment pipelines from five teams get HTTP 429 responses from a Premium registry, although the request rate for the registry as a whole is well below its limit. Every pipeline signs in with the registry's admin user. What should you do?

options.text: Spread the pipelines across the admin user's two passwords
Ask Azure Support to raise the registry's per-registry request limit
Give each pipeline its own Microsoft Entra identity for registry access
Enable anonymous pull access so that the pipelines skip authentication

questions.explanation: All requests that authenticate with admin credentials count as one identity for throttling, whichever of the two passwords they use, so five teams share one per-identity bucket and exhaust it while the registry still has spare capacity. Separate Entra identities each get their own per-identity limit. Anonymous requests are also throttled together as a single identity, and a higher per-registry limit doesn't help when the per-identity limit is the one being reached.

questions.prompt: A Standard registry in a region with availability zones shows zoneRedundancy as Disabled in the portal, and the registry must keep serving pulls during a single-zone outage. What change is required?

options.text: Upgrade to Premium and set zoneRedundancy to Enabled
Recreate the registry with --zone-redundancy and import the images
Leave it as it is; the registry is zone-redundant already
Add a geo-replica in another region of the same geography

questions.explanation: Zone redundancy is on by default, at no extra cost, for every tier in regions that support availability zones, and the zoneRedundancy property is a legacy value that no longer reflects or controls it. Upgrading, recreating or setting the property changes nothing in such a region, and a geo-replica is a Premium feature for regional resilience rather than something this requirement needs. Zone redundancy used to be a Premium-only opt-in, which is why the property can still read Disabled.

questions.prompt: You delete a repository whose images share some layers with images in another repository of the same registry. Which TWO statements are true? Select TWO.

options.text: Billing for the freed storage stops right away
Untagging the images first would have freed more space
The reported storage usage drops at the same moment
Layers that other images still reference are kept
All layers that the repository's images used are removed

questions.explanation: Billing for deleted image data ends immediately, but the registry reclaims the space in an asynchronous clean-up, so the usage figure falls only later. A layer's data is deleted only when no remaining image references it, so the layers shared with the other repository stay. Untagging frees nothing at all, because the manifests and layers remain.

questions.prompt: For each statement about Container Registry tiers and usage reporting, select Yes or No.

options.text: No
Yes

slots.text: Customer-managed encryption keys require the Premium tier.
Private endpoints are available in the Basic tier.
For a geo-replicated registry, total storage is the home region's usage multiplied by the number of replicas.
Basic and Standard registries have the same storage limit as Premium.

questions.explanation: Customer-managed keys appear only in the Premium column, and so does private link with private endpoints, which Basic and Standard registries lack. Usage in a geo-replicated registry is reported for the home region, so total storage is that figure times the replica count. Basic and Standard registries can grow to 40 TiB, while Premium allows 100 TiB.

questions.prompt: Complete the Python release script that locks the deployed build by using the azure-containerregistry package.

slots.text: ContainerRegistryClient(endpoint, DefaultAzureCredential(), audience=...), with endpoint set to

options.text: "https://acrml.azurecr.io"
"acrml.azurecr.io:443"
"https://management.azure.com"

slots.text: Block overwrite and deletion of the deployed digest: client.update_manifest_properties(repo, digest, ...)

options.text: can_write=False, can_delete=False
can_read=False, can_delete=False
can_write=True, can_delete=False

slots.text: Walk through each repository in the registry

options.text: client.list_manifest_properties(repo)
client.list_repository_names()
client.get_manifest_properties(repo, tag)

questions.explanation: The client takes the login server with its https scheme as the endpoint, while the Resource Manager URL belongs in audience. Setting can_write and can_delete to False locks the manifest against overwrite and deletion, whereas can_read set to False would block pulls of the build you just released, and can_write True leaves it open to overwrite. list_repository_names iterates the repositories; the manifest calls work inside one repository.

questions.prompt: Which registry tier is the lowest that meets Alpine Ski House's network requirement for its container registry?

options.text: Premium
Standard, with public IP network rules for the company's address range
Standard
Basic

questions.explanation: Private endpoints through Private Link are a Premium feature, so Premium is the lowest tier that can limit the registry to a private endpoint in the company's virtual network. Basic and Standard offer no private endpoints, and public IP network rules are Premium-only as well, so a Standard registry can't be restricted that way either.

questions.prompt: A pipeline agent has no Docker engine, but the pipeline must build the Dockerfile in the repository and push the result to the contosoai registry. Which command should the pipeline run?

options.text: az acr import --name contosoai --source docs-api:v7
az acr login --name contosoai, then docker build and docker push
az acr task logs --registry contosoai --name docs-api
az acr build --registry contosoai --image docs-api:v7 .

questions.explanation: az acr build runs an ACR quick task: it uploads the build context, builds the image in Azure and pushes it to the registry, so the agent needs no local Docker engine. Signing in and then running docker build and docker push still needs an engine on the agent, az acr import only copies an image that already exists, and az acr task logs shows the output of earlier runs.

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order so that docs-api is rebuilt automatically whenever its Python base image is patched.

options.text: Check the automatically started run with az acr task logs
Run the task once with az acr task run so that it records the base image dependency
Import the patched version of the base image into contosoai
Import the Python base image into contosoai and create a task that builds FROM the imported image

questions.explanation: Keeping a copy of the base image in your own registry means an update triggers the task at once instead of after a 10 to 60 minute check of the public repository. The task, whose base image trigger is on by default, has to run once before ACR Tasks knows the dependency; after that, updating the image behind the stable tag starts a rebuild, and runs started by a trigger keep their logs for az acr task logs.

questions.prompt: Match each build requirement to the ACR Tasks feature that meets it.

options.text: Timer trigger
Pull request trigger
Source code commit trigger
Quick task (az acr build)
Base image update trigger

slots.text: Rebuild whenever code is pushed to the main branch
Rebuild when the FROM image receives OS patches
Run an image maintenance step every night
Build once from a laptop that has no Docker engine

questions.explanation: Commit triggers, on by default for a Git context, react to pushes; base image triggers react to updates of the image named in FROM; timer triggers run a task on a schedule; and az acr build is the on-demand quick task. A pull request trigger is off by default and fires when a pull request is opened or updated, so it fits none of these requirements.

questions.prompt: An ACR task builds FROM python:3.12.7-slim. The maintainers then publish python:3.12.8-slim, yet the task never runs. Why?

options.text: Base image tracking works for images in Azure registries, not Docker Hub
ACR Tasks checks public base images once a day, so the run is still pending
A new version tag leaves 3.12.7-slim untouched; build FROM a stable tag like 3.12-slim
Base image triggers are off by default and must be enabled on each task

questions.explanation: A base image trigger fires when the image behind the referenced tag is updated, and publishing a new version tag leaves 3.12.7-slim exactly as it was. Building from a stable tag such as 3.12-slim, which the maintainers move to each patch, lets the trigger fire. Base image triggers are enabled by default, and public Docker Hub and Microsoft Container Registry images are checked every 10 to 60 minutes.

questions.prompt: An ACR task builds a two-stage Dockerfile: the build stage starts FROM python:3.12 and the final stage starts FROM python:3.12-slim. Patches to python:3.12 never start a run, while patches to python:3.12-slim do. Why?

options.text: Tracking covers the runtime stage's base image, not build stages
A task follows the first build stage's FROM line, not the last one
Docker Hub base images have to be imported before any tracking works
python:3.12 counts as a version tag, which can't trigger a task

questions.explanation: ACR Tasks discovers base image dependencies when it builds, but it currently follows updates only for the application, or runtime, image and not for intermediate build-time images in a multi-stage Dockerfile, so only patches to python:3.12-slim start a run. Docker Hub repositories are tracked by polling every 10 to 60 minutes without any import, and python:3.12 is a stable tag that receives patches.

questions.prompt: A quick task builds an image for edge devices with 64-bit ARM processors, and the image fails to start on them. What should you change?

options.text: Run the build on a dedicated agent pool in a Premium registry
Add --platform Linux/arm64 to the az acr build command
Push the image with a tag that ends in -arm64
Enable a base image trigger for the ARM variant of the FROM image

questions.explanation: ACR Tasks builds for Linux on AMD64 unless you say otherwise, so the default output doesn't run on ARM hardware; --platform takes an OS and architecture, with an optional variant such as Linux/arm64/v8. An agent pool changes where the build runs rather than what it targets, and neither a trigger nor a tag name changes the binaries inside the image.

questions.prompt: A developer runs az acr build from a project folder that holds a .env file with an API key, and the key ends up inside the image. What should the developer do?

options.text: List .env in a .dockerignore file at the root of the build context
Run the build on a dedicated agent pool in a Premium registry
Start the build with az acr task run instead of az acr build
Pass the key with --build-arg on the az acr build command line instead

questions.explanation: Keeping secrets out of images is the user's job, and az acr build applies .dockerignore rules before it uploads a local folder, so an ignored .env file never reaches the build. Passing the key on the command line is worse, because ACR diagnostic tracing can log command-line values. Another agent or another command still builds from the same folder contents.

questions.prompt: A multi-step task must push each image to the registry it runs in and to a second registry that production reads from. Which TWO actions are recommended? Select TWO.

options.text: Pass the second registry's login server with --context
Enable the pull request trigger on the task
Create a service principal with AcrPush on the second registry
Grant the service principal AcrPull on the second registry
Run az acr task credential add with the second registry's login server

questions.explanation: By default a task can push and pull only in the registry where it runs, so another registry needs credentials added to the task with az acr task credential add. Learn suggests a service principal for them, with AcrPush on a registry without ABAC repository permissions (Container Registry Repository Writer on one that uses them). AcrPull allows pulls only, and --context names the source code location, not a push target.

questions.prompt: Complete the multi-step task file and the command that registers it, so that each commit to main is built, smoke-tested and then pushed.

slots.text: Keep the test container running in the background while later steps call it (cmd step property)

options.text: async: true
background: true
detach: true

slots.text: Step type that sends the tested image to the run registry

options.text: cmd
build
push

slots.text: Tag value that differs for every run

options.text: {{.Run.ID}}
{{.Run.Registry}}
latest

slots.text: az acr task create --registry acrml --name ranker-ci --context <repository URL>#main

options.text: --file taskmulti.yaml --git-access-token $PAT
--cmd taskmulti.yaml --git-access-token $PAT
--file taskmulti.yaml --schedule "0 2 * * *"

questions.explanation: detach: true starts a cmd step's container in the background so that later steps can test it, and a push step then sends the tested image to the run registry. {{.Run.ID}} is a run variable that is unique to each run, whereas {{.Run.Registry}} names the registry and latest is reused. --file points the task at the YAML file in the repository and the Git access token lets ACR Tasks install the commit webhook; a timer schedule would build nightly instead of on each commit.

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order to rebuild an image on each commit to a private GitHub repository and confirm that the trigger works.

options.text: Run az acr task list-runs and check that the newest run shows the Commit trigger
Create a GitHub personal access token with full repo scope
Run az acr task create with the repository context and --git-access-token
Push a commit to the branch that the task watches

questions.explanation: The task needs the token when it's created, because ACR Tasks uses it to set up the webhook in the repository, and a private repository needs the full repo scope. A pushed commit can start a run only after the task and its webhook exist, and list-runs then shows Commit in the trigger column for that run.

questions.prompt: Which approach meets Margie's Travel's requirement for building container images on each merge?

options.text: Create an ACR task with a commit trigger so that each merge starts a build
Enable the pull request trigger on an ACR task for each repository
Run az acr build from the CI pipeline after each merge
Create a timer-triggered ACR task that builds main every 15 minutes

questions.explanation: ACR Tasks doesn't support commit or pull request triggers for GitHub Enterprise repositories, where Margie's Travel keeps its container projects, so a task can't react to merges on its own. A CI pipeline that runs on each merge can start a quick task with az acr build, which builds the image in Azure and pushes it to the registry. A timer builds on a schedule whether or not anything merged, so it doesn't tie one image to each merge.

questions.prompt: A Linux custom container on App Service runs gunicorn on port 8000, and the site fails to start because the platform sends requests to port 80. What should you configure?

options.text: A ports entry of 8000 in a Docker Compose file for the app
The WEBSITES_ENABLE_APP_SERVICE_STORAGE app setting set to true
The WEBSITES_PORT app setting with the value 8000
The CONTAINER_AVAILABILITY_CHECK_MODE app setting set to Repair
