questions.explanation: App Service assumes a custom container listens on port 80 and forwards traffic to the port named in WEBSITES_PORT when it listens elsewhere; only one HTTP port can be exposed. Docker Compose ignores ports other than 80 and 8080 and is being retired in favour of sidecars, the storage setting only controls whether /home persists, and the availability check mode applies to Windows containers.

questions.prompt: Complete the configuration that gives an App Service container the embeddings key from Key Vault.

slots.text: Reference string inside @Microsoft.KeyVault(...)

options.text: SecretName=<secret URI>
SecretUri=<secret URI>
KeyUri=<secret URI>

slots.text: Role for the app's managed identity on the vault

options.text: Key Vault Crypto User
Key Vault Reader
Key Vault Secrets User

slots.text: With an unpinned reference, a rotated version is picked up without a restart

options.text: only after the next deployment
within 30 minutes
within 24 hours

questions.explanation: A reference names its secret with SecretUri, or with VaultName plus SecretName, and the app's identity needs Key Vault Secrets User, because Key Vault Reader sees metadata but not secret values and Crypto User covers key operations. Without a pinned version, App Service caches resolved values and fetches them again every 24 hours, or at once when a configuration change restarts the app; 30 minutes is the Container Apps refresh window.

questions.prompt: Which TWO actions let App Service pull its image from Azure Container Registry without storing any registry credentials? Select TWO.

options.text: Grant the app's managed identity Key Vault Secrets User on a vault
Set WEBSITES_ENABLE_APP_SERVICE_STORAGE to true on the app
Grant the app's managed identity the AcrPull role on the registry
Set acrUseManagedIdentityCreds to true in the site configuration
Enable the registry admin user and save its password as an app setting

questions.explanation: A managed identity pull has two parts: the identity holds AcrPull on the registry, and the site is told to use it through acrUseManagedIdentityCreds (plus acrUserManagedIdentityID for a user-assigned identity); the registry must also accept ARM audience tokens. The admin user means storing a password, a Key Vault role grants nothing on the registry, and the storage setting only controls /home persistence.

questions.prompt: Staging and production slots must each keep their own Key Vault reference, pointing at kv-staging and kv-prod, after every swap. What should you do?

options.text: Give the production slot's identity access to the staging vault
Mark each Key Vault reference setting as a deployment slot setting
Pin each reference to a specific secret version in its URI
Put both references in one setting separated by a semicolon

questions.explanation: Slot settings stay with their slot during a swap, so each environment keeps the reference to its own vault; Learn suggests this for most Key Vault references because each environment should have a separate vault. Two references in one setting don't form a valid reference, pinning a version controls rotation rather than swap behaviour, and cross-vault access mixes the environments.

questions.prompt: After a deployment, an App Service container reads the literal text @Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=...) from its OPENAI_KEY setting instead of the key. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Linux custom containers receive changed app settings only after a manual restart of the app
The secret was rotated recently, and its new version reaches the app within 24 hours
App settings that hold references must be resolved in code with the Key Vault SDK
The reference wasn't resolved, for example because the identity can't read the secret

questions.explanation: When App Service can't resolve a Key Vault reference, it passes the reference string itself to the app, most often because the identity lacks Key Vault Secrets User or a Get permission, the secret no longer exists, or the syntax is wrong; the setting's edit dialog and the Key Vault Application Settings Diagnostics detector show the reason. References need no code changes, a pending rotation still delivers the previous value, and changing an app setting restarts the app by itself, with no manual step.

questions.prompt: After the registry is restricted as Alpine Ski House requires, the web app can no longer pull its image. What should you configure?

options.text: Virtual network integration plus the vnetImagePullEnabled setting
Anonymous pull access on the registry for the assistant's repository
The app's outbound IP addresses in the registry's network rules
The registry's admin credentials in place of the managed identity

questions.explanation: A registry that accepts only private endpoint traffic can be reached only from inside the virtual network, so the app needs virtual network integration, DNS that resolves the private endpoint, and the vnetImagePullEnabled site setting, which routes the image pull through that network. Outbound IP rules don't help when public access is closed, and anonymous access or admin credentials change how the pull authenticates, not the network path it takes.

questions.prompt: A Linux App Service app is integrated with a virtual network, and its Key Vault references stop resolving after the vault is limited to a private endpoint in that network. What should you change?

options.text: Give the app's identity the Key Vault Reader role on the vault
Allow the app's public outbound IP addresses in the vault's network firewall
Set vnetRouteAllEnabled to true to route all outbound traffic
Pin each Key Vault reference to a specific secret version

questions.explanation: Linux apps that call private endpoints must be configured to route all traffic through the virtual network, except function apps on Flex Consumption, which do it automatically, and vnetRouteAllEnabled turns that on. Learn advises against depending on the app's public outbound addresses, because the source address of secret requests can differ, and a pinned version or a metadata-only role doesn't change the network path.

questions.prompt: After you point a custom container app at a new image tag, responses keep coming from the old build for several minutes. What explains this?

options.text: The new tag has to be locked before App Service can pull it
The old container serves until the new one has started and is ready
Image settings are refetched on the platform's 24-hour cycle
Image changes reach the container only after a manual restart

questions.explanation: When container settings change, App Service pulls and starts the new container while the old one keeps answering, and it sends requests to the new container only once it has started and is ready, which can take a few minutes. The 24-hour refetch applies to Key Vault reference values, and no lock or manual restart is needed for the switch.

questions.prompt: A Linux custom container app is scaled out from two to six instances, and the new instances take far longer to start than restarts of the existing ones. Why?

options.text: New instances pull all layers; restarts reuse layers on local disk
Scaling out moves the app to a tier that has slower container storage
App Service builds the image from its Dockerfile on each new instance
New instances, unlike restarts, wait for the Key Vault references to refresh

questions.explanation: App Service keeps pulled layers on the instance's disk and, on a restart, pulls only the layers that changed, but an instance that is new to the app, after a scale-out or a tier change, has to pull them all. App Service runs the image it's given rather than building it, and scaling out adds instances in the same tier.

questions.prompt: Clients reach a Python custom container on App Service over HTTPS. How should the container handle TLS?

options.text: Load a certificate into gunicorn and listen on port 443
Enable persistent storage so that certificates survive restarts
Serve plain HTTP, because TLS ends at the platform's front ends
Set WEBSITES_PORT to 443 so that encrypted traffic is forwarded

questions.explanation: App Service terminates TLS at front ends inside Azure datacenters, so TLS requests never reach the container, and Learn says the app doesn't need to, and shouldn't, implement TLS itself. A certificate in gunicorn or a forwarded port 443 adds work the platform already does, and storage settings don't change where TLS ends.

questions.prompt: A team stores APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING for an App Service app as a Key Vault reference. Which TWO statements are true? Select TWO.

options.text: The portal can no longer show the app's telemetry through that setting
The setting has to be a deployment slot setting to resolve
The connection string isn't treated as a secret, so a plain setting is an option
The app sends no telemetry until the reference is pinned to a version
Resolving the connection string needs the Key Vault Crypto User role

questions.explanation: The portal reads this setting to surface the app's telemetry and can't when it holds a Key Vault reference, so you open the Application Insights resource directly instead. Because the connection string isn't considered a secret, Learn suggests a plain setting may be simpler. The reference resolves like any other, with Key Vault Secrets User or the Get permission, and needs no pinned version or slot setting.

questions.prompt: Complete the Azure CLI values for an App Service app that uses one user-assigned identity for both image pulls and Key Vault references.

slots.text: az webapp config set ... --generic-configurations, with acrUserManagedIdentityID set to

options.text: the identity's client ID
the identity's principal ID
the identity's resource ID

slots.text: az webapp update ... --set keyVaultReferenceIdentity= followed by

options.text: the identity's principal ID
the identity's resource ID
the identity's client ID

slots.text: Later, to return Key Vault references to the system-assigned identity, set keyVaultReferenceIdentity to

options.text: Default
None
SystemAssigned

questions.explanation: acrUserManagedIdentityID, used for image pulls, takes the identity's client ID, whereas keyVaultReferenceIdentity takes the identity's full resource ID, a difference that often breaks one of the two features. Setting keyVaultReferenceIdentity to SystemAssigned sends every reference in the app back to the system-assigned identity. The principal ID fits neither property.

questions.prompt: Match each App Service requirement to the app setting that meets it.

options.text: WEBSITE_ENABLE_SYNC_UPDATE_SITE
WEBSITE_SKIP_CONTENTSHARE_VALIDATION
CONTAINER_AVAILABILITY_CHECK_MODE
WEBSITES_ENABLE_APP_SERVICE_STORAGE
WEBSITE_MEMORY_LIMIT_MB

slots.text: Keep files written under /home across restarts of a Linux custom container
Mount an Azure Files content share whose connection string is a Key Vault reference
Finish an app settings update before a dependent template resource deploys
Cap the memory that a Windows container can use

questions.explanation: WEBSITES_ENABLE_APP_SERVICE_STORAGE turns on persistent /home storage, which is off by default for Linux custom containers. A Key Vault reference in the content share connection string can't be resolved during validation, so WEBSITE_SKIP_CONTENTSHARE_VALIDATION set to 1 skips the check and you create the share in advance. WEBSITE_ENABLE_SYNC_UPDATE_SITE makes the settings update synchronous, and WEBSITE_MEMORY_LIMIT_MB sets a Windows container's memory limit. CONTAINER_AVAILABILITY_CHECK_MODE decides what happens when a Windows container's health pings fail.

questions.prompt: For each statement about resolving App Service Key Vault references, select Yes or No.

options.text: No
Yes

slots.text: If a setting's edit dialog shows no resolution status, the value isn't recognized as a reference.
With a vault limited to the app's virtual network, a 403 SecretGet from the app's public IP address in the audit log means that resolution failed.
keyVaultReferenceIdentity applies to all Key Vault references in the app.
The VaultName and SecretName form can't select a specific secret version.

questions.explanation: A missing status message in the setting's edit dialog means the syntax wasn't recognized as a Key Vault reference. A failed SecretGet from the public outbound address can appear by design and is followed by a successful one from the private address. The identity property applies app-wide, and the VaultName form accepts an optional SecretVersion.

questions.prompt: Which change to a container app creates a new revision?

options.text: Changing traffic weights between revisions
Adding a secret to the app
Updating the image tag in the app template
Switching ingress from external to internal

questions.explanation: Revision-scope settings live under properties.template, such as the container image, its environment variables and scale rules, and changing them creates a new revision. Secrets, traffic weights and ingress settings live under properties.configuration, so they apply to every revision without creating one.

questions.prompt: Complete the settings Contoso uses to send 10 percent of docs-api traffic to a new revision and give testers a fixed URL for it.

slots.text: ARM property configuration.activeRevisionsMode

options.text: latest
multiple
single

slots.text: az containerapp ingress traffic set -n docs-api -g rg-docs

options.text: --revision-weight docs-api--v1=90 docs-api--v2=10
--label-weight docs-api--v1=90 docs-api--v2=10
--revision-weight docs-api--v1=100 docs-api--v2=10

slots.text: Tester URL that you can later point at the next revision without changing it

options.text: the app's main application URL
the docs-api--v2 revision's own URL
a label assigned to docs-api--v2

questions.explanation: Traffic can be split only when the app runs in multiple revision mode, and the weights of all rules must add up to 100, so 90 and 10 is the valid split. --label-weight expects label names, and docs-api--v1 can't be a label because label names may not contain two consecutive dashes. Each revision also has its own direct URL, but only a label's URL can be moved to a later revision while staying the same, and the main application URL follows the traffic weights.

questions.prompt: You run az containerapp create with --secrets that use keyvaultref and set identityref to the system-assigned identity, and creation fails. What should you change?

options.text: Grant the environment's Log Analytics workspace access to the vault
Move the keyvaultref value from --secrets into --env-vars
Wait for the system-assigned identity's role assignment to propagate, then retry
Use a user-assigned identity that already has access to the vault

questions.explanation: During az containerapp create the app's system-assigned identity doesn't exist yet, so a Key Vault reference can only resolve through a user-assigned identity that was given Key Vault Secrets User beforehand. Waiting can't help an identity that is created only with the app, Log Analytics plays no part in secrets, and environment variables point at secrets with secretref instead of holding keyvaultref values.

questions.prompt: You changed the value of the embeddings-key secret stored directly in a container app, but the running revision still uses the old value. What should you do?

options.text: Switch the app from single to multiple revision mode
Wait up to 30 minutes for the platform to refresh the value
Run az containerapp secret set again with the same value
Restart the active revision or deploy a new revision

questions.explanation: Secrets are application-scoped: changing one creates no revision and doesn't reach running replicas, so you restart the revision or deploy a new one to load the value. The automatic refresh within 30 minutes applies to Key Vault references without a version, not to values stored in the app, and neither the revision mode nor sending the same value again reloads it.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements describe a Workload profiles environment in Container Apps? Select TWO.

options.text: It can't scale any app to zero replicas
It's the legacy type kept for older environments
It's the default type for new environments
It supports the Consumption plan and nothing else
It supports both the Consumption and Dedicated plans

questions.explanation: Workload profiles is the default environment type, and it can run apps on the Consumption plan, with scale to zero, as well as on Dedicated workload profiles with reserved hardware. The Consumption only type is the legacy one, and it is the type that supports only the Consumption plan.

questions.prompt: Contoso's test and production container apps must never share compute and must write logs to different workspaces. What should you do?

options.text: Create a separate Container Apps environment for each stage
Use one container app in multiple revision mode with labels test and prod
Keep one environment and give each app its own dedicated workload profile
Keep one environment and set the test app's ingress to internal

questions.explanation: Learn advises separate environments when apps must never share compute or must be isolated by stage, and logging is configured per environment, so two environments give two workspaces. A dedicated workload profile in a shared environment still sends every app's logs to the environment's one destination, labels only route traffic between revisions of one app, and internal ingress changes reachability, not isolation.

questions.prompt: Which approach meets Lucerne Publishing's access requirement for its on-call operators?

options.text: The built-in Reader role, plus Key Vault Secrets User on the vault
A custom role that lists the actions they need and leaves out listSecrets
The built-in Container Apps Contributor role at the resource group scope
The built-in Container Apps Operator role at the app's scope

questions.explanation: Container Apps exposes a listSecrets operation that returns secret values in plain text, and both the Contributor and the Operator roles reach it through wildcard actions, whatever their descriptions suggest. A custom role that names only the operations the operators need, with no listSecrets and no wildcard action, lets them restart revisions without reading secrets. Reader can't restart anything, and Key Vault Secrets User would let them read the secret values directly from the vault.

questions.prompt: A container app in multiple revision mode has the ingress traffic rule latestRevision: true with weight 100, so each new revision takes all traffic once it's ready. New revisions must be tested on their own URLs before users reach them. What should you change?

options.text: Switch the app to single revision mode for the duration of testing
Deactivate each new revision until its testing has finished
Give weight 100 to the known-good revision by its name
Assign a label to the known-good revision and keep the weights as they are

questions.explanation: Pinning the main URL's traffic to a named revision keeps users on the known-good version while new revisions stay reachable on their own endpoints for testing. Single revision mode moves traffic to each new revision automatically, a deactivated revision can't be tested, and a label adds a separate URL for one revision without changing how traffic to the app's main URL is split.

questions.prompt: Revision search-api--r7 carries the label beta, and you run az containerapp revision label add with --label qa for the same revision. What is the result?

options.text: qa is added, and beta moves to the previous revision
qa replaces beta, because a revision carries one label at a time
The command fails until the beta label is removed
The revision carries both labels, and each label gets its own URL

questions.explanation: A label points at one revision at a time and a revision holds one label, so label add on a revision that already has a label replaces the existing one. The command neither fails nor moves the old label to another revision.

questions.prompt: You must remove the old-search-key secret from a container app whose active revision reads it through an environment variable. What should you do first?

options.text: Remove the secret, and then restart the active revision to pick up the change
Switch the app to multiple revision mode before you remove the secret
Set the secret's value to an empty string, and then remove the secret itself
Deploy a revision without the reference, then deactivate those that use it

questions.explanation: Learn's order is to deploy a new revision without the reference first and then deactivate every revision that still references the secret, so nothing that runs depends on it when it's deleted. Removing the secret while a revision still references it leaves that revision pointing at a secret that's gone, which a restart would expose, and blanking the value or changing the revision mode leaves the reference in place.

questions.prompt: A revision's running status shows Activation failed. What does this status mean?

options.text: Its first replica failed to provision
It has zero replicas and starts one when a scale rule fires
At least one of its running replicas is in a failed state
It's moving from active to inactive and removing its resources

questions.explanation: Activation failed means the revision had no running replicas and its first replica couldn't be provisioned. At least one failed replica among running ones is reported as Degraded, zero replicas waiting for a scale rule is Scale to 0, and moving to inactive is Deprovisioning.

questions.prompt: Which TWO changes to a running container app take effect without creating a new revision? Select TWO.

options.text: Assigning a user-assigned managed identity to the app
Changing CPU and memory with az containerapp revision copy
Switching the revision mode from single to multiple
Adding an environment variable to the app's container
Setting a new revision suffix for the app

questions.explanation: The revision mode sits in properties.configuration, and Learn states that changing it creates no revision; adding, removing or changing a managed identity neither restarts the app nor creates a revision, except for apps deployed before April 11, 2022. The revision suffix, container resources and environment variables live in properties.template, so each of those changes produces a new revision.

questions.prompt: Which TWO conditions lead to the automatic deletion of a Container Apps environment when they last for more than 90 days? Select TWO.

options.text: Its apps run on the Consumption profile with no Dedicated profile
No container apps or jobs are active in the environment
A virtual network or Azure Policy setting keeps it in a failed state
Its container apps haven't deployed a new revision in that time
The environment's Log Analytics workspace has reached its daily cap

questions.explanation: Learn lists three conditions that lead to automatic deletion after 90 days: the environment is idle, with no active apps or jobs; it's in a failed state because of virtual network or Azure Policy configuration; or such configuration blocks infrastructure updates. Logging caps, the mix of workload profiles and how recently a revision was deployed aren't among them.

questions.prompt: Complete the az containerapp revision commands for routine revision management.

slots.text: Create a revision from the latest one with 1 vCPU and 2 GiB, keeping its image: az containerapp revision

options.text: activate
copy
restart

slots.text: Show all revisions of the app in a table: az containerapp revision

options.text: restart
list
show

slots.text: Bring back an inactive revision for a rollback: az containerapp revision

options.text: copy
set-mode
activate

questions.explanation: revision copy creates a revision from an existing one with the settings you change, revision list shows all revisions while show returns one revision's details, and revision activate makes an inactive revision active again. restart restarts a revision that's already running, and set-mode switches between single and multiple revision mode.

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order to have a new container app pull its private image with a system-assigned identity.

options.text: Make sure that identity holds AcrPull on the registry
Create the container app with a public image
Turn on the app's system-assigned managed identity
Set the registry to use the system identity, then switch the app to the private image

questions.explanation: A system-assigned identity exists only once the app does, so Learn creates the app with a public image first and then gives it the identity. The identity needs AcrPull on the registry (the Azure CLI can make this assignment for you) before the registry is configured with the system identity and the app switches to the private image. A user-assigned identity, which Learn prefers where possible, avoids the two passes because it can be given access in advance.

questions.prompt: For each statement about Container Apps revisions and labels, select Yes or No.

options.text: No
Yes

slots.text: A label name can contain two consecutive dashes.
A revision that receives traffic through its label needs no traffic weight.
Inactive revisions are charged at a reduced rate.
By default, once more than 100 revisions are kept, the oldest ones are purged.

questions.explanation: Label names use lowercase letters, digits and dashes, and may not contain two dashes in a row. Traffic sent to a label's URL goes to its revision without any weight allocation. Container Apps doesn't charge for inactive revisions, and by default it purges the oldest ones once the count passes 100, a limit that --max-inactive-revisions can change.

questions.prompt: docs-worker uses an azure-servicebus scale rule with messageCount 5, minReplicas 0 and maxReplicas 20, and 47 messages are waiting. What desiredReplicas value does the scaling algorithm compute? Answer in replicas. Enter a number.
questions.explanation: Container Apps computes desiredReplicas as the ceiling of the current metric divided by the target, so ceil(47 / 5) gives 10, which is below maxReplicas 20. The app then grows toward that number in steps of 1, 4, 8 and so on, and it never goes past the configured maximum.

questions.prompt: A queue worker in Container Apps has ingress disabled, a minimum of zero replicas and no scale rules, and it never processes a message. What fixes it?

options.text: Raise the scale limit maxReplicas from 10 to 30 on the worker
Enable external ingress so that KEDA can poll the queue
Add an azure-servicebus scale rule, or set minReplicas to 1
Switch the worker to multiple revision mode

questions.explanation: With ingress disabled and no custom rule, only the default HTTP rule applies, and no HTTP traffic can arrive, so the app stays at zero replicas with no way to start. An azure-servicebus rule lets KEDA start replicas from the queue length, or minReplicas 1 keeps one running. KEDA polls the event source itself, so ingress isn't needed, and a higher maximum or another revision mode doesn't start a replica.

questions.prompt: Which TWO can a Container Apps scale rule use to authenticate to Azure Service Bus? Select TWO.

options.text: An Event Grid subscription key for the namespace
The KEDA operator's cluster-admin service account
The environment's Log Analytics shared key
A managed identity that has access to the namespace
An app secret mapped to the trigger's connection parameter

questions.explanation: Scale rules accept a Container Apps secret mapped to the scaler's trigger parameter (--scale-rule-auth on the CLI) and, for Azure Queue Storage, Service Bus and Event Hubs, a managed identity (--scale-rule-identity, set with the CLI or a template rather than the portal), which Learn prefers because no secret is stored. Container Apps runs KEDA for you, so there's no operator account to use, and Log Analytics or Event Grid keys don't grant access to a queue.

questions.prompt: After the last queue message is processed, a scale-to-zero worker keeps one replica for about five minutes before it stops. Which setting causes this delay?

options.text: The cool down period
The polling interval
The HTTP concurrency target
The scale down stabilization window

questions.explanation: The cool down period, 300 seconds by default, is how long KEDA waits after the last event before it takes a revision from its final replica to zero, and it has no effect while other replicas are removed. The scale down stabilization window delays scale-in decisions while load falls, the polling interval (30 seconds) sets how often the queue is checked, and the HTTP concurrency target drives HTTP rules only.

questions.prompt: insight-worker is running 4 replicas when 250 messages are waiting on its subscription. Following Container Apps' documented scale-up step, how many replicas does the next scale-out reach? Answer in replicas. Enter a number.
questions.explanation: KEDA computes desiredReplicas as ceil(250 / 10) = 25, but each step scales to the smallest of the maximum (30), the desired count (25) and max(4, 2 times the current replicas), which is 8 when 4 replicas run. Later polls keep doubling toward 25, so answering 25 skips the step rule.

questions.prompt: A container app defines both an HTTP scale rule and an azure-servicebus custom rule. When does it begin to scale out?

options.text: As soon as the condition of either rule is met
When the conditions of both rules are met together
When the rule that's listed first in the template is met
When the HTTP rule is met, because HTTP rules take priority

questions.explanation: With several rules, Container Apps starts to scale once the first condition of any rule is met, so either a surge of requests or a queue backlog adds replicas. The rules aren't combined, and neither their order nor their type gives one of them priority.

questions.prompt: A queue worker has scaled out to 12 replicas, and then the backlog drops so far that 2 replicas would be enough. How does KEDA scale it in on Azure Container Apps?

options.text: It removes one replica at each 30-second polling interval until 2 remain
It halves the replica count every 300 seconds until 2 replicas remain
It removes all 10 surplus replicas at once, after the 300-second window
It waits out the cool down period, then removes one replica at a time

questions.explanation: Scale-in waits until the lower demand has lasted for the 300-second scale-down stabilization window, and the scale-down step then removes 100 percent of the replicas that need to shut down. The cool down period applies only to the final step from one replica to zero, and there's no one-by-one or halving pattern.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements are true for an event-driven Container Apps job? Select TWO.

options.text: It can't use an HTTP scale rule
Its custom rules use ScaledObject-based KEDA scalers
It scales with the default HTTP concurrency of 10 requests
Its custom rules use ScaledJob-based KEDA scalers
It can use a TCP scale rule

questions.explanation: Container Apps jobs support neither HTTP nor TCP scale rules, so the HTTP concurrency setting doesn't apply to them. Event-driven jobs use custom rules built on ScaledJob-based KEDA scalers, while container apps use ScaledObject-based scalers.

questions.prompt: Complete the Bicep custom scale rule for a worker that drains a Service Bus queue without storing a connection string.

slots.text: custom.type, copied from the KEDA scaler specification

options.text: 'servicebus-queue'
'azure-servicebus'
'Microsoft.ServiceBus/namespaces'

slots.text: custom.metadata key that sets the target number of messages per replica

options.text: messageCount
queueLength
concurrentRequests

slots.text: Property that replaces the auth array to authenticate with a user-assigned identity

options.text: identity: '<identity resource ID>'
managedIdentity: true
auth: [{ identity: '<identity resource ID>' }]

questions.explanation: A custom rule's type is the KEDA trigger type, azure-servicebus, and its metadata keys come straight from the scaler, where messageCount is the per-replica target; queueLength belongs to the Azure Queue Storage rule and concurrentRequests to HTTP rules. To use a managed identity, the rule carries an identity property, set to a user-assigned identity's resource ID or to system, in place of the auth array.

questions.prompt: How does Container Apps measure load for an HTTP scale rule?

options.text: As the average across the 300-second stabilization window
As the peak number of concurrent requests in the last minute
Requests in the past 15 seconds divided by 15, every 15 seconds
Every 30 seconds, when KEDA polls the ingress endpoint for open requests

questions.explanation: For HTTP rules, the concurrent request count is recalculated every 15 seconds as the number of requests in the past 15 seconds divided by 15, and the app adds a replica when the count passes concurrentRequests. The 30-second polling interval applies to event-source rules and not to HTTP or TCP rules.

questions.prompt: In multiple revision mode, you add an azure-servicebus rule to a container app, and the revision that was active before the change keeps ignoring the queue backlog. Why?

options.text: KEDA loads a new rule after the 300-second cool down period has passed
The new revision got the rule; the older one keeps its old rules
A revision keeps ignoring the queue until it gets a label
Scale rules apply to the revision that has all of the traffic

questions.explanation: Scale rules are revision-scope settings, so adding one creates a new revision, and in multiple revision mode the old revision stays available with its old rules. Use revision management to shift traffic and retire the old revision; neither labels nor the cool down period add rules to an existing revision.

questions.prompt: New catalog-api pods on AKS show ImagePullBackOff, and the image and tag exist in acrcatalog.azurecr.io. What should you do?

options.text: Attach the registry with az aks update --attach-acr
Change the catalog-api Service type from ClusterIP to LoadBalancer
Add a liveness probe to the deployment manifest
Raise the memory limit of the catalog-api container

questions.explanation: When the image and tag are right, ImagePullBackOff points to the kubelet identity being unable to authenticate to the registry; --attach-acr assigns that identity the AcrPull role on it, and az aks check-acr can confirm access. Memory limits, probes and the Service type act only once a container has been pulled and started, so they can't fix a pull failure.

questions.prompt: Match each Kubernetes object or setting to its purpose.

options.text: Keeps a minimum number of pods up during voluntary disruptions
Gives a set of pods one stable IP address and DNS name
Decides whether a pod receives traffic from a Service
Runs a set number of identical pods and rolls out updates
Restarts a container that stops responding

slots.text: Deployment
Service
PodDisruptionBudget
readinessProbe

questions.explanation: A Deployment keeps the declared replica count and applies rolling updates, a Service groups pods behind one IP address or DNS name, a PodDisruptionBudget limits how many pods voluntary disruptions such as upgrades can take down, and a failing readiness probe removes a pod from load balancing. Restarting an unresponsive container is the liveness probe's job.

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order to deploy the catalog-api manifest to AKS from the command line and test it from the internet.

options.text: Watch kubectl get service catalog-api until EXTERNAL-IP shows a public address
Open the external IP address in a browser
Change the image values in catalog-api.yaml to the acrcatalog.azurecr.io login server
Run kubectl apply -f catalog-api.yaml
Remove the app with kubectl delete -f catalog-api.yaml

questions.explanation: The manifest must name its images by the registry's login server before kubectl apply creates the objects it defines. A LoadBalancer Service shows EXTERNAL-IP as pending until Azure assigns a public address, which you then open in a browser, and kubectl delete with the same file removes what apply created.

questions.prompt: Which Kubernetes Service type gives the catalog-api pods a public IP address that Azure manages for internet clients?

options.text: LoadBalancer
ExternalName
NodePort
ClusterIP

questions.explanation: A LoadBalancer Service makes AKS create an Azure load balancer resource with an external IP address and rules that forward to the pods. ClusterIP, the default, gives an address reachable only inside the cluster, NodePort maps a port on each node's own address, and ExternalName creates a DNS entry.

questions.prompt: A Deployment runs 4 replicas with a RollingUpdate strategy and maxUnavailable set to 1. How many pods, at minimum, stay available during an update? Answer in pods. Enter a number.
questions.explanation: maxUnavailable caps how many of the desired pods may be unavailable at once during a rolling update, so with 4 replicas and a value of 1, at least 3 pods keep serving. maxSurge works the other way: it allows extra pods above the desired count while new ones start.

questions.prompt: A Python model server takes about two minutes to load its model, and the kubelet keeps restarting it because the liveness probe fails during loading. What should you add?

options.text: A second replica so that one pod can serve traffic
A startup probe, so the other probes wait until the app has started
A readiness probe that uses the same endpoint as the liveness probe
A PodDisruptionBudget with minAvailable set to 1

questions.explanation: When a startup probe is configured, the kubelet runs the readiness and liveness probes only after it succeeds, so a slow model load is no longer mistaken for a hung container. A readiness probe only takes a pod out of load balancing and doesn't stop the liveness probe from restarting it, while a disruption budget or an extra replica protects availability, not the startup of each pod.

questions.prompt: How should Woodgrove Bank meet its requirement for doc-classifier pods that are stopped during a node upgrade?

options.text: A preStop hook, with terminationGracePeriodSeconds that covers it
A startup probe so that each pod waits until its database connections are open
A liveness probe that restarts any pod still holding an unfinished message
A PodDisruptionBudget with minAvailable set to 30 of the doc-classifier pods

questions.explanation: A preStop hook runs just before Kubernetes stops a container, which includes the evictions of a node upgrade, so doc-classifier can finish its message and close its database connections. terminationGracePeriodSeconds has to cover the hook, because the pod is killed when the grace period ends. A disruption budget limits how many pods go at once but gives a stopping pod no time to clean up, and probes deal with health and startup rather than shutdown.

questions.prompt: A Deployment runs 8 replicas, and its PodDisruptionBudget sets minAvailable to 75%. During a node drain, what is the largest number of these pods that can be voluntarily disrupted at the same time? Answer in pods. Enter a number.
questions.explanation: minAvailable can be a percentage of the desired number of pods, and 75 percent of 8 means 6 pods must stay available, so evictions can take down at most 8 - 6 = 2 pods at a time. A PDB acts through the Eviction API for voluntary disruptions such as drains and upgrades, so it doesn't cover a node that fails.

questions.prompt: An AKS API must be reachable from virtual machines in the same virtual network, with no public IP address. Which Service should you create?

options.text: A ClusterIP Service in the API's namespace with a fixed IP
An ExternalName Service that points to the API's DNS name
A LoadBalancer Service on an internal load balancer
A NodePort Service on nodes that have public IP addresses

questions.explanation: An internal load balancer is given only a private IP address, so the Service can be reached from the virtual network but not from the internet, and AKS manages the Azure load balancer for you. A ClusterIP address works only inside the cluster, ExternalName only creates a DNS entry, and node ports on public node addresses would face the internet.

questions.prompt: Before you set container limits, you want to see how much CPU and memory each AKS node can give to pods. Which command shows this?

options.text: az aks show, reading the node pool's agent pool profile
kubectl describe node, reading the Allocatable section
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
kubectl top pod for every pod that runs on the node

questions.explanation: kubectl describe node prints Capacity and Allocatable, and Allocatable is lower because AKS reserves CPU and memory on each node for Kubernetes components; Learn warns against pod limits above what a node supports. kubectl top pod shows current use, events record what happened, and the agent pool profile describes the node VMs rather than what pods can use.

questions.prompt: A team wants the Vertical Pod Autoscaler to recommend CPU and memory requests for a Deployment without applying them to any pod. Which updateMode should it set?

options.text: Manual
Initial
Off
Auto

questions.explanation: In Off mode, VPA only provides recommendations and changes nothing. Initial sets requests when pods are created and Auto updates them when pods restart, so both apply the values, and Manual isn't one of the VPA modes. VPA is on by default in AKS Automatic, while in AKS Standard you choose whether to enable it.

questions.prompt: Which TWO practices does Learn recommend for the system node pools of an AKS Standard cluster? Select TWO.

options.text: Deploy application pods to the kube-system namespace
Turn off the autoscaler so that the system node count stays fixed
Use B series VMs to lower the cost of the system nodes
Run at least two nodes in each system node pool
Apply the CriticalAddonsOnly taint so that application pods stay off

questions.explanation: System node pools host critical pods such as CoreDNS, so Learn asks for at least two nodes for resilience during upgrades and the CriticalAddonsOnly taint to keep user workloads from competing with them. kube-system isn't meant for your own applications, B series VMs are explicitly discouraged for AKS, and the system pool should be able to autoscale to meet the needs of system pods.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about the AKS pricing tiers for cluster management are true? Select TWO.

options.text: The Free tier has no financially backed uptime SLA
The Standard tier supports clusters of up to 5,000 nodes
The Free tier limits each cluster to 100 nodes
AKS Automatic clusters need the Premium tier
The Standard pricing tier and the AKS Standard cluster mode are the same thing

questions.explanation: Free includes every AKS feature and up to 1,000 nodes but no financially backed uptime SLA, while Standard turns the uptime SLA on by default and supports up to 5,000 nodes; Premium adds Microsoft maintenance beyond community support. The Standard pricing tier is separate from the AKS Standard cluster mode, and AKS Automatic comes preconfigured with the Standard tier.

questions.prompt: Complete the manifest fields for a Deployment that is updated gradually and protected during node upgrades.

slots.text: Deployment spec.strategy.type

options.text: Recreate
OnDelete
RollingUpdate

slots.text: kind of the object that keeps at least 2 of the pods running during voluntary disruptions

options.text: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
PodDisruptionBudget
VerticalPodAutoscaler

slots.text: apiVersion of that object

options.text: apps/v1
autoscaling.k8s.io/v1
policy/v1

questions.explanation: A RollingUpdate strategy replaces pods gradually within its maxSurge and maxUnavailable limits, which is the gradual update Learn describes, rather than replacing them all at once. A PodDisruptionBudget, declared with apiVersion policy/v1, keeps its minAvailable count of pods running during voluntary disruptions such as upgrades; the autoscalers change replica counts or resource requests instead.

questions.prompt: Put the events in order for an AKS Standard node pool that uses the cluster autoscaler when new pods don't fit on its nodes.

options.text: New pods stay Pending because no node has enough free resources
After load falls, the autoscaler finds nodes without running pods and removes them
The cluster autoscaler detects the pods that can't be scheduled
The pending pods are scheduled onto the new nodes
The autoscaler adds nodes to the node pool

questions.explanation: The cluster autoscaler watches for pods that can't be scheduled because of resource constraints and responds by raising the node count, after which the waiting pods can be placed on the new nodes. It also checks nodes regularly for a lack of running pods and scales the pool back down.

questions.prompt: Where does AKS place the virtual machines, scale sets and storage that back a new cluster's nodes?

options.text: In a subscription that Azure manages for the control plane
In the kube-system namespace of the cluster
In a node resource group that AKS creates automatically
In the resource group that holds the cluster resource

questions.explanation: When you create a cluster, the AKS resource provider creates a second resource group, the node resource group, which holds the VMs, scale sets and storage of the nodes. The cluster resource stays in the group you chose, the control plane is managed by Azure separately from your nodes, and kube-system is a Kubernetes namespace rather than a place for Azure resources.

questions.prompt: catalog-api pods are in CrashLoopBackOff, and you need the output the container wrote just before it crashed. Which command shows it?

options.text: kubectl get events --watch
kubectl describe deployment catalog-api
kubectl top pod <pod>
kubectl logs <pod> --previous

questions.explanation: kubectl logs with --previous returns the log of the last terminated instance of the container, which holds its exit messages, while plain kubectl logs shows the attempt that is running now. Events and describe output show scheduling and status changes, and top shows resource use, not what the application printed.

questions.prompt: Match each symptom to the first command you should run.

options.text: az containerapp logs show --type console
kubectl get endpoints catalog-api
az acr task logs --registry acrcatalog
az containerapp logs show --type system
kubectl describe pod, then read its Events

slots.text: AKS pod stuck in Pending
AKS Service catalog-api answers nothing: does any ready pod back it?
Container Apps revision unhealthy after a deployment
Container Apps stack traces printed by your own code

questions.explanation: For a pod stuck in Pending, the events that describe pod lists (for example FailedScheduling) show why it hasn't started. Pods that aren't ready don't become endpoints, so an empty endpoints list explains a silent Service. Container Apps system logs carry platform events such as image pulls and probe failures, console logs carry your process output, and ACR task logs cover image builds only.

questions.prompt: A new docs-api revision never becomes ready: system logs show readiness probe failures on port 80, and the new image runs gunicorn on port 8000. What should you change?

options.text: Switch the container app to multiple revision mode
Raise maxReplicas so that more replicas can pass the probe
Enable Dapr on the container app
Set the ingress target port, and any probe ports, to 8000

questions.explanation: Default probes for an app with ingress use TCP on the ingress target port, so a target port of 80 probes a port where nothing listens and the revision never turns ready. Setting the target port, and any custom probe ports, to 8000 lets the probes reach gunicorn. Replica counts, revision mode and Dapr leave the probed port unchanged.

questions.prompt: Complete the KQL query that counts docs-api console log lines from the last hour for each revision.

slots.text: Table

options.text: ContainerAppConsoleLogs_CL
ContainerAppSystemLogs_CL
AppRequests

slots.text: | where ContainerAppName_s == 'docs-api' and TimeGenerated >

options.text: bin(1h)
take(1h)
ago(1h)

slots.text: | summarize count() by

options.text: RevisionName_s
ContainerGroupName_g
Log_s

questions.explanation: Your container's stdout and stderr land in ContainerAppConsoleLogs_CL, while ContainerAppSystemLogs_CL holds platform events and AppRequests is an Application Insights table. ago(1h) returns the time one hour before now, which is what the TimeGenerated filter needs, whereas bin groups continuous values into units and take limits the number of rows. Grouping by RevisionName_s gives one count per revision; ContainerGroupName_g is the replica name.

questions.prompt: An on-call engineer runs kubectl get events the morning after a 02:00 pod failure and finds nothing about it. What should the team do so that this evidence is kept next time?

options.text: Raise the event retention period in the cluster's AKS settings
Run kubectl get events with --all-namespaces next time
Enable Container insights so that events are kept in Log Analytics
Run kubectl describe pod, which keeps the pod's full event history

questions.explanation: Kubernetes keeps events for one hour after they're generated and has no retention setting, so a kubectl view of them the next morning comes up empty. Container insights collects events into the KubeEvents table in a Log Analytics workspace, where they can be queried later; describe and --all-namespaces read the same short-lived events.

questions.prompt: From a debug pod in the frontend namespace, curl to the ClusterIP and port of the orders service in the backend namespace succeeds, but a DNS lookup of orders.backend.svc.cluster.local fails. Which TWO should you check next? Select TWO.

options.text: CoreDNS health, configuration and logs
The pod's /etc/resolv.conf and dnsPolicy
Ingress network policies in the backend namespace
The service selector and its endpoint slices
Whether the application listens on its targetPort

questions.explanation: A working ClusterIP and port show that service routing, endpoints, the backend's ingress rules and the application are fine, so name resolution is what's left: Learn's workflow says a failing DNS name with a working ClusterIP means investigating DNS, starting with CoreDNS health, configuration and logs and the pod's resolver settings (and, if an egress policy isolates the debug pod, whether it still allows DNS). Selectors, endpoint slices and the target port matter when the ClusterIP itself fails.

questions.prompt: Several pods on one AKS node show status Failed with reason Evicted, although none of their containers had reached its memory limit. What happened?

options.text: Their liveness probes failed, so the kubelet restarted them
The kernel's OOM killer ended containers that went over their memory limits
A PodDisruptionBudget evicted them during a node upgrade
The kubelet evicted them because the node ran short of memory

questions.explanation: Evictions act on whole pods: the kubelet evicts pods to relieve memory pressure on the node, and those pods report Failed with reason Evicted. OOMKilled is different, because the kernel ends the one container that exceeds its own limit, typically with exit code 137, and the container is restarted. Probe failures restart containers, and a disruption budget limits evictions rather than causing them.

questions.prompt: A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff, and kubectl describe pod shows its last state as Terminated with reason Completed and exit code 0. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The container exceeds its memory limit a few seconds after it starts
The node can't pull the image because the image tag is wrong
A ConfigMap that the application reads at startup is missing
The process finishes normally, so the container restarts in a loop

questions.explanation: CrashLoopBackOff usually comes with a non-zero exit code, but a container whose process simply finishes, such as an image started without a long-running command, exits with 0 and is restarted in a loop as well. A memory limit breach ends with exit code 137 and OOMKilled, a missing ConfigMap makes the app fail with an error, and an image that can't be pulled never runs to a terminated state.

questions.prompt: After a cluster moves from a service principal to a managed kubelet identity, pulls from Azure Container Registry fail with 401 Unauthorized, although az role assignment list shows AcrPull. Ten minutes later, pulls still fail. What should you do?

options.text: Reconcile with az aks update, then upgrade the node image if needed
Enable the registry's admin user and create an image pull secret
Change imagePullPolicy from Always to IfNotPresent in the Deployment
Delete and re-create the AcrPull role assignment for the identity

questions.explanation: The kubelet's credential provider caches tokens, so pulls can fail after a credential change even though the new role assignment is right. Learn's first solution is a reconcile with az aks update so every node picks up the new identity. The cache usually refreshes within a few minutes, so if pulls still fail after about five minutes, its second solution is a node-image-only upgrade, recommended especially after a service-principal-to-managed-identity move. Re-creating a correct role changes nothing, an admin secret works around the identity instead of fixing it, and the pull policy addresses rate limits.

questions.prompt: Apps in an internal Container Apps environment have healthy replicas, but every request from a VM in the virtual network returns HTTP 404 with the message Container App is stopped or does not exist. What should you change?

options.text: Add a private DNS record for each app's domain name
Set the apps' ingress to accept traffic from anywhere
Raise each app's minimum replica count to 1
Change the ingress target port to match the app

questions.explanation: In an internal environment, ingress that's limited to the Container Apps environment rejects callers elsewhere in the virtual network with exactly this 404, and accepting traffic from anywhere fixes it without public exposure, because an internal environment has no public endpoint. Name resolution and TLS already work here, the replicas are running, and a wrong target port would make the health probes fail instead.

questions.prompt: AKS pods fail to pull from a registry whose private endpoint is in another virtual network, and the pod events show 403 Forbidden while an anonymous token is fetched. What should you check first?

options.text: That imagePullPolicy is set to IfNotPresent for the private image
That the kubelet identity holds AcrPush on the private registry, not AcrPull
That the virtual network peering between the two networks is Connected
That the AKS network is linked to the registry's private DNS zone

questions.explanation: A 403 while a token is fetched points to network access, and when the registry's private endpoint sits in a different virtual network, the cluster's virtual network needs a link in the registry's private DNS zone, named privatelink.azurecr.io by default. Peering problems show up as i/o timeouts instead, pull permission comes from AcrPull rather than AcrPush, and the pull policy addresses rate limits.

questions.prompt: Which TWO image pull errors in AKS pod events point to the network path to the registry rather than to authorization? Select TWO.

options.text: dial tcp <IP address>:443: i/o timeout
failed to fetch oauth token: 401 Unauthorized
no basic auth credentials
exec /canipull: exec format error
net/http: TLS handshake timeout

questions.explanation: An i/o timeout on port 443 occurs with Private Link networking, for example when virtual network peering is missing, and a TLS handshake timeout points to a firewall, proxy or network virtual appliance in the path. 401 Unauthorized and missing basic auth credentials are authorization errors, and exec format error from az aks check-acr comes from an architecture mismatch.

questions.prompt: Match each AKS image pull error to its most likely cause.

options.text: The kubelet's default image pull rate limit
The image doesn't match the node's operating system or architecture
A public registry's pull limit on the node's outbound IP
An expired service principal secret
A wrong registry, repository or tag name

slots.text: no match for platform in manifest
pull QPS exceeded
429 Too Many Requests from Docker Hub
not found for the repository and tag

questions.explanation: A platform mismatch, such as a Linux image on a Windows node or an ARM64 image on an AMD64 node, gives no match for platform in manifest. pull QPS exceeded means the kubelet hit its own pull rate limit, which IfNotPresent eases, while a 429 from Docker Hub is the public registry's limit on the node's egress IP, which importing the image into ACR avoids. not found points to the name, for example azureacr.io typed for azurecr.io, and an expired service principal secret shows up as 401 Unauthorized.

questions.prompt: Put the checks in order for a pod that can't reach a service in another namespace, following Learn's AKS connectivity workflow.

options.text: Validate the service selector and its endpoint slices
Call the service's ClusterIP and port
Review network policies and the cluster network data plane
Call a destination pod's IP address directly
Resolve the service by its DNS name from the source pod

questions.explanation: Learn's workflow works outward from name resolution and stops at the first failing layer: DNS, then the ClusterIP and port, then whether the selector produces endpoints, then a destination pod directly, and only then network policies and the data plane. Each step rules out one layer before the next is tested.

questions.prompt: For each statement about troubleshooting pod-to-service connections in AKS, select Yes or No.

options.text: No
Yes

slots.text: A connection refused error points first to whether the application listens on the expected target port.
A timeout points first to the pod's DNS search domains.
Restarting system networking components before evidence identifies the failing component is the recommended way to clear transient faults.
When failures follow one node, you keep timestamps, pod placement and node conditions before you fix anything.

questions.explanation: Learn maps connection refused to the application's port and address, while a timeout calls for checking endpoints, network policies, routes, node health and the data plane; DNS is the starting point for name resolution errors. It warns against restarting system networking components before evidence points to one, because a restart can erase evidence, and it asks you to preserve node-specific evidence first.

questions.prompt: A Python service knows an item's id and partition key value, and by_id holds a parameterized SELECT on c.id. Which call returns that item for the fewest RUs?

options.text: container.read_item(item=item_id, partition_key=tenant)
container.query_items("SELECT * FROM c", enable_cross_partition_query=True)
container.query_items_change_feed(partition_key=tenant)
container.query_items(query=by_id, parameters=params)

questions.explanation: Naming both the id and the partition key makes a point read, which Cosmos DB serves directly; Learn puts it at about 1 RU for an item of roughly 1 KB, and point reads are cheaper than queries. The parameterized SELECT still goes through the query engine, the unfiltered cross-partition query has to visit every physical partition, and the change feed returns the partition's stream of changes rather than one item.

questions.prompt: A Python web API creates CosmosClient(url, credential=DefaultAzureCredential()) and signs in with its own identity. Which TWO statements are true? Select TWO.

options.text: The account key must also be passed for queries to succeed
Reading and querying items needs a data-plane role such as Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor
Creating containers through Azure Resource Manager needs a control-plane role
The Cosmos DB Operator role lets the identity read and write items
The data role is granted with az role assignment create, like other Azure roles

questions.explanation: Item reads, writes and queries are authorized by Cosmos DB's own data-plane role definitions, such as Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor, which you assign with az cosmosdb sql role assignment create. Managing databases and containers is control-plane work under Azure RBAC, and the vector quickstart traces a 403 at container creation to missing control-plane access. Cosmos DB Operator manages accounts without data access, and a client built with DefaultAzureCredential sends Entra tokens, so it needs no account key.

questions.prompt: Complete the azure-cosmos code that runs a parameterized query in pages and reports its RU charge.

slots.text: Dictionary key that carries the argument in parameters=[{"name": "@tenant", ...}]

options.text: "data"
"value"
"param"

slots.text: Keyword argument of query_items that caps the items returned in each page

options.text: max_page_count=100
page_size=100
max_item_count=100

slots.text: After iterating the results: container.client_connection.last_response_headers

options.text: ["x-ms-activity-id"]
["x-ms-documentdb-query-metrics"]
["x-ms-request-charge"]

questions.explanation: In azure-cosmos each query parameter is a dictionary with a name and a value, and max_item_count is the query_items argument that limits how many items come back per page; the other two names aren't query_items arguments. The x-ms-request-charge response header carries the RUs the request consumed and needs no extra flag, whereas the query-metrics header is filled only when populate_query_metrics is set, and the activity ID only identifies the request.

questions.prompt: For each statement about CosmosClient in the Python SDK, select Yes or No.

options.text: No
Yes

slots.text: Requests use Gateway connection mode, because Direct mode isn't available in Python.
Listing West US and then East US in preferred_locations sets the order in which regions are tried.
consistency_level=ConsistencyLevel.Strong on the client makes reads stronger than the account's default level.
The client isn't thread-safe, so each worker thread should create its own CosmosClient.

questions.explanation: The Python SDK reaches Cosmos DB through the gateway because it has no Direct mode, and preferred_locations gives the client a priority list of regions to try. A client-level consistency setting can only relax read consistency below the account default, never raise it. The client is thread-safe, and Learn recommends creating one instance and reusing it for the life of the application.

questions.prompt: An orders container is partitioned on /storeId, and a FastAPI endpoint runs a parameterized query for one store's open orders. How can the Python call avoid the query-plan request to the gateway?

options.text: Give query_items a partition_key argument
Create the client with consistency_level set to Eventual
Give query_items max_item_count=-1 to size its pages
Give query_items enable_cross_partition_query=True

questions.explanation: When a query is scoped to one partition, passing the partition key value as partition_key lets the Python SDK skip the network call that builds a query plan, which cuts latency. Allowing cross-partition execution does the opposite, since the SDK then has to consider every physical partition. max_item_count tunes how many items arrive per page, and a weaker client consistency level changes read guarantees, not query planning.

questions.prompt: You need a custom Cosmos DB for NoSQL data-plane role that allows all item operations except deletes. How should the role definition be written?

options.text: Put items/* in dataActions and scope the assignment to exclude deletes
Assign Data Contributor together with a second role that denies deletes
Put items/* in dataActions and the delete action in notDataActions
List each allowed item action in dataActions and leave delete out

questions.explanation: Cosmos DB's native data-plane RBAC doesn't support notDataActions: whatever isn't granted in dataActions is excluded automatically, so the definition must name the allowed actions and simply omit delete. An assignment scope selects the account, a database or a container, not individual operations, and there's no deny role to combine with Data Contributor, whose wildcard already includes deletes.

questions.prompt: An account accepts writes in West Europe and replicates reads to North Europe. A Python app in North Europe passes preferred_locations=["North Europe"], yet its upserts still travel to West Europe. Why?

options.text: The setting takes effect after the first regional failover
The client also needs consistency_level set to Strong
The region names must be written in lowercase, as northeurope
Its one write region handles them whatever the list says

questions.explanation: When an account isn't configured for multi-region writes, the client sends every write to the one writable region, and preferred_locations affects reads alone, so local reads come from North Europe while upserts go to West Europe. The Learn samples pass display names such as West US, a client consistency setting can only weaken reads and never applies to writes, and the list is used from the start rather than after a failover.

questions.prompt: Complete the Azure CLI command that lets a worker's managed identity read and write items in the orders container of the sales database, and nowhere else.

slots.text: az

options.text: role assignment create
cosmosdb sql role assignment create
cosmosdb sql role definition create

slots.text: --role-definition-id for Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor:

options.text: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/readMetadata

slots.text: --scope

options.text: "/databases/sales/containers/orders"
"/dbs/sales/colls/orders"
"/dbs/sales"

questions.explanation: Data-plane roles are Cosmos DB's own role system, so they're assigned with az cosmosdb sql role assignment create rather than the Azure RBAC command, and the definition command creates a role instead of granting one. The built-in Data Contributor definition has the ID ending in 0002, while the other GUID isn't one of the account's data-plane definitions, and a readMetadata data action is part of a definition, not its ID. The relative scope /dbs/<database>/colls/<container> limits the grant to one container, whereas /dbs/sales covers the whole database, and scopes use the dbs and colls segments rather than full resource names.

questions.prompt: For each statement about Cosmos DB for NoSQL clients and accounts, select Yes or No.

options.text: No
Yes

slots.text: upsert_item replaces the stored item when an item with the same id already exists.
Passing connection_timeout=10 to CosmosClient sets a 10-second connection timeout.
Setting disableLocalAuth to true on the account also blocks clients that sign in with Microsoft Entra ID.
A cross-partition query tends to run faster as the container gains physical partitions.

questions.explanation: upsert_item inserts a new item or replaces an existing one, and connection_timeout is one of the client options the Python SDK exposes, measured in seconds. disableLocalAuth turns off key-based authentication so that applications must use Microsoft Entra ID, which keeps working. A cross-partition query has to visit every partition, so more physical partitions can make it slower, not faster.

questions.prompt: A query sorts with ORDER BY c.docType ASC, c.updatedAt DESC and fails because no matching index exists. What should you add to the indexing policy?

options.text: A composite index of docType ascending, then updatedAt ascending
A composite index of updatedAt descending, then docType ascending
Included range paths /docType/? and /updatedAt/?
A composite index of docType ascending, then updatedAt descending

questions.explanation: Sorting on two or more properties needs a composite index whose paths come in the same sequence as the ORDER BY and whose directions match it, or are all reversed. Swapping the paths breaks the sequence, docType ascending with updatedAt ascending matches neither the query's directions nor their full reversal, and ordinary range paths support single-property sorts only.

questions.prompt: Users must see their own profile edits at once, other users may see them a little later, and reads should cost as few RUs as possible. Which default consistency level fits?

options.text: Session
Strong
Eventual
Bounded staleness

questions.explanation: Session consistency guarantees read-your-writes inside a client session while reading from a single replica, so its reads cost the same as the weaker levels. Strong and bounded staleness read from two replicas and charge about twice the RUs per read, and eventual consistency can hand even the writer a stale copy.

questions.prompt: Chunk items of about 2 KB hold a 1,024-dimension vector in embedding and long text in content, queries filter on tenantId and docType, and writes cost too many RUs. Which TWO changes cut write RUs and keep those filters efficient? Select TWO.

options.text: Change the account default consistency to Eventual
Add /content/? to the excluded paths
Set indexingMode to none for the container
Add a composite index on /content and /embedding
Add /embedding/* to the excluded paths
Add /tenantId/? to the excluded paths

questions.explanation: Every indexed path adds to the RU charge of each write, and neither the vector array nor the long text is used in a range filter, so excluding /embedding/* and /content/? lowers write cost while the root include keeps tenantId and docType indexed; vector search relies on its own vector index. Disabling indexing or excluding /tenantId/? would turn the filters into scans, a composite index adds index work, and write RU cost is the same at every consistency level.

questions.prompt: Query metrics for SELECT VALUE c.title FROM c WHERE UPPER(c.title) = @t show 60,000 retrieved documents, 7 output documents and 0% index utilization. What should you change?

options.text: Add a composite index on title ascending and on id ascending
Request bigger pages so that the query makes fewer round trips
Store an uppercase copy of title at write time and filter on it
Pass populate_index_metrics=True so the query picks its index

questions.explanation: The index can't evaluate UPPER, so the engine loads every document to test the filter, which is what the retrieved count and the zero index utilization show. Saving the uppercase value when the item is written, or indexing it as a computed property, lets a plain equality filter use the index. No composite index can serve the function either, the index-metrics flag only reports index use, and larger pages don't reduce the documents the query must load.

questions.prompt: A frequent query runs WHERE c.status = @s AND c.total > @min, and you want it to consume fewer RUs. Which composite index serves it?

options.text: (status ASC, total ASC, createdAt ASC)
(total DESC, status DESC)
(total ASC, status ASC)
(status ASC, total ASC)

questions.explanation: In a composite index for filters, properties with equality filters come first and the single range filter comes last, so status then total lets the engine use the index for both predicates. Putting total first breaks that rule whichever direction is used, and a composite index that contains a property the query doesn't filter on, such as createdAt, isn't used for the query.

questions.prompt: On a busy container, you're replacing the range index that a hot query uses on /region with a composite index on region and createdAt. How should you apply the change?

options.text: Add the composite index, wait for its transformation, then remove the old path
Remove the old path first, then add the composite index in a second update
Remove the old path and add the composite index together in one policy update
Apply the change through an SDK so that the new index skips the transformation

questions.explanation: Removing an indexed path takes effect at once, while a new index is used only after its index transformation completes, so Learn says to add the replacement first and remove the old index after the transformation finishes. Removing first, in the same update or an earlier one, leaves the hot query on a full scan in the meantime. Every policy change, from the portal or an SDK, runs as an online transformation.

questions.prompt: Proseware's dashboard query runs SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.clientId = @id ORDER BY c.endedAt DESC. Which change best meets the request unit requirement?

options.text: ORDER BY c.clientId, c.endedAt DESC with a composite index on clientId ASC, endedAt DESC
ORDER BY c.endedAt DESC with the account default consistency set to Strong
ORDER BY c.endedAt DESC with the /clientId/? path moved to the excluded paths
ORDER BY c.endedAt DESC with a composite index on endedAt DESC, clientId ASC

questions.explanation: When a query filters on one property and sorts on another, adding the filter property to the start of the ORDER BY lets a composite index on both properties serve the filter and the sort together, which costs fewer RUs than range indexes alone. A composite index with endedAt first doesn't match the query's property order, excluding clientId makes the filter scan, and Strong consistency roughly doubles the RU charge of reads.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about a container whose indexingMode is none are true? Select TWO.

options.text: Queries keep using the index that was built before the change
It suits a container used purely as a key-value store
Time to live can't be turned on for the container
Point reads by id and partition key stop working
Lazy indexing is a supported alternative for new containers

questions.explanation: TTL relies on indexing, so it can't be activated while the mode is none, and the mode fits containers that serve lookups by key without secondary indexes, or that are being bulk-loaded. With indexing disabled there's no index for queries to use, new containers can't select lazy indexing, and point reads don't depend on the index at all.

questions.prompt: A container has 4,000 RU/s of provisioned throughput, and its Cosmos DB account is associated with three regions. How much throughput is available to the container globally? Answer in RU/s. Enter a number.
questions.explanation: Throughput provisioned on a container is made available in each region of the account, and it can't be assigned to one region selectively. The global total is therefore the provisioned value times the number of regions: 4,000 times 3 gives 12,000 RU/s.

questions.prompt: Match each indexing requirement to the index path that expresses it.

options.text: /headquarters/*
/events/[]/name/?
/locations/[]/country/?
/headquarters/employees/?
/events/[]/{name, category}/?

slots.text: Index the employees value under headquarters, but nothing nested inside it
Index everything below the headquarters property
Index the country property of each element in the locations array
Filter on name and category together within each element of the events array

questions.explanation: A path that ends in /? indexes one scalar value, while /* matches every node below the property, and [] steps into each element of an array. A tuple index for filtering on several fields in the same array element uses the {} specifier after [] and ends in /?, whereas a path to name alone doesn't cover the pair.

questions.prompt: A container will hold about 3 million 3,072-dimension embeddings, and searches must keep latency and RU cost low across the whole set. Which vector index type should you choose?

options.text: quantizedFlat
flat
diskANN
range

questions.explanation: diskANN is the approximate index built for large search scopes, generally the best performer beyond about 50,000 vectors, with the lowest latency and RU cost, and it accepts up to 4,096 dimensions. flat stops at 505 dimensions, quantizedFlat is a brute-force scan over compressed vectors that suits scopes of 50,000 or fewer, and range belongs to the standard index, not the vector index types.

questions.prompt: Match each requirement to the container vector policy or vector index setting that meets it.

options.text: dataType float16
distanceFunction dotproduct
Index type flat
Index type quantizedFlat
distanceFunction euclidean

slots.text: Halve the storage of each stored vector at a small cost in accuracy
Rank by straight-line distance, where a lower score means more similar
Exact search with 100% recall over 384-dimension vectors
Compressed brute-force search over a scope that filters narrow to a few thousand vectors

questions.explanation: float16 stores each element in half the space of float32 with some loss of accuracy, and euclidean measures straight-line distance, where smaller values mean closer vectors. flat is a brute-force search with full recall for vectors of up to 505 dimensions, and quantizedFlat scans compressed vectors, which suits searches that filters have narrowed to a small set. Dot product is a similarity in which larger values mean more similar, so it matches none of the rows.

questions.prompt: Complete the Cosmos DB for NoSQL query that returns the five chunks closest to a query embedding for one tenant.

slots.text: Start of the query: SELECT

options.text: c.id, VectorDistance(c.embedding, @q) AS score
TOP 5 c.id, VectorDistance(c.embedding, @q) AS score
FIRST 5 c.id, VectorDistance(c.embedding, @q) AS score

slots.text: FROM c WHERE c.tenantId = @t ORDER BY

options.text: c._ts DESC, VectorDistance(c.embedding, @q)
c.id, VectorDistance(c.embedding, @q)
VectorDistance(c.embedding, @q)

questions.explanation: Cosmos DB limits results with TOP N in the SELECT clause, and Learn warns that a vector query without it tries to return far more results at a higher RU cost and latency; FIRST isn't Cosmos DB syntax. Ordering by the same VectorDistance expression ranks the chunks from most to least similar, whereas putting _ts or id ahead of it sorts by time or by id first, so the closest chunks no longer come first.

questions.prompt: A new container holds 600 chunk vectors under a diskANN index, and vector queries cost far more RUs than the team expected. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: diskANN takes over from a scan once a container holds 50,000 vectors
Fewer than 1,000 vectors are indexed, so a full scan runs instead
Shared database throughput doubles the charge of vector queries
Cosine distance bypasses diskANN and needs a flat index instead

questions.explanation: quantizedFlat and diskANN need at least 1,000 indexed vectors for their quantization to be accurate, and below that Cosmos DB runs a full scan, which raises the RU charge. The 50,000 figure is guidance on when diskANN outperforms quantizedFlat rather than a switch-on point, vector search isn't supported at all on shared-throughput accounts, and diskANN works with the cosine distance function, as the Learn quickstarts show.

questions.prompt: A container of 1,536-dimension product embeddings has a diskANN index. One high-value endpoint needs better recall, while the other endpoints are fine as they are. What should you change?

options.text: Replace the container's diskANN index with a flat vector index
Set the endpoint's client consistency level to Eventual
