Raise searchListSizeMultiplier in its VectorDistance call
Set quantizerType to product on the container's vector index

questions.explanation: diskANN recall can be tuned for each query: a larger searchListSizeMultiplier in VectorDistance buys higher recall at the price of more latency and RUs, and leaves other queries untouched. A flat index accepts at most 505 dimensions and would change every query, product is already the default quantizer, and a weaker consistency level has nothing to do with vector recall.

questions.prompt: Running the same vector query twice against an unchanged container with a diskANN index returns slightly different orderings, and a tester reports possible data corruption. What explains the behaviour?

options.text: The vector policy left out dimensions, so the vectors are truncated on read
Cosine scores are rounded differently depending on the SDK that sends them
Too few vectors are indexed, so a full scan with random order runs instead
Approximate search on per-replica indexes varies a little by design

questions.explanation: diskANN performs approximate nearest-neighbour search, each replica builds its own vector index and any replica can serve the query, so the same query can return a slightly different ordering without anything being wrong. A full scan below 1,000 vectors is a brute-force search rather than a random one, and a missing dimensions value defaults to 1,536 instead of truncating stored vectors.

questions.prompt: Lucerne moves its Azure OpenAI deployment to a model that returns 3,072 dimensions, and the article-vectors vector policy was created without a dimensions value. What must the team do?

options.text: Recreate the vector policy and index with 3,072 dimensions, then re-embed
Leave the policy as it is, because the policy adapts to each vector's length
Edit dimensions in the existing policy and let the index transformation re-embed
Keep the policy and set dataType to float16 so that longer vectors fit

questions.explanation: A policy without dimensions uses the default of 1,536, every vector in a path must have the same dimensions, and vector policy and index settings can't be changed in place, so the policy and index have to be dropped and added back before vectors from the new model are written. Re-embedding is needed anyway, since vectors from the old model can't be compared with new query vectors, and float16 changes the storage of each element, not the vector length.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about vector search in Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL are true? Select TWO.

options.text: float64 is among the supported vector data types
It needs no feature registration or account capability
One path can carry two policies with different distance functions
One container can have vector policies for several paths
Vector indexing can be switched off on the container later

questions.explanation: Vector indexing and search are on by default, so you only define a container vector policy and vector indexes, and a container can have several policies as long as each targets a different path. Each unique path has at most one policy, vector search can't be disabled on a container once enabled, and the supported data types are float32, float16, int8 and uint8.

questions.prompt: Complete the container policies for chunk embeddings that use very high-dimensional vectors.

slots.text: vectorEmbeddings and vectorIndexes entries: "path":

options.text: "/chunks/[]/embedding"
"/vectors/*/embedding"
"/embedding"

slots.text: vectorIndexes entry with "type": "diskANN", for steadier recall over time and faster indexing:

options.text: "quantizerType": "scalar"
"quantizerType": "product"
"quantizerType": "spherical"

questions.explanation: Vector paths can't contain wildcard characters or be nested inside arrays, so the vector must sit in a property such as /embedding. The spherical quantizer can shorten quantization time and give higher, more stable recall with very high-dimensional embeddings, whereas product is the balanced default and scalar isn't one of the documented quantizer types.

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order to add vector search over product descriptions to an existing Cosmos DB app.

options.text: Create a container whose vector policy and index use those dimensions
Write the products with their description embeddings to the container
Query with SELECT TOP 10 ordered by VectorDistance to the question's embedding
Check how many dimensions the chosen embedding model returns

questions.explanation: The vector policy needs the dimension count before the container exists, because policy settings can't be changed later, and items written afterwards are indexed under that policy. Only once embeddings are stored can a TOP N query ordered by VectorDistance rank them against the embedding of a question.

questions.prompt: A Python team wants to react to inserts and updates in a container, with checkpoints and load balancing across instances handled for them. What should they use?

options.text: An Azure Functions Cosmos DB trigger with a lease container
ChangeFeedProcessor from the azure-cosmos package with a lease container
query_items_change_feed polled by every instance over the whole container
A Cosmos DB trigger that reads in all versions and deletes mode

questions.explanation: The Functions trigger for Cosmos DB runs the change feed processor on your behalf, keeps its state in a lease container and spreads the work across function instances, and its default latest version mode is available in every Functions language. The processor library itself ships for .NET and Java only, the pull model leaves checkpoints and splitting the feed to your own code, and the trigger's all versions and deletes mode is limited to the .NET isolated worker.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about a container's change feed in latest version mode are true? Select TWO.

options.text: An item created and then updated between reads appears once, in its updated form
Each intermediate update of an item stays in the feed
Deletes can be caught by setting a soft-delete flag and a TTL
The feed can be filtered by operation type, such as updates
The account needs continuous backup to read in this mode

questions.explanation: Latest version mode keeps the current version of each created or updated item, so a create followed by an update before the next read shows up once. It doesn't record deletes, so Learn suggests marking items with a deleted flag and a TTL, which the feed captures as an update. The mode is on by default, while continuous backup and intermediate versions belong to all versions and deletes mode, and the feed can't be filtered by operation type.

questions.prompt: A Python worker reads a container's change feed with query_items_change_feed, and after a restart it must carry on from the last change it processed. What should it do?

options.text: Read the feed ranges again and start each range from Now
Call query_items_change_feed with start_time="Beginning" each time
Let the SDK checkpoint each batch into a lease container
Save the etag continuation token and pass it back as continuation

questions.explanation: In the pull model the continuation token, taken from the etag response header, is the bookmark: passing it as continuation resumes right after the last processed change and takes precedence over any start time. Starting from the beginning replays every change, starting each range from Now skips whatever changed while the worker was down, and lease containers belong to the change feed processor, which Python doesn't have and whose leases can't be converted to continuation tokens.

questions.prompt: A Cosmos DB trigger has processed a container for a week. To reprocess the container's history, the team turns on the trigger's start-from-beginning option and redeploys, but no older changes arrive. Why?

options.text: Existing leases already hold checkpoints, so the option has no effect
The option works in all versions and deletes mode alone
The change feed keeps changes for 24 hours, so older ones are gone
The option takes effect after the feed poll delay of 60 seconds

questions.explanation: Starting from the beginning sets the trigger's initial state, so it applies the first time the trigger starts; once leases exist, their stored checkpoints win and the option changes nothing. Latest version mode has no fixed retention period, the poll delay defaults to 5 seconds and governs polling for new changes, and all versions and deletes mode can't read from the beginning at all.

questions.prompt: A Python function app connects to Cosmos DB with a managed identity and sets create_lease_container_if_not_exists to true, and the function fails to start. What should you do?

options.text: Set the lease container's partition key path to /leases
Assign the identity Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor on the account
Switch the trigger to all versions and deletes mode
Provision the lease container beforehand and set the option to false

questions.explanation: Creating a container is a control-plane operation that isn't allowed through Microsoft Entra data-plane access, so with an identity connection the function can't create its lease container and won't start. Provisioning the container beforehand, for example with the Azure CLI or Bicep, and leaving the option off fixes it. A data-plane role still doesn't permit container creation, the mode is unrelated, and a partitioned lease container needs the /id partition key.

questions.prompt: Lucerne adds a second Python function that logs article edits for auditing, triggered by the same articles container and sharing the existing leases container. After deployment, one of the two functions stops receiving changes. What should you change?

options.text: Point both functions at the account through separate connection settings
Give each function its own lease prefix
Move the second function to a separate function app on its own plan
Set a larger maximum number of items per invocation on both functions

questions.explanation: When several functions use a Cosmos DB trigger on the same container, each needs a dedicated lease container or its own lease prefix; otherwise they compete for the same leases and only one is triggered. A prefix lets both share the leases container. Batch size, hosting and connection settings leave the two functions reading the same leases, so the conflict stays.

questions.prompt: A Python job must replay and process the changes of a single tenant, whose ID is the container's partition key, at a pace the job controls. Which approach fits?

options.text: A Functions Cosmos DB trigger filtered on the tenant's partition key
query_items with ORDER BY c._ts over the tenant's changes

A plain query ordered by _ts returns current items rather than a resumable feed of changes.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about the Azure Functions trigger for Azure Cosmos DB are true? Select TWO.

Python functions can use all versions and deletes mode
It polls for new changes at 60-second intervals by default
It doesn't say whether each document was inserted or updated
It works with any Cosmos DB API, including MongoDB

questions.explanation: The trigger hands over the changed documents without marking inserts and updates, so code that must treat them differently needs its own timestamp fields, and a lease that isn't renewed within the expiration interval expires and moves to another instance. The trigger supports the API for NoSQL alone, all versions and deletes mode is limited to the .NET isolated worker, and the default feed poll delay is 5 seconds.

questions.prompt: For each statement about reading the change feed with the Python pull model, select Yes or No.

An empty 200 response doesn't mean the feed is exhausted, so the client should keep polling, and Now, not Beginning, is the default start_time.

questions.prompt: A Python app connects to Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server with DefaultAzureCredential. Which scope should it request the access token for?

questions.explanation: The PostgreSQL quickstart asks Microsoft Entra ID for a token on the ossrdbms-aad scope and sends it as the password, because that's the audience the service accepts. The redis.azure.com and cognitiveservices.azure.com scopes are the ones the Azure Managed Redis and Azure OpenAI samples request, and the scope isn't named after the server's host name.

questions.prompt: A script signs in to PostgreSQL as a developer's Entra user and reuses the password it got at startup; about an hour later, opening further sessions fails authentication. What should you change?

Make the user a Microsoft Entra administrator on the server
Get a new token for each new connection from one reused credential
Turn off password authentication so the server refreshes tokens

questions.explanation: Entra user tokens for PostgreSQL last about an hour, and the token serves as the password, so a token obtained at startup stops working for new connections once it expires. Asking one long-lived credential for a token per new connection lets the SDK cache and renew it, as the quickstart advises. Rereading the same stored token doesn't renew it, and neither the password-authentication setting nor the administrator role changes how long a token lasts.

The quickstart makes inserts and updates permanent with conn.commit() before it closes the cursor and connection, whereas fetchall only reads results.

questions.prompt: A flexible server was created with private access through virtual network integration. A developer on a laptop at home can't reach it with a Python script. How can the developer run the script against the server?

options.text: Connect on port 6432 so the request goes through PgBouncer
Set sslmode=disable so the connection skips the TLS handshake
Add the laptop's public IP address to the server's firewall rules
Run it on a VM inside the server's VNet

questions.explanation: A server created with private access accepts connections from resources inside its virtual network, so the quickstart's advice is to connect from a virtual machine added to that network. Firewall rules for client IP addresses belong to servers created with public access, turning off TLS doesn't change network reachability, and the PgBouncer port is reached over the same network path as port 5432.

questions.prompt: An engineer's Microsoft Entra account was deleted by mistake and then recreated with the same user name. The engineer's PostgreSQL role still exists, but signing in with a fresh token fails. Why?

options.text: The deleted account's last token stays valid for 60 minutes
Tokens are matched to roles by Entra object ID, which is new
The server must restart before it accepts recreated accounts
Recreated accounts can sign in through an Entra group alone

questions.explanation: Azure Database for PostgreSQL maps an access token to a database role through the user's unique Microsoft Entra ID rather than the user name, so a new account with the old name counts as a different user and can't use the existing role. The up-to-60-minute window applies to a deleted user's existing token, no restart is involved, and group sign-in doesn't repair the mapping for an individual role.

questions.prompt: Members of the Microsoft Entra group pg-analysts must sign in to a flexible server through the group. What do they use as the user name and the password?

options.text: The group name, with a shared password from Key Vault
The group name, with their own Entra token
Their own user name, with the group's object ID
Their own user name, with an Entra token issued to the group

questions.explanation: Signing in as a group member differs from an individual sign-in only in the user name: the member gives the group name, and the password is the same individual Microsoft Entra token they'd use otherwise. A group doesn't receive tokens of its own, and neither a stored password nor an object ID serves as the credential in Entra authentication.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about Microsoft Entra authentication for Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server are true? Select TWO.

options.text: A server can have just one Microsoft Entra administrator at a time
Tokens for system-assigned managed identities can last up to 24 hours
Password authentication can't be switched off once it's turned on
Turning it on at the server level enables PGAadAuth and restarts the server
Deleting a user in Entra ID ends their current token's access at once

questions.explanation: Learn gives system-assigned managed identity tokens a validity of up to 24 hours, and enabling Entra authentication on the server turns on the PGAadAuth extension, which restarts the server. Password authentication can be deactivated for auditing and compliance, several Entra administrators can be configured after provisioning, and a deleted user's existing token works until it expires unless the user is also removed from the server.

The fully qualified server name always takes the form <server>.postgres.database.azure.com. The quickstart sets sslmode to require, while the other two parameters aren't the libpq setting for encrypted connections.

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order so that a Python app can connect to a new flexible server with its managed identity instead of a password.

options.text: Create a database role for the app's managed identity
Sign in to the server as a Microsoft Entra administrator
Grant that role the privileges the app needs on its tables
Have the app request an access token and pass it as the password
Turn on Microsoft Entra authentication for the server

questions.explanation: Entra sign-in has to be enabled before anyone can use it, and at first only a Microsoft Entra administrator can connect with an Entra identity and configure further Entra database users. Once the identity has a role with privileges, the app can request a token for its managed identity and present it as the password when it connects.

questions.prompt: A chunks table will store text-embedding-ada-002 output and needs an HNSW index on it. Which column definition should you use?

options.text: embedding vector(1536)
embedding real[]
embedding vector
embedding vector(1024)

questions.explanation: text-embedding-ada-002 returns 1,536 dimensions, and a pgvector column has to declare a dimension count that matches the model before it can be indexed. A vector column without dimensions fails index creation with a column-does-not-have-dimensions error, real[] is a plain array that must be cast to vector before pgvector can compare it, and 1,024 dimensions don't match what the model returns.

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order to add vector search to a new database on flexible server so that the index builds as fast as possible.

options.text: Bulk-load the rows with COPY
Create the chunks table with its vector column
Run CREATE EXTENSION vector in the database
Create the HNSW index on the vector column
Add vector to the azure.extensions server parameter

questions.explanation: An extension must be allowlisted in azure.extensions before CREATE EXTENSION can install it in a database, and the vector type has to exist before a table can declare a vector column. Learn advises loading data before indexing it, because the build is faster and the resulting layout is better, so the HNSW index comes after the COPY load.

questions.prompt: An ingestion job re-embeds revised chunks and must update the stored vector when a chunk's id already exists, or insert the row when it doesn't. Which statement fits?

options.text: UPDATE chunks SET embedding = %s WHERE chunk_id = %s for each revised chunk
INSERT with ON CONFLICT (chunk_id) DO NOTHING so that duplicate ids are skipped
INSERT with ON CONFLICT (chunk_id) DO UPDATE SET embedding = EXCLUDED.embedding
COPY chunks (chunk_id, embedding) FROM STDIN WITH (FORMAT BINARY) for each batch

questions.explanation: ON CONFLICT on the key column turns one INSERT into an upsert: new ids are inserted, and with DO UPDATE an existing row's embedding is overwritten by the value proposed in EXCLUDED. DO NOTHING keeps the stale vector, a plain UPDATE never adds chunks that are new, and COPY is the bulk-load path, listed separately from upserts, that doesn't resolve key conflicts.

questions.prompt: A team stores 3,072-dimension embeddings in a vector(3072) column, and CREATE INDEX ... USING hnsw fails. Which change keeps an HNSW index using only generally available features that Learn documents for flexible server?

options.text: Reduce the vectors to 2,000 dimensions or fewer and store those
Create the index WITH (m = 64) so it can hold 3,072 dimensions
Build an IVFFlat index instead, which has no dimension limit
Declare the column as vector so the index ignores dimensions

questions.explanation: For the vector type, HNSW and IVFFlat indexes accept up to 2,000 dimensions, and Learn's flexible-server guidance for larger columns, which can be stored but not indexed, is to reduce their dimensionality. The pgvector project also indexes up to 4,000 dimensions through halfvec half-precision vectors or half-precision indexing, but Learn's flexible-server pages don't document that, which the stem rules out, and DiskANN's higher-dimension support relies on product quantization, which is preview. The m option sets graph connections rather than the dimension cap, IVFFlat has the same 2,000-dimension limit, and a column without a dimension count can't be indexed at all.

questions.prompt: On a flexible server, CREATE EXTENSION pgvector fails although the team believes the extension is allowlisted. What should they do?

options.text: Allowlist pgvector in azure.extensions and run the command again
Run CREATE EXTENSION pgvector in the postgres database instead
Run CREATE EXTENSION pgvector CASCADE to pull in its dependencies
Allowlist and create the extension under the name vector

questions.explanation: The community calls the project pgvector, but the binary and the extension are named vector, and that name is the one to put in azure.extensions and to pass to CREATE EXTENSION. Allowlisting or creating pgvector fails whichever database you use, and CASCADE installs dependencies of an extension that exists rather than fixing a wrong name.

questions.prompt: The vector extension works in the app1 database, but creating a table with a vector(768) column in the new app2 database on the same server fails because the type doesn't exist. What should you do?

options.text: Create the table in app1 and reference it from app2 by name
Add vector to azure.extensions again and save the parameter
Restart the server so that app2 loads the allowlisted extension
Connect to app2 and run CREATE EXTENSION vector there

questions.explanation: Allowlisting in azure.extensions is a server-level step, but CREATE EXTENSION installs the extension in the database you're connected to, so it has to be repeated for every database that needs the vector type. The allowlist already contains vector, a restart doesn't install extensions, and PostgreSQL tables can't be referenced across databases by name.

questions.prompt: An embeddings table is range-partitioned on vec_date, one partition per year, and indexed. EXPLAIN for a query meant to cover only recent rows shows index scans on every partition. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: PostgreSQL prunes partitions just for tables below a million rows
An index on a partitioned table covers just its first partition
Its WHERE clause doesn't filter on the vec_date column
ivfflat.probes is too low to skip partitions

questions.explanation: The planner can skip partitions only when the query filters on the partition key, here a range on vec_date, so Learn's EXPLAIN checklist asks whether partitions that aren't needed were pruned. An index created on the partitioned table gives every partition its own index, probes tunes the search inside an IVFFlat index rather than pruning, and no row-count limit applies to partition pruning.

questions.prompt: Match each pgvector operator or function to the calculation it performs.

Euclidean norm

questions.prompt: For each statement about storing embeddings in Azure Database for PostgreSQL, select Yes or No.

options.text: Yes
No

A vector column can be added to an existing table with ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN.
AVG over a vector column returns the average of the stored vectors as a vector.
Cosine distance returned by <=> ranges from -1 to 1.

questions.explanation: Learn's examples keep embeddings either in their own table, linked to the source rows by a foreign key, or in a column added later with ALTER TABLE, and pgvector's AVG aggregate returns a vector. Cosine distance runs from 0 for identical directions to 2 for opposite ones; the -1 to 1 range belongs to cosine similarity.

questions.prompt: Complete the SQL that keeps 1,536-dimension chunk embeddings for an existing chunks table.

INHERITS chunks(chunk_id),
REFERENCES chunks(chunk_id),

ALTER COLUMN embedding vector(1536);
ADD INDEX embedding vector(1536);

questions.explanation: A REFERENCES clause makes chunk_id a foreign key to the source rows, as Learn's sessions example does; INHERITS and PARTITION OF are table-level clauses that copy or attach a whole table structure. ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN adds the vector column to existing rows, whereas ALTER COLUMN changes a column that already exists and ADD INDEX isn't PostgreSQL syntax.

questions.prompt: A nearest-neighbour query that ranks rows with the <=> operator shows a sequential scan in EXPLAIN, although an HNSW index built with vector_l2_ops exists. What should you do?

options.text: SET enable_seqscan TO OFF and keep the index
Rewrite the ORDER BY to use the <#> operator
Rebuild the HNSW index with vector_cosine_ops
Raise hnsw.ef_search to 200 so the scan visits more vectors

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL considers a vector index only when its operator class matches the query's operator: <=> is cosine distance and needs vector_cosine_ops, whereas vector_l2_ops serves <->. ef_search tunes an HNSW index that's already in use, <#> would need vector_ip_ops, and discouraging sequential scans can't make the planner use an index that doesn't serve the operator.

questions.prompt: Match each description to the pgvector indexing option.

options.text: No vector index
HNSW
B-tree index on the filter column
IVFFlat
DiskANN

slots.text: Clusters the rows into lists with k-means and searches the lists nearest the query
Layered graph that a search enters at a sparse top layer and narrows down to the densest layer
Graph index from a separate extension that depends on vector, aimed at billion-point scale
Exact search with perfect recall, at the cost of scanning every row

questions.explanation: IVFFlat groups the rows into k-means lists and, at query time, probes the lists whose centres are closest to the query, while HNSW builds a layered graph that a search enters at the top and narrows layer by layer. DiskANN comes from the pg_diskann extension, which needs vector, and targets very large datasets, and with no vector index pgvector runs an exact search. A B-tree on a filter column narrows the rows exactly without scanning all of them, so it fits none of the descriptions.

questions.prompt: A table holds 600,000 embeddings, and you create an IVFFlat index with the starting lists value that Learn suggests. What lists value should you use? Answer in lists. Enter a number.
questions.explanation: For tables of up to 1 million rows Learn's starting point is lists = rows / 1000, so 600,000 rows give 600 lists; beyond a million rows it switches to the square root of the row count. The matching starting point for probes is lists / 10, which would be 60 here.

questions.prompt: With pg_diskann, a filtered query that asks for 200 rows stops at 100 in one session, and results must stay in exact distance order. What should that session set?

options.text: SET LOCAL enable_seqscan TO OFF
SET diskann.iterative_search TO 'strict_order'
SET diskann.l_value_is TO 20
SET diskann.iterative_search TO 'relaxed_order'

questions.explanation: A cap at 100 rows is what pg_diskann does when iterative search is off: it fetches l_value_is candidates, 100 by default, in a single step, so a query can't return more rows than that whatever its LIMIT. strict_order keeps searching the graph in batches until the LIMIT is met and returns rows sorted by distance, while the default relaxed_order may return them slightly out of order. A lower l_value_is shrinks the candidate list further, and discouraging sequential scans doesn't lift the cap.

questions.prompt: An IVFFlat index with 2,000 lists returns poor recall, and the queries run with settings at values that no session or transaction has changed. What should you change first?

options.text: Rebuild the index with ten times as many lists
Set enable_seqscan to off for the session
Raise hnsw.ef_search, which IVFFlat reads at query time
Raise ivfflat.probes from its default of 1

questions.explanation: IVFFlat searches only the lists closest to the query, and with probes at 1 it searches a single one of the 2,000, so recall suffers; Learn's starting point is probes of about lists / 10. hnsw.ef_search tunes HNSW indexes only, more lists make each probe cover a smaller share of the data, and discouraging sequential scans doesn't widen the index search.

questions.prompt: To get perfect recall, a developer sets ivfflat.probes equal to the index's lists value, and EXPLAIN now shows a sequential scan. Why?

options.text: The index has to be rebuilt after the probes value changes
IVFFlat accepts a probes value only through SET LOCAL
The probes setting resets to 1 whenever it's above 1,000 lists
All lists probed means exact search, so the index isn't used

questions.explanation: When probes equals the number of lists, every list is searched, which is the same as a brute-force search of the whole table, so the planner doesn't use the index. probes is a query-time setting that needs no rebuild, and it can be set for the session or, with SET LOCAL, for one transaction.

questions.prompt: A new chunks table is empty when the app goes live, rows arrive continuously, and approximate search must work from the first day. Which index should you create?

options.text: IVFFlat with lists = 1000
A B-tree index on the embedding column
HNSW
IVFFlat with lists = 1

questions.explanation: HNSW has no training step, so it can be created on an empty table and stays useful as rows arrive. IVFFlat builds its lists from the data with k-means, which is why Learn advises loading data before creating it; a single list gives no speed-up at all, and a B-tree can't order rows by vector distance.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about pgvector index settings on flexible server are true? Select TWO.

options.text: pg_stat_progress_create_index reports the progress of an HNSW build
ivfflat.probes can be chosen only when the index is created
SET LOCAL hnsw.ef_search applies only until the transaction ends
The m option sets the candidate list size during queries
hnsw.ef_search defaults to 64 candidates per query

questions.explanation: SET LOCAL scopes ef_search or probes to the current transaction, after which the session value applies again, and on PostgreSQL 12 and later pg_stat_progress_create_index shows how far an index build has got. ef_search defaults to 40, while 64 is the ef_construction default, probes is a query-time setting, and m is the maximum number of connections per layer, fixed when the index is built.

The index uses vector_cosine_ops, so the query must order by the cosine operator <=>; <-> and <#> need the L2 and inner-product operator classes.

questions.prompt: A 20 GB HNSW index has to be held entirely in the server's buffers under steady production load, and the server is limited to 4 vCores. Which compute tier fits?

options.text: General Purpose
Burstable
General Purpose with Premium SSD v2 storage
Memory Optimized

questions.explanation: Memory Optimized gives 6.75 to 9.5 GiB of memory per vCore, and its 4-vCore sizes have 32 GiB, room for the index, and Learn positions the tier for workloads that need in-memory performance. General Purpose gives 4 GiB per vCore, 16 GiB at 4 vCores, and Premium SSD v2 raises IOPS and throughput but adds no memory; the 4-vCore Burstable size also has 16 GiB and runs on CPU credits that sustained load drains.

questions.prompt: Building a DiskANN index over 5 million vectors on flexible server is slow. Which TWO changes speed up the build? Select TWO.

options.text: Raise maintenance_work_mem for the session that builds the index
Rebuild with REINDEX CONCURRENTLY so it runs in the background
Move the server to the Burstable tier during the build
Set parallel_workers on the table and allow parallel maintenance workers
Lower diskann.l_value_is before running CREATE INDEX

questions.explanation: pg_diskann builds faster with more maintenance_work_mem, and Learn suggests scaling memory up for the build and back down afterwards; parallel workers, set through the table's parallel_workers storage parameter and allowed by max_parallel_maintenance_workers and related settings, also shorten it. Burstable has less compute to give, l_value_is only affects index scans at query time, and REINDEX rebuilds the same index without making the build any faster.

questions.prompt: A flexible server on Premium SSD has 256 GiB of storage and storage autogrow enabled. What size does the storage grow to when autogrow triggers? Answer in GiB. Enter a number.
questions.explanation: On Premium SSD, autogrow always doubles the provisioned size, which also doubles the storage cost, so 256 GiB becomes 512 GiB; Premium SSD v2 grows in finer steps. Storage can't be scaled down afterwards, and the online grow stops at the 4,096 GiB disk boundary, which needs a manual, offline scale.

questions.prompt: A flexible server on Premium SSD has 2 TiB of storage with storage autogrow enabled. How much free space is left when autogrow activates? Answer in GiB. Enter a number.
questions.explanation: Above 1 TiB, autogrow triggers when free space falls below 10% of capacity or below 64 GiB, whichever is smaller. Ten percent of 2 TiB is about 204.8 GiB, so the 64 GiB threshold applies.

questions.prompt: During a large import, a Premium SSD server without autogrow became read-only at 95% storage used. You must restore writes now without increasing the storage cost. What should you do?

options.text: Restart the server, which clears the read-only state
Move the server to the Burstable tier to free disk space
Set the session to read-write and delete data you no longer need
Scale the storage down and back up again to reset the flag

questions.explanation: The server switches to read-only at 95% used or under 5 GiB free, and Learn's remedy without adding storage is to run SET SESSION CHARACTERISTICS AS TRANSACTION READ WRITE and delete unneeded data. Storage can only be scaled up, never down, a restart doesn't free space, and the compute tier has no effect on disk usage.

questions.prompt: A vector workload on a 256 GiB server needs a sustained 15,000 IOPS, and the team doesn't want to buy capacity it won't use. Which storage choice fits?

options.text: Premium SSD at 256 GiB on a Memory Optimized compute size
Premium SSD v2, with IOPS raised separately from size
Premium SSD scaled to 1 TiB for its 5,000 provisioned IOPS
Premium SSD at 256 GiB with storage autogrow switched on

questions.explanation: Premium SSD v2 lets you set capacity, IOPS and throughput independently, and a 256 GiB disk can scale to 80,000 IOPS, so the size can stay small. Premium SSD's included IOPS come from the disk size: 256 GiB gives 1,100 provisioned and up to 3,500, and even 1 TiB gives only 5,000. The compute size must also support the IOPS, since VM types have their own limits.

questions.prompt: A production vector search API runs on a B2s server, and under sustained load queries time out while the CPU Credits Remaining metric sits at zero. What should you do?

options.text: Increase the storage size to raise the IOPS limit
Move the server to the General Purpose tier
Restart the server so that its CPU credits refill
Raise max_connections so that queued queries can start

questions.explanation: Burstable servers run on CPU credits and drop to baseline CPU once credits are spent, which under sustained load causes timeouts; the tier targets nonproduction use, and General Purpose suits most production workloads. Learn advises against restarting while credits are near zero, and neither more IOPS nor more connections adds CPU.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about compute and storage on Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server are true? Select TWO.

options.text: Memory Optimized servers have 4 GiB of memory per vCore
The number of vCores can be scaled down after the server is created
Premium SSD autogrow crosses the 4,096 GiB boundary online
A Premium SSD v2 disk can be sized in steps of 1 GiB
Storage can be scaled down once data has been deleted

questions.explanation: vCores can be changed up or down after creation, and Premium SSD v2 has no fixed sizes, so it grows in 1 GiB increments. Storage only ever scales up, autogrow isn't triggered when Premium SSD would have to cross 4,096 GiB, which needs a manual offline scale, and 4 GiB per vCore is General Purpose, whereas Memory Optimized has 6.75 to 9.5 GiB.

questions.prompt: Complete the Azure CLI command that turns on storage autogrow for an existing flexible server.

update

slots.text: --resource-group rg-ai --name pg-ai --storage-auto-grow

questions.explanation: An existing server's storage settings are changed with az postgres flexible-server update, while create provisions a new server and parameter set changes server parameters. The --storage-auto-grow option takes the values enabled and disabled rather than a Boolean.

questions.prompt: Fabrikam's chunks table has an HNSW index on its embedding column, and a query that filters on tenant_id and ranks chunks by cosine distance asks for five; small tenants often get one or two while large tenants get five. What should you change?

options.text: List-partition the table on tenant_id so each partition gets its own index
Rebuild the HNSW index with a larger ef_construction value
Lower hnsw.ef_search on each tenant's connection so the index answers sooner
Normalize the vectors and move the table's index and query to inner product

questions.explanation: With an approximate index the WHERE filter is applied after the index scan, so a shared HNSW index returns about ef_search candidates (40 by default) and a small tenant's few matches among them are what's left after filtering. The pgvector project recommends list partitioning or separate tables for tenant isolation, which gives each tenant its own index and recall, and Learn shows that partitioned tables can be indexed. A smaller ef_search returns even fewer candidates, and inner product or a better-built graph still filters after the scan.

questions.prompt: Complete the SQL that the Python API sends through psycopg to fetch the five closest chunks of one document type for a tenant.

slots.text: SELECT content FROM chunks WHERE tenant_id = %s

options.text: GROUP BY doc_type
HAVING doc_type = %s
AND doc_type = %s

slots.text: ORDER BY embedding <=> %s

options.text: ::vector
::jsonb
::real[]

slots.text: End of the query

options.text: OFFSET 5
LIMIT 5
TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM (5)

questions.explanation: Metadata filters go in the WHERE clause beside the tenant filter, whereas GROUP BY and HAVING turn the result into groups. The ::vector cast turns the query embedding that psycopg passes as a parameter into a vector value that pgvector's distance operators accept, which a plain real[] array or jsonb isn't. LIMIT caps the rows, as every Learn example does, whereas OFFSET 5 skips the five closest chunks and TABLESAMPLE belongs after a table name in FROM, where it samples rows at random.

questions.prompt: A RAG endpoint retrieves the top chunks from PostgreSQL and calls a chat model, but answers still include facts that aren't in the manuals. What should the prompt to the model contain?

options.text: The chunks' embedding vectors, which keep their meaning more precisely than text
Every chunk above the similarity cutoff, so the model has the widest context
The retrieved chunks merged into one summary, with source labels removed
Retrieved chunks labelled by source, with an instruction to stay within them

questions.explanation: RAG adds the retrieved text to the prompt as grounding data, and Learn's remedy when grounded answers still drift is clear instructions to stick to that content, plus source labels so the answer can cite it. Passing every chunk above a cutoff spends tokens without telling the model how to use them, a merged summary drops the labels that make citations possible, and embedding vectors carry no readable content for the model.

questions.prompt: Stored chunks were vectorized with text-embedding-ada-002, while the API now vectorizes incoming questions with text-embedding-3-small; queries run without errors, but retrieval quality drops. What should you do?

options.text: Normalize each question embedding to length 1 before comparing it
Rebuild the HNSW index over the chunks so that it adapts to the new model
Embed questions with the same model as the chunks, or re-embed them all
Switch from <=> to <#>, which suits the newer model

questions.explanation: Embeddings from different models live in different vector spaces, so Learn's guidance is to use one embedding model consistently for a vector index, with matching dimensions and distance metric; a matching dimension count only hides the mismatch. Rebuilding the index or normalizing the query vector leaves the two spaces incompatible, and a different operator doesn't make vectors from different models comparable.

questions.prompt: Which change to the planner's retrieval step best meets Margie's Travel's requirement for suggested places?

options.text: Return more chunks per request so that the right places are more likely
Put the city and price band filters in the similarity query's WHERE clause
Ask the chat model to remove places outside the city and price band
Add the city name to the request text before it's turned into an embedding

questions.explanation: Filtering on the stored metadata in the WHERE clause of the vector query guarantees that only chunks from the requested city and price band can be retrieved, so the model never sees other places. An instruction to the model can still be ignored, adding the city to the embedded text only shifts similarity without excluding anything, and retrieving more chunks adds tokens while still including places that break the rule.

questions.prompt: A query with WHERE category = 'tour' asks an HNSW-indexed table for its ten nearest chunks, and tours are about 10% of the rows; it usually returns about four. What explains this?

options.text: HNSW indexes cap any filtered query at four rows to protect recall
PostgreSQL applies LIMIT before WHERE in a nearest-neighbour query
The <=> operator ignores WHERE clauses on tables with HNSW indexes
The filter is applied after an index scan of about 40 candidates

questions.explanation: An approximate index returns hnsw.ef_search candidates, 40 by default, and the WHERE condition is evaluated on those afterwards, so a condition matching 10% of rows leaves about four of them. The filter is still applied, LIMIT isn't evaluated before WHERE, and the shortfall comes from the candidate count rather than a fixed cap.

questions.prompt: Each partner's listing chunks are a tiny share of a 20-million-row table, and partner pages need the nearest chunks for one partner_id with exact results. What should you add?

options.text: The partner ID added to the text before it's embedded
A B-tree index on partner_id
An HNSW index rebuilt with a larger m value
An IVFFlat index with more lists than the HNSW index

questions.explanation: For a condition that matches a low percentage of rows, an ordinary index on the filter column lets PostgreSQL find those rows quickly and then rank them exactly by distance. A better-connected HNSW graph or an IVFFlat index is still approximate and filters after the scan, and putting the ID into the embedded text doesn't restrict which rows are returned.

questions.prompt: Which TWO practices does Learn recommend for a production RAG endpoint? Select TWO.

options.text: Use API keys rather than Microsoft Entra ID for the model
Send every retrieved passage whatever the token budget
Fine-tune the chat model whenever the source content changes
Treat retrieved passages as untrusted input
Apply access control when content is retrieved

questions.explanation: Grounded answers can leak whatever retrieval returns, so access should be enforced at retrieval time, and passages can carry prompt-injection text, so the system message and app logic should treat them as untrusted. Learn prefers Entra ID over API keys in production, uses RAG rather than fine-tuning for changing knowledge, and advises filtering or ranking passages to stay within the token budget.

questions.prompt: Put the request-time steps of a RAG endpoint backed by PostgreSQL in order.

options.text: Run the filtered similarity query against the chunks table
Embed the question with the model used for the stored chunks
Combine the question, the chunks and instructions into a prompt
Send the prompt to the chat model
Return the answer with citations to the chunks' sources

questions.explanation: Retrieval comes first: the question must become a vector from the same embedding model before it can be compared with stored chunks. The augment step then builds the prompt from the question and the retrieved grounding data, and only the generate step calls the model, whose answer can cite the sources that came back with the chunks.

questions.prompt: Complete the SQL that returns the five most similar chunks with a cosine similarity score.

slots.text: SELECT content,

options.text: (embedding <=> %s::vector) AS similarity
1 - (embedding <=> %s::vector) AS similarity
(embedding <-> %s::vector) * -1 AS similarity

slots.text: FROM chunks ORDER BY embedding <=> %s::vector

options.text: ASC LIMIT 5
DESC LIMIT 5
ASC OFFSET 5

questions.explanation: <=> returns cosine distance from 0 to 2, and cosine similarity is 1 minus that distance, so the first expression gives a score where higher means more similar; the raw distance runs the other way, and negated Euclidean distance isn't cosine similarity. Ordering the distance ascending puts the closest chunks first, whereas DESC returns the least similar and OFFSET skips the top five.

questions.prompt: During imports a Flex Consumption function app scales to 60 instances, and the General Purpose server starts refusing connections with too many clients. What should you do first?

options.text: Use the built-in PgBouncer on port 6432 with a small pool per instance
Run a PgBouncer sidecar container next to each function instance's code
Raise max_connections well above the default and then restart the server
Move the server to Burstable, whose built-in pooling absorbs the bursts

questions.explanation: PgBouncer holds a server connection only while a transaction or query is active, so pointing each instance at port 6432 with a small pool keeps 60 instances within the server's limits, and Learn recommends this over raising max_connections, which costs memory as connections become active and needs a restart. Learn's pooling guidance lists sidecars for container platforms, not Functions, and 60 sidecars with their own pools would still multiply server connections, while Burstable servers can't use the built-in PgBouncer at all.

questions.prompt: For each statement about connection limits on Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server, select Yes or No.

options.text: No
Yes

slots.text: A new max_connections value takes effect after the server restarts.
Scaling the server to a larger compute size leaves its max_connections value unchanged.
Idle connections use no server resources until they run a query.
Applications can use the whole max_connections value, because no connection slots are reserved.

questions.explanation: max_connections gets its default from the compute size chosen at provisioning and isn't recalculated when the compute changes, so Learn advises adjusting it yourself, and a changed value needs a restart. Every connection, idle or active, takes server resources, and the service keeps reserved slots, currently 15, for replication and monitoring, so user connections are fewer than max_connections.

questions.prompt: An app runs 2,000 AKS pods, each with its own PgBouncer sidecar, and the PostgreSQL server runs short of connections. Which change fits?

options.text: Give each sidecar a larger pool size so that its clients wait less
Switch each sidecar's pool mode from transaction to session
Run one central PgBouncer service in the cluster instead of sidecars
Add a second PgBouncer sidecar to each pod to spread the load

questions.explanation: Learn warns that a sidecar per pod multiplies the connections the server sees, so large AKS deployments with hundreds of pods should run PgBouncer as a standalone service that pools for all of them, at the cost of an extra network hop. Bigger pools or a second sidecar per pod add even more server connections, and session pooling keeps a server connection for each client's whole session.

questions.prompt: Woodgrove's 40 doc-classifier pods connect through the built-in PgBouncer with one database user and one database. Which PgBouncer setting bounds the server connections that all the pods share?

options.text: pgbouncer.max_client_conn
pgbouncer.server_idle_timeout
pgbouncer.default_pool_size
pgbouncer.pool_mode

questions.explanation: default_pool_size sets how many server connections PgBouncer allows for each user and database pair, 50 by default, so pods that share one user and one database share that pool however many clients they open. max_client_conn limits client connections to PgBouncer (5,000 by default), server_idle_timeout drops server connections idle for longer than its value, and pool_mode decides when a server connection can be reused by another client.

questions.prompt: You set pgbouncer.enabled to true on a Memory Optimized server. What else is needed before an app can pool its connections through it?

options.text: Use the server's separate pooler host name
Set pgbouncer.pool_mode to session
Restart the server to start PgBouncer
Change the app's port from 5432 to 6432

questions.explanation: PgBouncer listens on port 6432 of the same host, so the app keeps its host name and changes only the port, and enabling the parameter needs no restart. There's no separate pooler host, and the default transaction mode is what Learn recommends for most users.

questions.prompt: The built-in PgBouncer already has max_prepared_statements above 0, yet a worker that sends PREPARE get_doc AS SELECT ... and then EXECUTE get_doc keeps failing at random. What should you change?

options.text: Raise max_prepared_statements further so more names are kept
Raise default_pool_size so that each worker gets its own connection
Set pool_mode to statement so each statement keeps its connection
Prepare through the driver's protocol-level calls, not PREPARE text

questions.explanation: PgBouncer's prepared-statement support covers protocol-level commands, such as libpq's PQprepare, which it can intercept, whereas a PREPARE statement sent as SQL text isn't interpreted, so in transaction mode a later EXECUTE can reach a server connection that never saw it. A higher limit doesn't change what is tracked, statement mode can't be used with prepared statements, and a bigger pool still doesn't tie a client to one server connection.

questions.prompt: Apps on Azure App Service share a Burstable flexible server that must stay on that tier, and the server needs connection pooling that survives the loss of one pooler. What should you deploy?

options.text: A higher max_connections value, applied with a restart
The built-in PgBouncer, enabled with pgbouncer.enabled
One PgBouncer VM that all the apps connect to directly
Several PgBouncer VMs behind a load balancer

questions.explanation: The built-in PgBouncer isn't available on Burstable, so pooling has to run elsewhere, and Learn's pattern for managed hosts such as App Service is PgBouncer on VMs behind a load balancer, which removes the single point of failure. Raising max_connections doesn't pool anything, and a lone VM is exactly the single point of failure the requirement rules out.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about the built-in PgBouncer are true? Select TWO.

options.text: Turning it on with pgbouncer.enabled needs no server restart
Existing client connections stay open while the server restarts
After an HA failover it runs on the new primary with the same connection string
Its metrics are emitted by default once PgBouncer is on
default_pool_size caps server connections for the whole server

questions.explanation: In zone-redundant HA, PgBouncer restarts on the promoted standby, so apps keep their connection string, and the enable parameter is dynamic. default_pool_size applies per user and database pair, a server restart also restarts PgBouncer so connections must be re-established, and its metrics need metrics.pgbouncer_diagnostics as well.

questions.prompt: Complete the psql connection string an operator uses to see how many connections each pool holds in each state.

dbname=

options.text: pgbouncer_admin
postgres
pgbouncer

SHOW POOLS;
SHOW DATABASES;

questions.explanation: The admin console is the internal pgbouncer database on port 6432, reachable by users listed in pgbouncer.stats_users. SHOW POOLS reports the connections in each state for each pool, whereas SHOW DATABASES lists the applied connection limits and SHOW HELP lists the commands; port 8432 serves worker nodes of elastic clusters.

questions.prompt: A profile service uses cache-aside with a 5-minute TTL, and after editing their profile, users keep seeing the old value for minutes. What should the update path do?

options.text: Switch the eviction policy to allkeys-lru
Raise the TTL to 30 minutes to cut cache misses
Delete the cached key, then write to the database
Write to the database, then delete the cached key

questions.explanation: Cache-aside invalidates on write: update the data store first and then remove the cached item, so the next read loads the new value. Removing the key first leaves a window in which another reader can load the old row and put it back in the cache, a longer TTL keeps stale data around longer, and eviction only removes keys under memory pressure.

questions.prompt: For each statement about expiration in Azure Managed Redis, select Yes or No.

options.text: No
Yes

slots.text: With the default eviction policy, keys without a TTL aren't evicted under memory pressure.
EXPIREAT sets a key to expire at a specific date and time.
A key with a TTL takes no more memory than the same key without one.
The TTL command sets how many seconds a key may live.

questions.explanation: Azure Managed Redis defaults to volatile-lru, so only keys that carry a TTL can be evicted, and EXPIREAT sets expiry at a chosen date and time, whereas EXPIRE counts seconds. Expiration tracking adds memory for each key that has a TTL, and the TTL command only reports how long a key has left.

questions.prompt: A 60 GB Azure Managed Redis cache must work with a client library that doesn't support the Redis Cluster API. Which clustering policy should you choose?

options.text: OSS
Enterprise
Non-clustered
Active geo-replication

questions.explanation: The Enterprise policy puts a proxy behind a single endpoint, so clients that don't speak the cluster protocol still work, and it isn't limited to small caches. OSS needs a cluster-aware client that connects to each shard, Non-clustered applies only to caches of 25 GB or less, and active geo-replication is a replication feature rather than a clustering policy.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of a cache-aside read in order for an app that caches product records in Azure Managed Redis and, on a miss, caches the record before returning it.

options.text: Try to read the product's key from the cache
On a miss, read the product from the database
Return the product to the caller
Store the product in the cache with an expiration time

questions.explanation: Cache-aside loads data on demand: the app checks the cache first, goes to the data store only on a miss, adds the item to the cache and then returns it, as the stem requires. Setting an expiration when the item is stored limits how long it can go stale if another process changes the record.

questions.prompt: Which TWO actions meet Alpine Ski House's requirements for cached lift status? Select TWO.

options.text: Set EXPIREAT on each status to the end of the ski day
Delete a lift's key as soon as the lift is reported closed
Store each status with an expiration of 120 seconds
Seed every status at startup with no expiration set
Switch the cache's eviction policy to allkeys-lru

questions.explanation: A two-minute expiration caps how old any cached status can be, and removing the key when a closure is reported invalidates it at once instead of waiting for it to expire. Eviction runs only under memory pressure, seeded entries without expiration go stale indefinitely, and an expiry at the end of the day lets a status be hours old.

questions.prompt: An order's processing status is rewritten several times a minute and read back only when a customer opens the order page. A developer proposes write-through caching for it. What should the write path do?

options.text: Write to the cache alone and copy statuses to the database nightly
Write-through, with a one-day TTL on each cached order status
Write-through, so the cache matches the database after each write
Write to the database and invalidate the key, or bypass the cache

questions.explanation: Learn keeps write-through for read-heavy paths that need read-after-write freshness, because it adds latency and coordination to every write; data that's rarely read after it's written or that changes constantly should be invalidated on write or not cached at all. A TTL doesn't remove the write-through cost, and the cache must never be the only store for important changes.

questions.prompt: Which data is the best candidate for cache-aside in a shared Azure Managed Redis cache?

options.text: Session state for a web farm that depends on server affinity
Catalogue descriptions read thousands of times an hour and edited weekly
Payroll records that several apps and many users read from one cache
Search results that each user requests once and not again

questions.explanation: Caching pays off for data read often and changed rarely, which is exactly how the catalogue behaves. Learn warns against caching sensitive data in a cache that several applications or users share, and the pattern gives little when most requests miss, as with results read only once. It also advises against caching web-farm session state in a way that depends on client-server affinity.

questions.prompt: An Azure Managed Redis cache with High Availability enabled holds about 12 GB of data. About what value does the Used Memory metric report? Answer in GB. Enter a number.
questions.explanation: With High Availability, Used Memory adds the primary and replica shards, so it reports roughly twice the dataset: about 24 GB for 12 GB of data. The SKU memory limit already allows for replication, so Learn suggests watching Used Memory Percentage instead.

questions.prompt: For each statement about memory and eviction in Azure Managed Redis, select Yes or No.

options.text: Yes
No

slots.text: With the noeviction policy, writes fail once memory is full.
Used Memory Percentage already accounts for High Availability replication.
With High Availability, choose a SKU twice the size of your dataset.
MEMORY USAGE returns how many seconds a key has left before it expires.

questions.explanation: noeviction refuses writes when memory is exhausted, and the percentage metric is measured against a SKU limit that already includes replica memory. For the same reason you size the SKU on the dataset alone. MEMORY USAGE reports the bytes a key consumes, while TTL reports its remaining lifetime.

questions.prompt: After each deployment, every app instance loads the whole 50 GB product catalogue into Redis at startup, and database CPU spikes for minutes. What should you change?

options.text: Remove the TTLs so that the seeded items never need reloading
Run the seeding from all instances in parallel
Load items on demand, seeding only the most-used subset
Switch the eviction policy to allkeys-lru before seeding

questions.explanation: Seeding a large cache puts a sudden heavy load on the source database, so Learn suggests analysing usage and prepopulating only data that's heavily used, leaving the rest to cache-aside. Parallel seeding makes the spike sharper, dropping TTLs doesn't stop each deployment from reloading, and eviction choice has no effect on how much is read from the database.

questions.prompt: Fabrikam is creating a 40 GB Azure Managed Redis instance for its semantic cache. Which TWO settings must be chosen at creation for vector search to work? Select TWO.

options.text: Turn on data persistence for the cache
Enable the RediSearch module
Enable the RedisTimeSeries module
Choose the Enterprise clustering policy
Choose the Flash Optimized tier

questions.explanation: Vector search in Azure Managed Redis runs on RediSearch, which has to be enabled at creation because modules can't be added afterwards, and RediSearch can't run under the default OSS policy. Learn also allows RediSearch under Non-clustered, but that policy applies only to caches of 25 GB or less, so a 40 GB cache needs Enterprise clustering, which can't be changed in place later. The Well-Architected guidance also requires the NoEviction eviction policy for RediSearch. Flash Optimized doesn't offer RediSearch, TimeSeries isn't needed for vectors, and data persistence is an optional recovery feature rather than a vector search requirement.

questions.prompt: Complete the RedisVL semantic cache code that a Python API uses with Azure Managed Redis.

options.text: score_threshold=0.1,

distance_threshold=0.1,

duration=1800)
