options.text: check(prompt=question, num_results=3)
query(prompt=question, num_results=3)
store(prompt=question, num_results=3)

questions.explanation: RedisVL's SemanticCache takes distance_threshold in Redis cosine-distance units from 0 to 2, where lower is stricter, and a default ttl in seconds; check looks up semantically similar prompts and store saves a new prompt and response after a miss. score-threshold and duration are attributes of the API Management policies for gateway-level caching, which use their own units.

questions.prompt: A multitenant API's semantic cache returns an answer cached for one tenant to a user of another tenant who asked a similar question. Which TWO changes each stop this? Select TWO.

options.text: Store a tenant field with each entry and filter lookups on it
Lower the ttl so that a tenant's cached answers expire within a minute
Rebuild the cache's vector index as HNSW instead of FLAT
Give each tenant its own cache index
Raise distance_threshold so that fewer prompts count as a match

questions.explanation: Similarity matching ignores who asked, so Learn's guidance is to partition a semantic cache by tenant, through separate cache indexes or filterable fields, before any entry is reused. Raising distance_threshold loosens matching, because lower values are stricter, a shorter TTL only narrows the window in which the leak can happen, and the index type changes search speed and precision, not who can see an entry.

questions.prompt: During a busy weekend, Alpine Ski House's operations team raises the RedisVL distance_threshold for answer matching from 0.10 to 0.30. What is the effect?

options.text: More questions match an answer, including less similar ones
Nothing changes until the vector index has been rebuilt
Fewer questions match, because higher values are stricter
Cached answers start expiring three times as quickly

questions.explanation: distance_threshold is measured in Redis cosine-distance units from 0 to 2, where lower values are stricter, so raising it accepts matches that are further away and increases the risk of unrelated answers. The threshold is applied at lookup time, so no rebuild is needed, and expiry is governed by the ttl setting, not the threshold.

questions.prompt: A recommendation service stores 20 million product embeddings in Azure Managed Redis, and low latency matters more than exhaustive precision. Which vector index should it use?

options.text: A sorted set scored by similarity
HNSW
FLAT
JSON documents with no vector index

questions.explanation: RediSearch offers FLAT, an exact brute-force index for smaller datasets or exhaustive search, and HNSW, an approximate graph index for larger datasets where lower latency matters more than exhaustive precision. A sorted set or unindexed JSON documents give RediSearch no vector index to search.

questions.prompt: A semantic cache keeps returning answers that were produced before the team changed the prompt template. What should you change?

options.text: Include the template version in the cache's index name or filters
Lower distance_threshold to 0 so that only exact prompts match
Raise num_results so answers from the new template come back
Rebuild the cache's vector index as FLAT instead of HNSW

questions.explanation: Learn advises partitioning or versioning cache entries by prompt template, model and embedding model, because an entry created under an old template can be stale or incompatible after a change. A threshold of 0 nearly turns semantic matching off without separating old entries from new ones, the index type changes search precision, and more results still include the old answers.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about vector search in Azure Managed Redis are true? Select TWO.

options.text: Query vectors must have the dimensions of the indexed field
Vector indexes work under the OSS clustering policy
RediSearch is available on the Flash Optimized tier
API Management thresholds use RedisVL's distance units
Vectors can be stored in hashes or in JSON documents

questions.explanation: RediSearch indexes vectors held in hash or JSON structures, and a vector index only accepts query vectors with the same dimensions as its field. RediSearch isn't supported with the OSS policy, Flash Optimized doesn't support RediSearch, and API Management's score-threshold runs from 0.0 to 1.0, so values shouldn't be copied from RedisVL without validation.

questions.prompt: For each statement about using a semantic cache in front of a chat model, select Yes or No.

options.text: Yes
No

slots.text: Answers to public product FAQ questions can use a TTL of hours to days.
Answers about operational status call for a TTL of seconds to minutes.
Answers about a user's own account balance are good candidates for the cache.
On a cache miss, the request avoids the cost of creating a prompt embedding.

questions.explanation: Learn suggests long TTLs for stable content such as public FAQ answers and short ones for volatile status data. Highly personalized or time-sensitive answers shouldn't be cached semantically, and every eligible request pays for the prompt embedding and lookup; a miss then pays for the model call too.

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order for handling one prompt with an app-level semantic cache in Azure Managed Redis.

options.text: Receive the prompt from the caller
On a miss, call the chat model for a response
Search the cached prompt embeddings in the caller's partition
Store the prompt, response, embedding and TTL in Redis
Create the prompt's embedding with the cache's embedding model

questions.explanation: The prompt has to be embedded with the same model as the cached prompts before Redis can compare it by vector similarity, and the search is limited to the caller's tenant or version partition. Only when no entry falls within the threshold does the app call the model, and it then stores the new entry so that later similar prompts can hit.

questions.prompt: Messages with a malformed payload disappear from a payments queue after about ten failed processing attempts, and no code dead-letters them. Where are they now?

options.text: In the queue's dead-letter subqueue, with reason MaxDeliveryCountExceeded
Discarded by duplicate detection, which drops repeated deliveries
Removed for good, because Service Bus deletes messages it can't deliver
In the queue's transfer dead-letter queue, waiting to be forwarded

questions.explanation: Each failed peek-lock delivery raises the message's delivery count, and once the count passes the queue's maximum, 10 by default, Service Bus moves the message to the queue's dead-letter subqueue and records MaxDeliveryCountExceeded as the reason. Nothing cleans that subqueue up, so the messages wait there until someone receives and completes them. The transfer dead-letter queue holds only messages that auto-forwarding couldn't pass on, and duplicate detection looks at resent MessageIds, not at repeated deliveries.

questions.prompt: Complete the azure-servicebus code for an invoices worker that settles each message itself.

slots.text: Malformed payload, so reject it at once with no further deliveries: receiver.____(msg)

options.text: dead_letter_message
complete_message
abandon_message

slots.text: A downstream call timed out, so make the message available again right away: receiver.____(msg)

options.text: abandon_message
defer_message
complete_message

slots.text: An operator tool reads the rejected messages: client.get_queue_receiver(queue_name="invoices", ____=ServiceBusSubQueue.DEAD_LETTER)

options.text: receive_mode
session_id
sub_queue

questions.explanation: dead_letter_message moves the message to the dead-letter subqueue straight away (its optional reason and error_description arguments record why), while abandon_message only releases the lock, so the message would come back until the max delivery count dead-letters it, and complete_message deletes it. After a transient failure, abandon_message makes the message receivable again at once; defer_message would park it until someone asks for it by sequence number. The dead-letter subqueue is opened by passing sub_queue=ServiceBusSubQueue.DEAD_LETTER to get_queue_receiver; receive_mode picks peek-lock or receive-and-delete, and session_id targets a session.

questions.prompt: A worker needs about eight minutes per message, the queue's lock duration is already at its maximum, and some messages are processed twice. What should you do?

options.text: Enable sessions on the queue so that a single receiver owns each message
Receive in RECEIVE_AND_DELETE mode so that no lock can expire
Register each message with AutoLockRenewer until the worker settles it
Turn on duplicate detection for the queue that the worker reads

questions.explanation: The lock lasts at most five minutes, so an eight-minute job outlives it, the message becomes visible again and a second worker takes it; AutoLockRenewer (or calls to renew_message_lock) keeps extending the lock until the message is completed. Receive-and-delete removes the message on receipt, so a crash mid-job loses it. Duplicate detection only drops resends that carry a known MessageId, and sessions give a receiver an exclusive session lock that also expires and must be renewed, so they don't stop the redelivery.

questions.prompt: Match each requirement to the Service Bus feature that meets it.

options.text: Receive-and-delete mode
Scheduled messages
Message sessions
SQL filter rule
Duplicate detection

slots.text: Handle each customer's messages in order, one at a time
Ignore a resend that carries the same MessageId within 10 minutes
Make a reminder message appear in the queue 24 hours from now
Give one subscription only the messages whose amount property exceeds 1000

questions.explanation: Sessions give one receiver an exclusive lock on all messages with a session ID, which keeps their processing in order. Duplicate detection remembers MessageIds for a window that defaults to 10 minutes, scheduling (schedule_messages or scheduled_enqueue_time_utc) holds a message back until its enqueue time, and a SQL filter can compare a property with a relational operator. Receive-and-delete only changes how a message is settled, so it meets none of these needs.

questions.prompt: You added a filter rule for high-priority messages to a topic's alerts subscription, but the subscription still gets every message. What's the most likely cause?

options.text: Filters apply only to messages that were sent with a session ID
Rules without an action are skipped until one is added
Its $Default rule, a true filter, selects all messages
Priority is in the message body, and filters ignore the body

questions.explanation: A new subscription starts with a default rule, named $Default in Learn's filter examples, whose true filter selects everything, and a message enters the subscription when any rule matches, so the new rule changes nothing until $Default is removed. Filters never read the body, but a misplaced property would make the new rule match nothing, which can't explain receiving every message. Sessions play no part in filtering, and rules without actions are combined with OR rather than skipped.

questions.prompt: Which TWO events increase the delivery count of a message received in peek-lock mode? Select TWO.

options.text: The sender sends a copy with the same MessageId
Another client reads the message with peek_messages
The receiver abandons the message
The receiver completes the message
The lock expires before the receiver settles the message

questions.explanation: The delivery count goes up whenever a peek-locked message is abandoned or its lock runs out, and it is this count that eventually sends a poison message to the dead-letter queue. Completing removes the message, a resend with a known MessageId is a new send that duplicate detection may drop, and peek_messages takes no lock, so a peeked message isn't delivered under peek-lock and can't be settled.

questions.prompt: During a burst, some upload jobs wait in the documents queue longer than their time to live and then vanish, so operators can't inspect them. What should Contoso change?

options.text: Turn on sessions for the documents queue
Raise the queue's lock duration to the 5-minute maximum
Enable dead-lettering on message expiration
Enable duplicate detection on the documents queue

questions.explanation: With the expiration option off, Service Bus simply drops messages whose time to live has passed; turning it on moves them to the dead-letter queue with the reason TTLExpiredException, which keeps them available for investigation as Contoso requires. Sessions group related messages for ordered handling and still let expired messages be dropped, the lock duration only matters once a receiver holds a message, and duplicate detection drops resends.

questions.prompt: For each statement about Service Bus tiers, sessions and dead-letter queues, select Yes or No.

options.text: No
Yes

slots.text: A Basic tier namespace supports topics and subscriptions.
Messages in a dead-letter queue can be received in peek-lock mode, as in any other queue.
After sessions are enabled on a queue, clients can still send it messages without a session ID.
Session state on a Standard tier namespace can hold up to 256 KB.

questions.explanation: Topics and subscriptions need the Standard or Premium tier, and a dead-letter queue supports the normal receive operations, peek-lock and receive-and-delete included. Once sessions are enabled, every message sent to the queue must carry a session ID, and session state can be as large as one message: 256 KB on Standard and 100 MB on Premium.

questions.prompt: A subscription must receive only messages whose region property is EU and whose tier property is gold, with the least effect on throughput. Which filter should you use?

options.text: A SQL filter with a rule action that sets both properties
A correlation filter that matches both properties
A SQL filter: region = 'EU' AND tier = 'gold'
A filter that reads both values from the JSON body

questions.explanation: A correlation filter matches property values by equality and combines several conditions with AND, and Learn advises choosing it over SQL filters because it is much cheaper to evaluate. The SQL filter would select the same messages, but SQL rules lower throughput at the subscription, topic and namespace level. A rule action changes properties rather than selecting messages, and no filter can read the body.

questions.prompt: Python code must read the messages that the audit subscription of the orders topic receives. Which call creates the receiver?

options.text: client.get_subscription_receiver(topic_name="orders", subscription_name="audit")
client.get_queue_receiver(queue_name="audit")
client.get_topic_sender(topic_name="orders")
client.get_subscription_receiver(topic_name="audit", subscription_name="orders")

questions.explanation: Consumers never read a topic directly: each subscription acts as a virtual queue, and the azure-servicebus client opens it with get_subscription_receiver, naming the topic and then the subscription. Swapping the two names points at a topic called audit that doesn't exist, a subscription isn't a queue that get_queue_receiver can open by its name, and get_topic_sender only sends messages to the topic.

questions.prompt: Woodgrove's doc-classifier pods take messages from the applications queue. Which processing approach meets the requirements about lost and repeated applications?

options.text: Receive-and-delete, then record each classification result in the database
Peek-lock, complete each message on receipt, then classify its documents
Peek-lock, skip messages whose result is already recorded, then complete
Peek-lock with duplicate detection on, completing once the result is recorded

questions.explanation: Peek-lock leaves the message in the queue, locked, until the pod completes it, so a pod that crashes or is stopped part-way doesn't lose the application. That is at-least-once delivery, so a message can arrive again, and checking the application's ID (for example its MessageId) before writing keeps a retry from producing a second result. Receive-and-delete, or completing before the work is done, loses the application if the pod fails, and duplicate detection only drops a sender's resends of a known MessageId, not a redelivery of the same message to a receiver.

questions.prompt: A worker normally needs about three minutes per message, and its queue's lock is left at the default. Some messages are processed twice. Which change addresses the cause?

options.text: Enable duplicate detection with a three-minute history window
Set the queue's lock duration to a value above three minutes
Receive from the queue in receive-and-delete mode instead
Raise the receiver's prefetch_count so messages are cached ahead

questions.explanation: The default lock lasts one minute, so a three-minute job outlives it and the message becomes visible to another receiver. Learn advises a lock duration above the normal processing time, up to the five-minute maximum, so that no renewal is needed. Prefetching only caches messages ahead of processing, which makes lock expiry more likely rather than less, receive-and-delete trades duplicates for lost messages, and duplicate detection drops a sender's resends, not redeliveries.

questions.prompt: A session receiver accepts a session, receives three of its messages without settling them, and then closes the session. What happens to those messages' delivery counts?

options.text: They don't matter, because closing the session completes the messages
They stay as they were, and the messages can be received again
Each rises by one, as for a message the receiver abandons
Each rises by one, and the messages go to the dead-letter queue

questions.explanation: Learn's table for sessions says that when a session is accepted and closed with its messages still unsettled, the delivery count isn't incremented, and the messages remain available to the next receiver that accepts the session. The count rises when the session lock expires through a timeout, not when the session is closed, and closing a session never completes its messages.

questions.prompt: A topic's default message time to live is one hour, and its subscription's is one day. A message is sent with no time to live of its own. When does it expire in the subscription?

options.text: One day after it's enqueued
Never, because the message carries no time to live
Fourteen days after it's enqueued
One hour after it's enqueued

questions.explanation: An entity's default time to live applies to every message sent without one, and when a topic specifies a smaller time to live than its subscription, the topic's value is applied. The message therefore still expires, after one hour. Fourteen days is the default and maximum entity expiration on the Basic tier, which has no topics.

questions.prompt: A subscription has five rules: two with actions and three without. One message matches both rules with actions and two of the rules without actions. How many copies of it does the subscription receive? Answer in messages. Enter a number.
questions.explanation: Each matching rule with an action produces its own copy of the message, marked with the rule's name, so the two action rules give two copies. Rules without actions are combined with OR and yield a single message however many of them match, so the total is 2 + 1 = 3.

questions.prompt: Complete the ServiceBusAdministrationClient.create_queue call for a new orders queue.

slots.text: Discard a resend that reuses a MessageId: ____=True

options.text: requires_session
requires_duplicate_detection
duplicate_detection_history_time_window

slots.text: Move messages whose time to live passes to the dead-letter subqueue: ____=True

options.text: forward_dead_lettered_messages_to
enable_batched_operations
dead_lettering_on_message_expiration

slots.text: Give each customer's messages to one receiver at a time, in order: ____=True

options.text: requires_session
enable_express
enable_partitioning

questions.explanation: requires_duplicate_detection turns on MessageId tracking, while the history time window is a duration that sets how long IDs are kept. dead_lettering_on_message_expiration moves expired messages to the dead-letter subqueue instead of dropping them, whereas forward_dead_lettered_messages_to names another entity. requires_session makes the queue session-aware, so one receiver holds each session's messages in order; partitioning, express entities and batched operations affect storage and throughput, not these behaviours.

questions.prompt: Complete the azure-servicebus code that sends a few hundred order events to the orders topic in as few calls as possible.

slots.text: Sender for the topic: client.____(topic_name="orders")

options.text: get_queue_sender
get_topic_sender
get_subscription_receiver

slots.text: Empty batch sized for the entity: batch = sender.____()

options.text: create_message_batch
ServiceBusMessage
send_messages

slots.text: batch.add_message(msg) when the batch is already full

options.text: raises ValueError, so start a new batch
drops the message without an error
sends the full batch automatically

questions.explanation: A topic is sent to through get_topic_sender, because subscriptions are only for receiving, and create_message_batch returns an empty ServiceBusMessageBatch sized to what the entity accepts. add_message raises ValueError once the batch reaches its maximum size, so the code sends the full batch with send_messages and starts a new one; nothing is dropped or sent on its own.

questions.prompt: Match each cause to the dead-letter reason that Service Bus records.

options.text: MaxDeliveryCountExceeded
Session ID is null
MaxTransferHopCountExceeded
HeaderSizeExceeded
TTLExpiredException

slots.text: A message expires on a queue that dead-letters expired messages
A message without a session ID is sent to a session-enabled queue
A message is forwarded through more than four chained queues
A message's header exceeds the size quota for its stream

questions.explanation: Service Bus sets TTLExpiredException for messages dead-lettered on expiry, Session ID is null when a session-enabled entity gets a message without one, MaxTransferHopCountExceeded when forwarding goes past four hops, and HeaderSizeExceeded when the header size quota is exceeded. MaxDeliveryCountExceeded is recorded only when a message's delivery count passes the entity's limit, which none of these causes involves.

questions.prompt: On a session-enabled queue with dead-lettering on expiration, one message of an active session passes its time to live while a receiver is listening. What happens?

options.text: All of that session's messages are moved to the dead-letter queue
The messages stay put until the receiver closes the session
The expired message is dropped and the session carries on
The expired message alone is moved to the dead-letter queue

questions.explanation: Messages on a session-enabled entity are locked at the session level, so when any message in a session passes its time to live, every message of that session expires, and the entity's dead-lettering on expiration setting decides whether they're dropped or dead-lettered. With the setting on, they all go to the dead-letter queue. Treating just the one message as expired is how an entity without sessions behaves, and dropping happens only when the setting is off.

questions.prompt: Three worker replicas, which can process any tenant, each call get_queue_receiver with session_id="tenant-7" on a session-enabled queue, and two of them fail with SessionCannotBeLockedError. What should the workers do?

options.text: Receive in receive-and-delete mode so that no session lock is held
Give each replica its own subscription on the session queue
Pass session_id=NEXT_AVAILABLE_SESSION when each creates its receiver
Register the session with AutoLockRenewer in every replica

questions.explanation: Only one receiver can hold a session's lock, so the replicas that ask for the same session ID are refused with SessionCannotBeLockedError. For a session-enabled queue, get_queue_receiver needs a session_id, and passing NEXT_AVAILABLE_SESSION makes each receiver take whichever session is free, which spreads the replicas across sessions. AutoLockRenewer only keeps a lock that a receiver already holds, a session still has to be accepted whatever the receive mode, and queues have no subscriptions.

questions.prompt: A Python script loops with for msg in receiver over a queue receiver and never exits when the queue is empty. How can it stop after five seconds with no messages?

options.text: Pass max_message_count=5 when it creates the receiver
Pass receive_mode=RECEIVE_AND_DELETE to the receiver
Pass prefetch_count=5 when it creates the receiver
Pass max_wait_time=5 when it creates the receiver

questions.explanation: max_wait_time, given on the receiver or on receive_messages, is how long receiving waits with no traffic before it stops, and it also ends a generator-style loop, which otherwise keeps waiting. prefetch_count controls how many messages are fetched ahead, max_message_count limits how many messages one receive_messages call returns, and the receive mode changes settlement, not how long the loop waits.

questions.prompt: A web API's managed identity sends messages to one Service Bus queue and never receives. Which role assignment grants it no more than it needs?

options.text: Azure Service Bus Data Sender, scoped to that queue
Azure Service Bus Data Sender, scoped to the namespace
Azure Service Bus Data Owner, scoped to that queue
Azure Service Bus Data Receiver, scoped to that queue

questions.explanation: Data Sender gives send access only, and scoping the assignment to the one queue keeps the identity away from the namespace's other entities. Data Owner also allows receiving and managing entities, a namespace scope covers every queue and topic in it, and Data Receiver allows receiving but not sending.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about a Service Bus dead-letter queue are true? Select TWO.

options.text: Messages reach it only when code calls dead_letter_message
Its messages don't expire, because time to live isn't observed there
A topic keeps one dead-letter queue for all its subscriptions
A message in it can't be dead-lettered a second time
It can be deleted on its own while its queue is kept

questions.explanation: The dead-letter queue ignores time to live, and a message in it can't be dead-lettered again; it stays until someone receives and completes it. Service Bus itself also moves messages there, for example on expiry or after too many deliveries. Each queue and each subscription has its own dead-letter queue, since messages don't stay at the topic level, and it can't be deleted or managed apart from its parent entity.

questions.prompt: Duplicate detection is on for a queue without partitioning. Which TWO statements are true? Select TWO.

options.text: Two messages with different MessageIds and the same body count as copies
A shorter history window reduces the effect on throughput
A duplicate send raises an exception, which tells the sender to stop retrying
A resend with a known MessageId is reported to the sender as accepted
The history window can be set to at most 24 hours

questions.explanation: When a message arrives with a MessageId logged in the window, Service Bus reports the send as accepted and silently drops the copy, and because every new ID is matched against the recorded ones, a smaller window keeps fewer IDs and affects throughput less. Only the MessageId is compared, never the body, and the window ranges from 20 seconds to 7 days, with a default of 10 minutes.

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order to reprocess a message that was dead-lettered because of a bug in its consumer.

options.text: Peek the message in the dead-letter queue and read its dead-letter reason
Complete the dead-lettered message
Fix and redeploy the consumer code that the reason points to
Send a copy of the message to the original queue

questions.explanation: The dead-letter reason and description identify the cause, and the cause has to be fixed before the message is resubmitted, or it fails again. Sending the copy before completing the dead-lettered message means a failure between those two steps leaves a spare copy rather than losing the message, and the dead-letter queue never cleans itself up, so the message stays there until it's completed.

questions.prompt: Proseware adds a quality-review service that must get every transcript message, while insight-worker keeps getting all of them too. What should Proseware do?

options.text: Add a second subscription on the topic for the new service
Have the new service peek the analysis subscription's messages
Forward the analysis subscription to a queue that both services read
Have the new service also read from the analysis subscription

questions.explanation: Each subscription receives its own copy of every message sent to the topic, so a new subscription gives quality-review all transcripts without taking any from insight-worker. Two services reading one subscription, or one shared queue, become competing consumers, each message going to only one of them, and peeking takes no lock and settles nothing, so it can't reliably process every message.

questions.prompt: You create an event subscription on an Event Grid custom topic (basic tier, push delivery) and keep the default retry policy. What is the policy's maximum number of delivery attempts? Answer in attempts. Enter a number.
questions.explanation: The retry policy of such a subscription allows 1 to 30 attempts, with 30 as the default, next to an event time to live of 1 to 1,440 minutes that defaults to 1,440 (24 hours). You can lower either value when you create the subscription, for example with --max-delivery-attempts in the Azure CLI, and Event Grid namespace topics have delivery settings of their own.

questions.prompt: An event subscription on an Event Grid custom topic has no dead-letter location, and its webhook answers an event with 400 Bad Request. What happens to that event?

options.text: Event Grid drops it without retrying
Event Grid keeps it until the webhook returns 200 OK
Event Grid retries it until the event's time to live runs out
Event Grid stores it in the topic's built-in dead-letter queue

questions.explanation: A 400 (like 413, and 401 or 403 from a webhook) tells Event Grid that delivery can never succeed, so the event isn't retried: it is dead-lettered if a location is set and dropped otherwise. The retry schedule applies to other failures such as timeouts or 503, there is no built-in dead-letter store because dead-lettering is off until you name a blob container, and Event Grid doesn't hold events indefinitely.

questions.prompt: Match each routing need to the event subscription filter that meets it.

options.text: Advanced filter IsNullOrUndefined
Included event types
Advanced filter NumberGreaterThan
Subject begins with
Subject ends with
Retry policy

slots.text: Only events of type Orders.Shipped or Orders.Cancelled
Only blobs whose names end in .pdf
Only blobs in the invoices container
Only events whose data.weightKg is above 20

questions.explanation: Event type filtering lists the types a subscription wants, subject filters match the start or end of the subject (for blob events, a container path or a file extension), and advanced filters compare fields in the event data, such as NumberGreaterThan for a numeric threshold. IsNullOrUndefined only tests whether a key is missing or null, and the retry policy controls delivery, not which events are routed.

questions.prompt: An Event Grid custom topic subscription has a 30-minute event time to live and 20 maximum delivery attempts, and its webhook is down for two hours. When does Event Grid stop trying to deliver an event?

options.text: When the time to live runs out, after about six attempts
After the first failure, because unreachable webhooks aren't retried
When the webhook is back, as retries go on until delivery succeeds
After the 20th attempt, however long it takes

questions.explanation: Event Grid ends delivery at whichever retry-policy limit is reached first, and its backoff schedule (10 seconds, 30 seconds, 1 minute, 5 minutes, 10 minutes, 30 minutes and so on) fits only about six attempts into 30 minutes, so the time to live wins and a higher attempt count changes nothing. An endpoint that doesn't respond is retried, since only codes such as 400 or 413 stop retries at once, and the policy never extends delivery past its limits.

questions.prompt: Complete the Python code that publishes an order event to an Event Grid custom topic whose input schema is CloudEvents v1.0.

slots.text: Client that signs in with the topic's access key: EventGridPublisherClient(endpoint, ____)

options.text: key
AzureKeyCredential(key)
DefaultAzureCredential(key)

slots.text: Event object: client.send(____(type="Orders.Shipped", source="/sales/orders", data=order))

options.text: ServiceBusMessage
CloudEvent
EventGridEvent

slots.text: Same client for a topic in an Event Grid namespace: EventGridPublisherClient(endpoint, credential, ____="orders")

options.text: subscription
namespace_topic
topic_name

questions.explanation: The access key is passed wrapped in AzureKeyCredential from azure.core.credentials, because the client expects a credential object rather than a bare string, and DefaultAzureCredential takes no key because it signs in with Microsoft Entra ID. A topic created for CloudEvents expects CloudEvent objects (azure.core.messaging), and sending another schema to it raises errors. The default client targets Event Grid basic topics, and passing namespace_topic makes it publish to a topic in an Event Grid namespace instead; subscription is an EventGridConsumerClient argument, and topic_name isn't one of the client's parameters.

questions.prompt: Each new blob in a storage account must start three independent handlers within seconds. What should you set up?

options.text: An Event Grid system topic for the account with three event subscriptions
Messages that the uploading client writes to a storage queue
A timer function that lists the account's new blobs every minute
One Service Bus queue that all three handlers read from

questions.explanation: Blob Storage publishes blob-created events to an Event Grid system topic, and each event subscription pushes its own copy to its handler, which suits reactive fan-out with no polling. A queue gives each message to only one competing consumer, so three handlers on one queue would split the work instead of each seeing every blob; a timer adds up to a minute of delay on every pass, and client-written messages miss blobs uploaded by other paths.

questions.prompt: Fabrikam's ingestion webhook gets no ManualPublished events: its event subscription uses the Event Grid schema, and creating it reported a failed validation. What should the webhook do?

options.text: Present a self-signed certificate that Event Grid can check
Move the subscription to CloudEvents to skip the handshake
Echo the validationCode from the validation event in its response
Answer every validation request with 202 Accepted instead of 200 OK

questions.explanation: Before delivering to a webhook, Event Grid sends a SubscriptionValidationEvent, and the endpoint proves ownership by returning its validationCode as validationResponse with 200 OK (or by calling the validationUrl within 10 minutes). A 202 isn't accepted as a validation response, self-signed certificates aren't supported, and CloudEvents delivery still needs a handshake, an HTTP OPTIONS exchange.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about CloudEvents v1.0 on Event Grid basic-tier custom and system topics are true? Select TWO.

options.text: CloudEvents deliveries are limited to webhook endpoints
A topic with Event Grid schema input can deliver CloudEvents to a subscription
CloudEvents deliveries carry the content type application/cloudevents+json
System topics can't deliver their events in the CloudEvents schema
A topic with CloudEvents input can deliver the Event Grid schema to a subscription

questions.explanation: Event Grid can turn Event Grid schema input into CloudEvents output, but not the other way round, because the Event Grid schema can't carry CloudEvents extension attributes; CloudEvents deliveries are marked with the application/cloudevents+json content type. System events such as Blob Storage events can use CloudEvents too, and an Azure Functions Event Grid trigger can receive them as CloudEvent objects.

questions.prompt: Margie's Travel keeps undeliverable ListingUpdated events in a dead-letter container and wants the data team alerted as each one arrives there. What should it set up?

options.text: A Service Bus queue as the original subscription's dead-letter location
An event subscription on the dead-letter storage account's blob-created events
Output batching on the original subscription, so failed events arrive together
A second retry policy on the original subscription, with 30 attempts

questions.explanation: Dead-lettered events are written as blobs to the container, and Learn's way to react to them is an Event Grid subscription on that dead-letter Blob storage, which notifies a handler every time an undelivered event lands. An event subscription has one retry policy, already 30 attempts by default, the dead-letter location has to be a blob container in a storage account, and batching changes delivery, not alerting.

questions.prompt: During short CRM outages, the gateway in front of the CRM webhook answers with an error status. Which status would break Proseware's requirement for ChurnRisk events?

options.text: 503 Service Unavailable
403 Forbidden
500 Internal Server Error
408 Request Timeout

questions.explanation: Event Grid doesn't retry a webhook delivery that gets 400, 401, 403 or 413, because those codes say that retrying can't succeed, so a 403 makes it drop the event, or dead-letter it if a location is set, instead of waiting for the CRM to come back. 503 is retried after 30 seconds or more, 408 after 2 minutes or more, and codes such as 500 follow the normal exponential backoff, so those events still arrive once the webhook recovers.

questions.prompt: An HTTP-triggered function receives events from a subscription that delivers in the CloudEvents v1.0 schema, and validation never completes. What must the function do?

options.text: Echo the validationCode from the SubscriptionValidationEvent in the response body
Reply to the HTTP OPTIONS request with 405 Method Not Allowed and an Allow header
Answer the OPTIONS request with WebHook-Allowed-Origin and WebHook-Allowed-Rate headers
Call the validationUrl from the event data within 10 minutes of creation

questions.explanation: With CloudEvents output, Event Grid uses the CloudEvents v1.0 abuse protection instead of the validation event: it sends an HTTP OPTIONS request carrying WebHook-Request-Origin, and the target agrees by replying with both WebHook-Allowed-Origin, set to that origin or an asterisk, and WebHook-Allowed-Rate. The validationCode echo and the validationUrl belong to the Event Grid schema handshake, and 405 is how a target says it doesn't support OPTIONS, which isn't consent.

questions.prompt: A third-party endpoint can't return the validationCode, and nobody opened the validationUrl in the time allowed. What must you do now?

options.text: Set the subscription's provisioning state back to AwaitingManualAction
Re-create the subscription and open its new validationUrl in time
Wait for Event Grid to resend the validation event
Open the original validationUrl, which stays valid until it's used

questions.explanation: The validationUrl is valid for 10 minutes, while the subscription waits in AwaitingManualAction; after that, its provisioning state becomes Failed, and Learn says you have to create the event subscription again before starting manual validation. The old URL has expired, Event Grid doesn't resend the validation event on its own, and the provisioning state isn't a value you set.

questions.prompt: A Python app publishes events to an Event Grid custom topic with DefaultAzureCredential. Which role does its identity need on the topic?

options.text: EventGrid EventSubscription Reader
EventGrid Data Sender
Reader
EventGrid Data Receiver

questions.explanation: To send events with a token credential, the identity needs the EventGrid Data Sender role, while EventGrid Data Receiver is for receiving events from an event subscription with a token credential. Reader and EventGrid EventSubscription Reader are management-plane roles that let an identity view resources, not send events to them.

questions.prompt: A subscription must get only events whose data.category is hotel or tour and whose data.priceBand is budget. How should its advanced filters be set?

options.text: One StringIn filter on data.category with both values, and one on data.priceBand
One StringIn filter on data.category whose values are hotel, tour and budget
Two StringIn filters on data.category, one per value, plus one on data.priceBand
A subject begins-with filter for hotel and tour, plus one on data.priceBand

questions.explanation: Values listed in one advanced filter are combined with OR, and separate filters are combined with AND, so one filter holding both categories plus a second filter for the price band selects exactly the wanted events. Two category filters would both have to match, which no event can do, adding budget to the category values tests the wrong field, and a subject filter reads the subject rather than the event data.

questions.prompt: A handler sometimes gets a listing's newer ListingUpdated event before an older one and then overwrites good data. What should you change?

options.text: Turn on output batching to keep publish order
Limit the handler's subscription to a single delivery attempt
Turn on sessions for the subscription so the events stay in order
Have the handler compare versions and ignore stale ones

questions.explanation: Event Grid doesn't guarantee delivery order, so subscribers can receive events out of order, and the handler has to protect itself, for example by comparing a version or timestamp in the event with what it already stored. Event Grid has no sessions, which are a Service Bus feature, batching only groups events for HTTP efficiency, and allowing a single attempt would lose events rather than order them.

questions.prompt: A subscription delivers batches of up to 500 events, and the handler returns 500 when any event in a batch fails. Events it already stored arrive again. Why?

options.text: Event Grid retries the whole batch, which can't partly succeed
Event Grid splits a failed batch and resends its events one at a time
The batch passed its preferred size, so the rest was resent
Event Grid delivers each batch twice so that the handler can confirm it

questions.explanation: Batched delivery is all or none: a failure response fails every event in the batch, so the retry resends events the handler had already stored, and Learn advises asking only for as many events per batch as the handler can process in 30 seconds. Event Grid doesn't split a failed batch into single events, the preferred batch size is a best-effort target rather than a reason to resend, and batches aren't sent twice by design.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about advanced filters on an Event Grid event subscription are true? Select TWO.

options.text: Their string comparisons aren't case-sensitive
A string value in a filter can be up to 4,096 characters long
A key whose name contains a dot can be escaped with a backslash
A key can be an array of objects, such as a list of line items
A key can be a string array once enableAdvancedFilteringOnArrays is true

questions.explanation: Learn states that all string comparisons in advanced filters ignore case, and arrays of one type, such as strings or integers, can be keys once enableAdvancedFilteringOnArrays is set. Arrays of objects aren't supported, keys that contain a dot can't be escaped, and each string value is limited to 512 characters, within 25 advanced filters and 25 values per subscription.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about Event Grid namespaces and the azure-eventgrid client library are true? Select TWO.

options.text: A basic custom topic supports pull delivery to consumers
A namespace topic accepts only the CloudEvents v1.0 schema
EventGridConsumerClient receives events from namespace topics alone
Publishing to a namespace topic needs EventGridEvent objects
EventGridPublisherClient can't send events to namespace topics

questions.explanation: Namespace topics support only CloudEvents v1.0, so they take CloudEvent objects or their dict form, and EventGridConsumerClient's receive, acknowledge, release and reject operations work only with namespaces, which support pull as well as push delivery. Basic topics support push delivery only, and EventGridPublisherClient publishes to a namespace topic when it's given namespace_topic.

questions.prompt: Complete the az eventgrid event-subscription create command for a webhook subscription on a custom topic.

slots.text: Keep undeliverable events: ____ $storageid/blobServices/default/containers/failed

options.text: --delivery-identity-endpoint

questions.explanation: --deadletter-endpoint takes the resource path of a blob container for events that Event Grid gives up on, while --endpoint is where events are delivered. --event-ttl sets the time to live in minutes, from 1 to 1,440, whereas --max-delivery-attempts counts attempts and --expiration-date ends the subscription itself. --event-delivery-schema cloudeventschemav1_0 selects CloudEvents output, a conversion that Event Grid supports from Event Grid schema input.

questions.prompt: Match each webhook response to how Event Grid treats the delivery.

options.text: Retried after 30 seconds or more
Not retried
Retried every 12 hours for 7 days
Counted as a successful delivery
Retried after 2 minutes or more

slots.text: 413 Request Entity Too Large
503 Service Unavailable
408 Request Timeout
204 No Content

questions.explanation: Event Grid treats only 200 to 204 as success, so 204 completes the delivery. 413 is one of the codes it doesn't retry, 503 is retried after 30 seconds or more and 408 after 2 minutes or more, while other failures follow the exponential backoff. No schedule runs for 7 days, since an event's time to live is at most 1,440 minutes.

questions.prompt: For each statement about retries and dead-lettering on an Event Grid custom topic subscription, select Yes or No.

options.text: No
Yes

slots.text: Event Grid waits 30 seconds for a response before it queues the event for a retry.
You can change the intervals of the retry schedule on an event subscription.
A dead-lettered event reaches its location about five minutes after the last attempt.
If the dead-letter location is unavailable for four hours, the event waits until it's back.

questions.explanation: Event Grid waits 30 seconds for a response and then queues the event for retry, and while you can set the maximum attempts and the time to live, the retry schedule itself can't be configured. Dead-lettered events are written about five minutes after the last attempt, to reduce Blob storage operations, and an event whose dead-letter location is unavailable for four hours is dropped.

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order to start delivering events from an existing Event Grid custom topic to a new webhook handler.

options.text: Deploy the handler with code that answers the validation event
Wait for the subscription's validation to succeed
Publish events to the topic with EventGridPublisherClient
Create the event subscription that points to the handler

questions.explanation: Event Grid sends the validation event when the subscription is created, so the handler must already be running to return the validation code, and events are delivered to it only after the endpoint has proved ownership. Events published before then have no validated subscription to go to.

questions.prompt: A timer-triggered function must run at 07:30 UTC from Monday to Friday. Which schedule expression should it use?
questions.explanation: The six-field NCRONTAB form reads second, minute, hour, day, month and day of week, so 0 30 7 is 07:30:00, and day-of-week values 1-5 are Monday to Friday because 0 is Sunday. Swapping minute and hour asks for hour 30, 0-4 runs Sunday to Thursday, and 30 0 7 fires at 07:00:30 because the first field is seconds. Schedules run in UTC unless the plan supports a time zone setting.

questions.prompt: Complete the Python v2 code that serves GET requests such as /api/products/42 on a function app with the default route prefix.

slots.text: @app.route(methods=["GET"], route=____)

options.text: "products/{product_id}"
"api/products/{product_id}"
"products?product_id={product_id}"

a product_id argument on get_product
req.params.get("product_id")

options.text: /api/products/42
/products/42
/runtime/products/42

questions.explanation: Routes are prefixed with api by default, so the template is products/{product_id}; writing api into it would double the prefix, and a query string isn't a route template. The v2 model exposes route values through req.route_params, while req.params holds the query string, and Learn says not to add route parameters as extra function arguments. An empty routePrefix in host.json removes api from the URL, and /runtime is reserved for the Functions host.

questions.prompt: Partner companies call an HTTP-triggered function, and one partner's access must be revocable without affecting the others. How should you configure access?

options.text: auth_level FUNCTION and one host key shared by all partners
auth_level ANONYMOUS and partner names checked in the query string
auth_level FUNCTION and a separate function key for each partner
auth_level ADMIN and the master key shared by all partners

questions.explanation: At the function level a request must present a key, in the code query parameter or the x-functions-key header, and each key has its own name, so one partner's key can be rotated or deleted while the others keep working. A single shared host key would also pass the check, but revoking it cuts off every partner at once; the master key is an administrative credential that Learn says not to give to third parties, and anonymous access checks no key at all.

questions.prompt: A @app.service_bus_queue_trigger uses connection="SB", and the app must connect with its system-assigned managed identity. Which TWO should you configure? Select TWO.

options.text: An app setting SB that holds the namespace connection string
An app setting SB__fullyQualifiedNamespace with the namespace host name
An app setting SB__clientId that holds the managed identity's object ID
The Azure Service Bus Data Receiver role for the identity on the queue
The Azure Service Bus Data Sender role for the identity on the queue

questions.explanation: An identity-based connection is a group of app settings that share the connection prefix, and for Service Bus it needs <prefix>__fullyQualifiedNamespace; the app's system-assigned identity is used by default, while a user-assigned one also needs the credential and clientId properties. The identity also needs a role that allows receiving, such as Azure Service Bus Data Receiver (Data Owner also works, and gives the most accurate scaling). A connection string brings back a stored secret, Data Sender only sends, and clientId is for choosing a user-assigned identity.

questions.prompt: Without using the Service Bus SDK, an HTTP-triggered Python function must also send a message to a Service Bus queue. What should you add?

options.text: A return of the message text, which the runtime then sends on to the queue
@app.service_bus_queue_output and a func.Out[str] parameter that the code sets
@app.queue_output with the name of the Service Bus queue
@app.service_bus_topic_output with topic_name set to the Service Bus queue's name

questions.explanation: An output binding lets the runtime write the message: the decorator names the queue and connection, and the function calls set on its func.Out parameter. With @app.route the return value is bound to the HTTP response, so returning the text answers the caller instead of queueing anything. The topic output binding sends to a topic named by topic_name, which a queue isn't, and queue_output writes to Azure Queue Storage.

questions.prompt: A Python function should receive an authenticated BlobClient for its input blob instead of the blob's bytes. What does this need?

options.text: A function.json input binding in the v1 model whose type is BlobClient
The v1 programming model with the blob input's dataType set to binary
An Event Grid trigger that passes each new blob in as a BlobClient
The v2 programming model and SDK type bindings for Blob Storage

questions.explanation: SDK type bindings let a Blob Storage trigger or input binding hand the function SDK objects such as BlobClient, and for Python they work only in the v2 decorator model, through the Blob bindings extension package. The v1 model, with or without a binary dataType, still passes the content rather than a client, and an Event Grid trigger delivers the event, not a Blob Storage client.

questions.prompt: Match each binding extension to the binding types that Azure Functions supports for it.

options.text: Input only
Trigger only
Trigger, input and output
Output only
Input and output, but no trigger

slots.text: Timer
Table Storage
SendGrid
Blob Storage

questions.explanation: Learn's supported-bindings table shows the timer as a trigger alone, Table Storage with input and output bindings but no trigger, SendGrid as an output binding only, and Blob Storage with all three. No extension in that table is input-only, so that option fits none of them.

questions.prompt: An HTTP-triggered summary function can run for up to ten minutes, and callers get HTTP 502 after about four minutes although the plan allows 30-minute runs. What should you change?

options.text: Raise the HTTP concurrency limit so requests don't wait behind others
Move to a Dedicated plan with Always On so that the limit is lifted
Queue the job, reply at once with a status URL, and process it from the queue
Raise the app's function timeout from 30 to 60 minutes for this work

questions.explanation: Whatever the timeout setting or plan, an HTTP-triggered function has 230 seconds to respond before Azure Load Balancer gives up and returns 502, although the function keeps running. Learn's advice for long work is an asynchronous pattern: hand the job off, answer immediately with a location to poll, and do the work elsewhere, for example in a queue-triggered function or with Durable Functions. A longer timeout or another plan leaves the 230-second limit in place, and concurrency doesn't shorten one request.

questions.prompt: One piece of Python logic must run both for HTTP requests and for messages on a Service Bus queue. How should you build it?

options.text: Two functions, each with its own trigger, that call shared code
One HTTP function with a Service Bus input binding for the queue
One timer function that polls the queue and also answers HTTP calls
One function decorated with both @app.route and @app.service_bus_queue_trigger

questions.explanation: A function has exactly one trigger, so the two entry points become two functions in the same app that call a shared helper, which can live in a shared module or a blueprint. Stacking two trigger decorators on one function isn't valid, Service Bus offers a trigger and an output binding but no input binding, and a timer trigger can't serve HTTP requests.

questions.prompt: Lucerne wants the change-feed function to write each article's vector to article-vectors without creating a Cosmos DB client in its code. How should the function be defined?

options.text: Keep its trigger on articles and add a Cosmos DB output binding for article-vectors
Add a Cosmos DB input binding for article-vectors and edit the documents it passes in
Move its trigger to article-vectors and add an output binding for articles
Add a second Cosmos DB trigger, on article-vectors, to the same function

questions.explanation: A function has exactly one trigger, which here stays on the articles change feed, and an output binding lets the runtime write data out to another resource, so the vectors reach article-vectors without SDK code in the function. A second trigger isn't allowed, an input binding only passes data in, and moving the trigger to article-vectors would stop the function from seeing article edits.

questions.prompt: To revoke a partner's access, you deleted an HTTP function and recreated it with the same name, yet the partner's old key still works. Why?

options.text: Deleted functions keep serving requests until the function app restarts
Callers cache function keys and keep using them for up to 24 hours
Stored keys outlive the function and are reused for the same name
The recreated function's authorization level now defaults to anonymous

questions.explanation: Access keys have their own lifecycle in the app's secret store, so deleting a function doesn't delete or rotate them, and because a key's storage location comes from the name, a function recreated with the same name picks up the stored keys again; the fix is to revoke or regenerate the key itself. An HTTP function with no explicit level defaults to the function level, not anonymous, and keys aren't cached by callers.

questions.prompt: A timer function on a Flex Consumption app must run at 09:00 New York time, and a first attempt set WEBSITE_TIME_ZONE to America/New_York. What should you do?

options.text: Remove the setting and write the schedule in UTC
Set TZ to America/New_York in place of WEBSITE_TIME_ZONE
Keep the setting but use the Windows name Eastern Standard Time
Switch to a TimeSpan schedule that repeats every 24 hours

questions.explanation: WEBSITE_TIME_ZONE and TZ aren't supported on Flex Consumption, where they can cause SSL issues and stop metrics, so the NCRONTAB expression has to be written in UTC, which is the default, and adjusted if daylight saving time matters. Windows zone names apply only on Windows, TZ is unsupported in the same way, and a TimeSpan schedule works only on an App Service plan.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about timer-triggered functions are true? Select TWO.

options.text: When the app scales out, a single instance runs each occurrence
The next occurrence starts even if the last run is still going
A TimeSpan schedule works on every hosting plan
use_monitor defaults to false for an hourly schedule
run_on_startup also fires when the app scales out

questions.explanation: The timer trigger takes a storage lock so that one instance runs each occurrence across a scaled-out app, and it doesn't fire again while an invocation is still running. run_on_startup fires whenever the runtime starts, which includes waking from idle and scaling out, so Learn says to set it rarely, if ever, in production. TimeSpan schedules need an App Service plan, and use_monitor defaults to true for schedules with an interval of a minute or more.

questions.prompt: Complete the Python v2 decorator for a function that processes the audit subscription of the orders topic.

slots.text: Decorator: @app.____(arg_name="msg", topic_name="orders", ...)

options.text: service_bus_queue_trigger
service_bus_topic_output
service_bus_topic_trigger

slots.text: subscription_name=____

options.text: "orders"
"audit"
"orders/audit"

slots.text: connection="SB", where SB is

options.text: the name of an app setting or setting prefix
the namespace connection string itself
the name of the topic to monitor

questions.explanation: A topic subscription is monitored with service_bus_topic_trigger, which takes topic_name and subscription_name separately, so subscription_name is just audit; the queue trigger watches a queue, and the topic output binding sends rather than receives. connection names an app setting, or the prefix of a group of identity-based settings, rather than holding the connection string, and the topic is already named in topic_name.

questions.prompt: Complete the Python v2 code for a signup function that reads a JSON body and needs no key, while the app's other HTTP functions keep requiring one.

slots.text: App object: app = func.FunctionApp(http_auth_level=____)

options.text: func.AuthLevel.ANONYMOUS
func.AuthLevel.FUNCTION
func.AuthLevel.ADMIN

func.AuthLevel.ANONYMOUS
func.AuthLevel.FUNCTION

options.text: req.params.get("body")
req.route_params
req.get_json()

questions.explanation: http_auth_level on FunctionApp sets the level for the app's HTTP functions, so FUNCTION keeps a key required, and the auth_level argument of @app.route sets the level for one function, here ANONYMOUS so that no key is needed; ADMIN would require the master key. req.get_json() parses the JSON body, whereas req.params holds query-string values and req.route_params holds values from the route template.

questions.prompt: A Service Bus queue feeds a Python function, and the team wants a message that keeps failing to be dead-lettered after 3 failed deliveries instead of 10. Where should that be set?

options.text: In host.json, under the Service Bus extension's settings
On the Service Bus entity, as its maximum delivery count
In a max_delivery_count argument on the trigger decorator
In the function app's application settings, as MaxDeliveryCount=3

questions.explanation: Poison message handling can't be controlled or configured in Azure Functions: Service Bus moves a message to the dead-letter queue when its delivery count passes the entity's maximum, 10 by default, and the runtime's abandon after each failed run is what raises that count. host.json's Service Bus settings cover things such as automatic completion and lock renewal, and neither app settings nor the trigger decorator hold the queue's limit.

questions.prompt: Put the events in order for a Service Bus-triggered function whose run lasts longer than the queue's lock duration and then succeeds.

options.text: The runtime renews the message lock while the function runs
The function starts with the message as its input
The runtime completes the message
The function returns without raising an exception
The runtime receives the message in peek-lock mode

questions.explanation: The Functions runtime receives Service Bus messages in peek-lock mode and passes each one to the function. While the function runs past the lock duration, the runtime keeps renewing the lock, up to maxAutoRenewDuration (5 minutes by default), and once the function finishes successfully the runtime calls Complete, which removes the message from the queue.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about HTTP-triggered Python functions are true? Select TWO.

options.text: Run locally with Core Tools, they don't check access keys
The key can be sent only in the code query string parameter
A host key works for one function but not for the others
With no explicit auth level, a request in Azure needs an access key
Requests to /admin reach functions whose routes start with admin

questions.explanation: For Python, an HTTP function with no explicit level uses the function level, so a request in Azure needs a function key or a host key, and Core Tools removes access key checks when you run the project locally. The key can go in the code query parameter or the x-functions-key header, a host key works for every function in the app, and /admin and /runtime are reserved for the host, so those requests never reach a function.

questions.prompt: A queue-triggered function creates a new CosmosClient in every invocation, and latency rises under load as sockets run short. What should you change?

options.text: Raise the function timeout for slow connections
Close each client at the end of its invocation
Build one client at module level and share it across invocations
Move the app to a plan with a higher outbound connection limit

questions.explanation: Learn's guidance for client SDK connections is to create one shared client that every invocation reuses, never a new client per invocation, which reduces latency and avoids socket exhaustion on every plan. Closing each client still opens a new connection every time, a longer timeout doesn't touch the cause, and while only the legacy Consumption plan caps outbound connections per instance, reuse is recommended on all plans.

questions.prompt: The same function code goes to a test app and a production app, and each must monitor a differently named Cosmos DB container. How should you set container_name?

options.text: To CONTAINER_NAME, which the runtime looks up as an app setting
To %CONTAINER_NAME%, with an app setting of that name in each app
To os.environ["CONTAINER_NAME"], read inside the function body
To each app's container name, edited into the code before deploying

questions.explanation: Binding properties such as container_name accept the %VAR_NAME% syntax, which the runtime replaces with the value of the app setting of that name, so each app picks up its own container from its own settings. A bare name is used literally, editing the code breaks the shared-code requirement, and a value read in the function body comes too late, because the trigger is configured before the function runs.

questions.prompt: Match each Python v2 decorator to what it declares for a function.

options.text: A second trigger on the same function
An output binding that sends events
A trigger that runs on a schedule
An input binding that reads documents
An HTTP trigger

slots.text: @app.route
@app.timer_trigger
@app.cosmos_db_input
@app.event_hub_output

questions.explanation: In the v2 model, @app.route and trigger-specific decorators such as @app.timer_trigger say how the function is invoked, input decorators such as @app.cosmos_db_input pass data in, and output decorators such as @app.event_hub_output let the function write data out. A function has exactly one trigger, so no decorator adds a second one.

questions.prompt: A Python function serves /api/products/{category}/{id}, and requests whose id isn't a whole number must not reach it. Which route should it use?

options.text: api/products/{category:alpha}/{id:int}
products/{category:alpha}/{id:int}
products/{category}/{id}?type=int
products/{category:string}/{id:number}

questions.explanation: Route parameters accept ASP.NET Core route constraints after a colon, so {id:int} matches only integers and {category:alpha} only letters, and the api prefix is added automatically. Writing api into the template would double the prefix, a query-string suffix isn't a constraint, and string and number aren't route constraint names.

questions.prompt: A function's managed identity serves a Cosmos DB trigger and an Event Hubs output binding. Which TWO role assignments match the minimum roles that Learn lists? Select TWO.

options.text: Azure Event Hubs Data Sender on the event hub
Owner on the resource group that holds both resources
Cosmos DB Built-in Data Reader on the Cosmos DB account
Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor on the Cosmos DB account
Azure Event Hubs Data Receiver on the event hub

questions.explanation: Learn's table of minimum roles for identity-based bindings gives Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor for the Cosmos DB trigger and Azure Event Hubs Data Sender for the Event Hubs output binding. Data Reader is listed for the Cosmos DB input binding, Data Receiver for the Event Hubs trigger, and Learn warns against broad roles such as Owner.

questions.prompt: A Python v2 Service Bus-triggered function should receive messages in batches instead of one at a time. What should you set on its decorator?

options.text: arg_name="messages"
is_sessions_enabled=True
queue_name="orders-batch"
cardinality="many"

questions.explanation: Setting cardinality to "many" (or func.Cardinality.MANY) makes the trigger pass a batch of messages, while omitting it or setting one passes a single message. is_sessions_enabled connects the trigger to a session-aware queue or subscription, arg_name only names the parameter, and queue_name chooses which queue is monitored.

questions.prompt: A function app works locally but fails in Azure because INVENTORY_API_URL is missing; the value is in the Values section of local.settings.json. What should you do?

options.text: Add INVENTORY_API_URL to the app's application settings
Remove local.settings.json from .funcignore so the settings are deployed
Commit local.settings.json to the repository so that the deployment includes it
Restart the function app so that it rereads INVENTORY_API_URL from local.settings.json

questions.explanation: local.settings.json serves local runs only and isn't published; in Azure, the Values entries are mirrored by the app's application settings, which the code reads as environment variables. You can add the setting in the portal or CLI, or upload local values with func azure functionapp publish --publish-local-settings. Shipping or committing the file doesn't help, because the app in Azure doesn't read it (and Learn says never to store it in a remote repository), and a restart only reloads the existing app settings.

questions.prompt: A new Python API must reach a database that only accepts traffic from a virtual network, and it should cost nothing for compute while no requests arrive. Which hosting plan should you choose?

options.text: Dedicated (App Service) plan
Flex Consumption plan
Consumption plan
Premium plan

questions.explanation: Flex Consumption is Learn's recommended serverless plan: it supports virtual network integration and, with no always-ready instances configured, scales to zero and bills only for executions. The legacy Consumption plan has no virtual network integration, a Premium plan keeps at least one instance warm and billed, and a Dedicated plan charges App Service plan rates whether or not requests arrive.

questions.prompt: A Python function app needs system libraries that you can supply only in your own container image, using generally available hosting only. Which option fits?

options.text: Consumption plan on Linux
Premium plan on Linux
Premium plan on Windows
Consumption plan on Windows

questions.explanation: Python runs only on Linux, and Windows plans deploy code only because Functions doesn't support Windows containers, which rules out both Windows options. The Consumption plan doesn't support containers on Linux either, whereas the Premium plan (like Dedicated and Container Apps hosting) runs Linux containers as a generally available feature.

questions.prompt: Match each file in a Python v2 function project to its role.

options.text: Configuration for the Functions host and every function in the app
Python packages that the app depends on
Files and folders left out of the deployment
Functions with their triggers and bindings, declared by decorators
A binding file that each function needs in its own folder

slots.text: host.json
function_app.py
requirements.txt
.funcignore

questions.explanation: In the v2 model, function_app.py (or a blueprint it registers) defines the functions with decorators, host.json holds app-wide host configuration, requirements.txt lists the packages to install, and .funcignore excludes items such as .venv or tests from deployment. A per-function binding file is the v1 model's function.json, which a v2 project doesn't use.

questions.prompt: In one region, a pay-as-you-go subscription runs only Flex Consumption apps on 4,096 MB instances, with the default regional quota and maximum instance counts that don't limit them. How many of these instances can run at the same time? Answer in instances. Enter a number.
questions.explanation: The default regional quota for all Flex Consumption instances in a subscription is 250 cores, and a 4,096 MB instance counts as 2 cores, so 250 / 2 gives 125 instances across those apps. Always-ready instances count against the quota too, and a support request can raise it; free trial and student subscriptions start from 15 cores instead.

questions.prompt: Put the commands in order to create a Python v2 project with Core Tools, test it locally and publish it to an existing function app.

options.text: func init OrdersProj --worker-runtime python --model V2
func azure functionapp publish <APP_NAME>
func start
func new --template "Http Trigger" --name orders
cd OrdersProj

questions.explanation: func init creates the project folder and files for the chosen worker and programming model, and the remaining commands run from that project root, where func new adds a function from a trigger template. func start runs the Functions host locally so you can call the endpoint, and func azure functionapp publish packages the project and deploys it to an app that already exists in Azure.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about the Flex Consumption plan are true? Select TWO.

options.text: HTTP triggers scale as one group; most other triggers scale on their own
One Flex Consumption plan can host several function apps side by side
Function apps on this plan can run on either Linux or Windows workers
Deployment slots give zero-downtime swaps between staging and production
Always-ready instances add a baseline charge even when idle

questions.explanation: Per-function scaling groups all HTTP triggers, all Event Grid-based Blob triggers and all Durable Functions triggers, while other functions get instances of their own; always-ready instances are billed for their provisioned memory as a baseline, with no free grant. The plan is Linux-only, has no deployment slots, and allows one app per plan.

questions.prompt: Which TWO ways deploy a code package to a Flex Consumption app? Select TWO.

options.text: The Visual Studio Code Deploy to Azure command
An FTPS upload to the app's wwwroot folder
Copying the zip package straight into the app's deployment container
az functionapp deployment source config-zip with the package
A push to the app's Local Git endpoint

questions.explanation: Flex Consumption uses its own package deployment, which the Azure CLI, Core Tools and Visual Studio Code (and the CI/CD tasks) select automatically; the package goes to the app's deployment endpoint, and the service then stores it in the deployment container. Uploading a zip into that container yourself doesn't deploy it, and Local Git and FTPS aren't available on this plan.

questions.prompt: Complete the app settings of a Python function app on a Linux Premium plan that uses ZIP deployment.

slots.text: Storage connection that the Functions host itself needs

options.text: AzureWebJobsStorage
WEBSITE_CONTENTSHARE
APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING

slots.text: Setting that makes the app run straight from the deployed zip package

options.text: FUNCTION_APP_EDIT_MODE=readonly
WEBSITE_CONTENTOVERVNET=1
WEBSITE_RUN_FROM_PACKAGE=1

slots.text: FUNCTIONS_EXTENSION_VERSION value that tracks the newest 4.x runtime

options.text: latest

questions.explanation: AzureWebJobsStorage names the storage account the host uses for keys, timer management and other internal work; WEBSITE_CONTENTSHARE names a file share and the Application Insights setting carries telemetry. On Premium, WEBSITE_RUN_FROM_PACKAGE=1 mounts the deployed zip read-only, while the edit-mode setting only reports whether the portal may edit code. A tilde with the major version, ~4, picks up new 4.x minor versions automatically; 2.x and 3.x are no longer supported.

questions.prompt: How should Margie's Travel set up the planner app's deployment storage to meet its deployment requirement?

options.text: Authenticate with a managed identity that has Storage Blob Data Contributor
Allow anonymous read access on the deployment container
Set WEBSITE_RUN_FROM_PACKAGE to a SAS URL for the package blob
Keep DEPLOYMENT_STORAGE_CONNECTION_STRING but make it a Key Vault reference

questions.explanation: Flex Consumption keeps the deployment package in a blob container and by default reaches it through the DEPLOYMENT_STORAGE_CONNECTION_STRING setting, a storage connection string; setting the deployment storage authentication to a system-assigned or user-assigned managed identity with Storage Blob Data Contributor on that account removes the dependency on keys. A Key Vault reference only hides the same connection string, WEBSITE_RUN_FROM_PACKAGE isn't used for Flex Consumption deployments, and anonymous access would expose the package.

questions.prompt: A Flex Consumption app has 3 always-ready instances for its http group and a maximum instance count of 40. At most, how many instances can serve its HTTP functions at once? Answer in instances. Enter a number.
questions.explanation: The maximum instance count limits only on-demand instances, and it applies to each function group, so the http group can run its 3 always-ready instances in addition to 40 on-demand ones: 3 + 40 = 43. The regional memory quota can lower that in practice, and always-ready instances count against it.

questions.prompt: On Flex Consumption, a Service Bus-triggered function can run for 40 minutes, and functionTimeout is 50 minutes. What happens to a run in progress when its instance is scaled in?

options.text: It gets a grace period of up to 60 minutes to finish
It's stopped at once and its message is delivered again
It's stopped after 10 minutes, the grace period for updates
It's moved to another instance and resumes where it stopped

questions.explanation: On Flex Consumption and Premium, a running execution gets a 60-minute grace period during scale-in, so a 40-minute run within a 50-minute functionTimeout can finish. The 10-minute grace period applies to platform updates, not scale-in, and Functions doesn't move a running execution to another instance.

questions.prompt: A Python app on a Linux Premium plan is zipped on a Windows laptop with its packages included, and it fails in Azure with import errors. What should you do?

options.text: Add the packages folder to .funcignore and redeploy the zip
Deploy the project source and request a remote build instead
Move the app to a Windows Premium plan that matches the laptop
Set WEBSITE_RUN_FROM_PACKAGE to 1 and deploy the same zip

questions.explanation: Building a Python package on Windows for a Linux app can bundle the wrong libraries, which is one of the cases where Learn says to request a remote build; on Linux Premium that means ENABLE_ORYX_BUILD and SCM_DO_BUILD_DURING_DEPLOYMENT set to true, which Core Tools and Visual Studio Code set for you, with WEBSITE_RUN_FROM_PACKAGE left unset. Running from the same package keeps the wrong libraries, excluding them leaves the imports missing, and Python runs only on Linux.

questions.prompt: A PowerShell function app depends on a Windows-only module and must bill only while functions run, scaling to zero when idle. Which hosting option fits?

options.text: Consumption plan on Windows
Premium plan on Windows
Flex Consumption plan
Container Apps with a minimum of zero replicas

questions.explanation: Learn suggests the legacy Consumption plan when an app depends on Windows, because Flex Consumption is Linux only, and Consumption on Windows bills only while functions run and scales to zero when idle. A Premium plan keeps prewarmed instances that are billed even when idle, and Container Apps hosting runs Linux containers only, whatever its replica minimum.
